{
"translation": "Ballad of the Pipa

At dusk by the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat,
We raise our cups but lack the sound of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, sorrowful at parting,
When we leave, the vast river drowns the moon's reflection.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the pipa's song;
The host forgets to go home, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, we ask secretly who plays,
The pipa pauses, hesitant to speak.
We move our boats closer, inviting her to appear,
Add more wine, relight the lamp, resume the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half covering her face.
She adjusts the pegs, tests the strings with two or three notes,
Before the melody forms, emotion is already present.
Each string suppressed, each note full of longing,
As if telling all her life's frustrated ambitions.
With lowered brows, she plays continuously without effort,
Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking,
First playing "Rainbow Garment," then "Six Yao."
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private conversation.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing among flowers,
Choked as spring water flowing under ice, struggling.
The icy spring freezes stiff, the strings halt abruptly,
Blocked and unyielding, the sound momentarily ceases.
Then arises hidden sorrow and secret resentment,
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Suddenly, like a silver vase breaking, water spurts forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ends, the plectrum sweeps across the center,
Four strings ring once sharply, like tearing silk.
On east and west boats, people sit quietly, speechless,
Only seeing the white autumn moon in the heart of the river.
She hesitates long, places the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with a composed countenance.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My home lived near Hama Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Named in the first troupe of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, skilled masters would admire me,
When fully dressed, beautiful women would envy me.
Young nobles from the Five Tombs vied to give me gifts,
For one piece of music, countless rolls of red silk were given.
Gold-ornamented combs broke beating time,
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, my looks fade.
Cold and desolate before my door, few horses and carriages,
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit above separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
The bright moon circles the boat, the river water cold.
Deep at night, I suddenly dream of youthful days,
Waking crying, makeup tears run down my face.
I heard the pipa and sighed,
Hearing these words, my sighs grew heavier.
We are both lost souls wandering the horizon,
Meeting here—why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Demoted, bedridden, sick in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music,
All year round, no sound of silk and bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, the land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and drink alone.
Are there mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are rough and harsh, difficult to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa words,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are briefly cleared.
Do not refuse; sit again and play another tune,
I will write for you the 'Ballad of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Sat back down, tightened the strings, which played faster.
Mournful, unlike the previous sounds,
All seats listened anew, everyone covering their faces to weep.
Who among them wept the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."
}

message.content:
{"translation":"The Ballad of the Pipa

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, in the night I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts as the guest boards his boat,
We raise our cups to drink, yet lack music's note.
Drunk but not joyful, sorrowful we part,
At leaving, vast is the river where moonlight lies.
Suddenly from the water comes a pipa's song,
The host forgets to return, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I quietly ask who plays,
The pipa ceases, she hesitates to speak.
I move my boat closer, invite her to meet us,
Pour more wine, trim the lamp, resume the banquet.
After thousand calls and ten thousand summons she emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the tuning pegs, plucks two or three strings,
Before the melody forms, emotion already stirs.
Each string suppressed, every tone full of longing,
As if telling a life spent unfulfilled.
Eyes downcast, fingers casually strum on,
Expressing all infinite matters of the heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping, then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Sweet as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Labored as springs flowing under ice.
When icy springs turn cold and sluggish, the strings seem frozen;
Frozen and halted, the sound briefly stops.
Hidden sorrows and secret resentments arise—
This silence surpasses any sounding voice.
Then silver vases burst, water spurts out,
Iron cavalry charges, swords clash loud.
The piece ends; she draws the pick across the center,
Four strings strike once, like silk tearing apart.
Boats east and west fall silent, no one speaks,
Only seeing white autumn moon upon the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she puts the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, stands with composed demeanor.
She says: "I was originally a girl of the capital city,
My home lay near the Shrimp Mound Hill.
At thirteen I mastered playing the pipa,
My name ranked first among the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing songs, great masters admired me,
Once dressed up, beauties like Qiu Niang envied me.
Young dukes and nobles competed to give gifts,
For one song, red silk bolts knew no count.
Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Joy this year, joy next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Brother went off to war, aunt died,
Days and nights wear on, fading beauty remains.
Front gate deserted, horse carriages rare,
Getting older, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit over separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He leaves and returns; I guard an empty boat,
Around the ship bright moon, river waters cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of youthful days,
In dreams I weep, makeup tears streak red across my face.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
Hearing these words, I sigh even more heavily.
Both are drifters fallen far from home—
To meet here, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, ill, resting in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, no strings or flutes heard.
Near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Dusky cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower morns, autumn moonlit nights,
Often take wine, pour alone.
Are there mountain songs and village flutes?
Crude and harsh sounds hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa melodies,
Like celestial music, ears suddenly clear.
Don’t refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you I shall compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Sat back down, tightened strings, tempo sped up.
Mournful unlike the previous tones,
Full audience hears again, all cover faces weeping.
Who among them sheds the most tears?
The Sima of Jiazhou—his blue robe is wet."}

{"translation":"At Xunyang River's head, I bid a guest goodnight;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat.
We raise our wine to drink, but there are no flutes or strings.
Drunk, yet joyless, we grieve at parting,
As vast moonlight soaks into the river.

The host forgets to return home, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask who plays;
The pipa stops, hesitant to speak.
I move my boat closer, inviting her to appear;
We add more wine, bring back the lamp, renew the feast.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings;

Each string suppresses sorrow, each note carries thought,
Seeming to tell of a life thwarted by fate.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely in succession,
They express all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking
Starting with "Rainbow Skirt," then following with "Six Strings."
The thick strings roar like heavy rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
The roaring and whispering intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Clear as orioles singing beneath the flowers,
Muffled as spring water flowing under ice.
The icy spring grows cold and sticky, strings freeze silent;
Silence blocks the flow, sound briefly ceases.
Another hidden sorrow, another secret resentment arises;
This wordlessness surpasses any spoken word.
A silver vase suddenly bursts, water splashing out;
Iron cavalry charges forth, blades and spears clanging.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
Four strings sound once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall quiet, none speaks;
Only the white autumn moon shines on the river's heart.
She meditates, places the plectrum between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with solemn dignity.
She says she was originally a girl of the capital,
Living near the Shrimp-Leeching Mound.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed among the first troupe of the teaching guild.
When her songs ended, skilled masters would praise her;
When made up, courtesans would envy her beauty.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to give gifts,
For one song, red silk bolts numbered countless times.
Gold-ornamented hairpins snapped when beating time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter continued,
Idly spending bright moons and gentle breezes.
Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died;
Dusk passed, dawn came, her beauty faded.
The street before her door grew desolate, horses rare;
Past youth, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit, cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and here she guards an empty boat;
Surrounding her, bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, she dreams suddenly of youthful days,
Waking in tears, her makeup running down her cheeks.
I heard the pipa and sighed already;
Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.
Both of us are wanderers fallen far from home;
What need be knowing if we meet today?
Since last year I left the imperial city,
Exiled to lie sick in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, no sound of silk or bamboo.
My dwelling is near Penjiang, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, apes wailing sadly.
On spring river nights, flower mornings, autumn moon evenings,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.  
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
But they are harsh and discordant, hard to bear.
Tonight hearing your pipa play,
It is like hearing celestial music, ears momentarily clear.
Please sit down again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose this "Song of the Pipa."""}

{"translation":"At dusk by the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
I dismount; my guest boards his boat. We raise our cups,
But no music sounds to warm this lonely drink.
Drunkenness brings no joy, only the gloom of parting;
As we leave, the vast river soaks the moon's reflection.
Suddenly, over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to go home, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa stops, the player hesitates, slow to speak.
We move our boats close together, invite her to appear,
Refill the wine, trim the lamps, and restart the feast.
Called repeatedly, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa before half her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings,
And before the melody forms, emotion is already present.
Each string suppresses its voice, every note carries sorrow,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled.
With lowered brows, she plays on freely,
Unburdening the infinite sorrows within her heart.
Her fingers lightly gather, slowly twist, sweep, and pluck;
First 'Rainbow Garment,' then 'Six Beats.'
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private murmurs.
Loud and soft notes intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Chattering like birds hidden among flowers, smooth and flowing,
Then choked and low, like spring water struggling under ice.
The cold, sluggish stream chokes the strings, silence falls;
When blocked, they cannot flow, and the sound pauses briefly.
A new kind of deep melancholy and hidden resentment arises;
Here, silence speaks louder than sound ever could.
Then suddenly, a silver bottle bursts, water splashes out,
Iron cavalry charges forward, swords and spears clash.
The song ends as she draws the plectrum across the center,
One strum from four strings, tearing like silk cloth.
The boats east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon remains in the middle of the river.
She sighs deeply, puts the plectrum between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with composed dignity.
She says: "Originally a woman of the capital city,
My home was near Shrimp Pond Mound.
By thirteen I had mastered the pipa,
My name belonged to the first class of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After playing a tune, even great masters would admire;
Once made up, courtesans like Qiuniang were jealous.
The sons of the five districts vied to give me gifts,
For one performance, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Gold-inlaid combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes taken for granted.
My brother went off to war, my aunt died;
Days passed, nights came, and my beauty faded.
The gate grew desolate, guests became rare;
Past my prime, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit over love, careless of parting;
Last month he bought tea in Fuliang.
He left, I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
The ship surrounded by bright moonlight, the river waters cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of youth's affairs,
Waking weeping, tears staining my makeup into red streaks.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed long ago,
Now hearing these words, I lament anew.
We are both wanderers lost at heaven's edge;
Since we meet, why must we have known each other before?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted here to lie sick in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year round, not a single strand of silk or bamboo is heard.
Living near Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing in grief.
On spring river flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
I often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Rough and discordant, unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightened the strings, which played faster.
The sound was mournful, unlike the previous tunes;
The entire audience heard it again and covered their faces, weeping.
Who among us shed the most tears?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked."}

As we depart, the vast river is steeped in moonlight.

Blood-crying cuckoos and mournful-gibbing apes.

{"translation":"The Ballad of the Pipa

By Bai Juyi

At night I bid farewell to a guest by the Xunyang River,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted, his guest was aboard the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Tipsy yet joyless, we faced our sad parting;
In that moment of leaving, vast was the river, bathed in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of pipa playing;
The host forgot to return, and the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who played it;
The pipa music stopped, as if about to speak, then hesitated.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to appear;
More wine was added, lamps turned up, and the feast resumed.
After countless calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked a few strings;
Before the melody took shape, emotion had already arisen.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing,
As if telling of unfulfilled ambitions in life.
With lowered brow, she casually played on and on,
Expressing all the boundless thoughts within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sliding then plucking,
First playing 'Rainbow Feather,' then 'Sixth String.'
The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like secret confessions.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Chirping like an oriole gliding through flowers below,
Sobbing like spring water struggling under ice.
Ice-cold springs grew sluggish, strings froze tight;
Frozen and impassable, the sound momentarily ceased.
Hidden sorrows and secret resentments arose;
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly bursting, water spraying forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, blades and spears clashing.
When the tune ended, she drew the pick across the center strings,
All four strings rang out once, like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and west fell silent without a word;
Only the white autumn moon remained visible in the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the pick among the strings,
Smoothed her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: "Originally I was a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Mound Hill.
By thirteen I had mastered the pipa,
My name recorded in the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After performing a piece, even master musicians admired me;
Once made up, often envied by courtesans like Qiuniang.
Young nobles from Five Tombs fought over gifts of silk;
For one song, red silks arrived beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
My brother went off to war, my aunt died;
Evenings came, mornings followed, and beauty faded.
The door was cold and deserted, horses rare;
Growing old, I married a merchant wife.
The merchant values profit above separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left me guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Around the ship, bright moon and cold river waters.
Deep in night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful days;
Waking tears streaked down my painted cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed longingly;
Hearing these words, I groaned again deeply.
Both are wanderers fallen low beneath heaven;
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
Throughout the year, I hear no wind or string instruments.
Living near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers amid flowering mornings, on autumn nights under full moons,
Often I take wine and pour alone.
Are there none mountain songs or village flutes?
Unharmonious and harsh, difficult for ears to bear.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece;
For you, I will compose 'The Ballad of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then sat back down, tightening strings which played faster.
Mournful sounds unlike those from before;
The entire audience, hearing again, covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among them?
The Blue-robed Sima of Jiangzhou."}

{
 "translation": "On the banks of Xunyang River, at night I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is aboard his boat,
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no strings or pipes.
Drunk yet joyless, we prepare for sorrowful parting;
When we leave, the vast river bathes the moon in light.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays departure.
Following the notes, I ask softly who plays such music;
The pipa stops, the player hesitates before speaking.
I move my boat closer and invite her to meet us;
More wine is poured, lamps trimmed, the feast resumes.
Called out to again and again, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings two or three times—
Before the melody forms, emotion is already present.
Each string is muffled, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Eyes downcast, fingers moving with ease, she continues playing,
Unfolding all the infinite matters of her heart.
Light strumming, slow twirling, brushing then picking back,
First 'Rainbow Feather,' then 'Six-One' follow on.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering mingled together,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Choked as spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound pauses briefly.
Then hidden sorrow and secret resentment arise;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
A silver vase bursts suddenly, water splashing forth;
Iron cavalry charge out, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends, the plectrum drawn across the center,
Four strings strike once, tearing silk apart.
Boats east and west fall silent without word;
Only the white autumn moon hangs in the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she puts down the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her expression.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital,
Her home near Xiama Ling.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first among the imperial musicians.
After finishing a piece, even skilled masters would admire her;
Once made up, every beauty grew envious.
Young men of Five Tombs vied to give gifts;
For one song, countless bolts of red gauze were paid.
Gold hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Joy year after year, laughing again next year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died;
Evenings pass, mornings come, her looks fade.
Few horses remain before her door, visits rare;
Getting older, she married a merchant as wife.
Merchants value profit above separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I stayed alone guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night I suddenly dreamed of youthful days;
Waking weeping, tears reddened through makeup.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, my sighs grew heavier still.
Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace at heaven's edge;
Meeting now, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the Imperial City,
Exiled to live ill in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year long I hear neither silk nor bamboo sounds.
Living near Penjiang where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries and monkeys wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often taking wine, I pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Hoarse and harsh, they are hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa language,
It's like listening to fairy music; ears momentarily clear.
Please don't refuse; sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Touched by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down, tightening strings until they sounded urgent.
Mournful, unlike earlier tones;
The whole audience heard again and wiped their tears.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou was soaked."
}

Cold and sluggish as icy streams, the strings seem frozen; Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceases. Then suddenly, as if a silver vase bursts, water spurts forth; Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clash. East and west, ships fall silent, no word is spoken; Only the autumn moon shines white on the river’s heart. She pauses, inserts the pick among the strings, Straightens her clothes, rises with a composed demeanor. Young men of Five Tombs vied to give her gifts, For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given. Ornate hairpins and silver combs broke against rhythm, Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine. Before her door, coldness settles, horses rare; Growing old, she married a merchant’s wife. Merchants value profit, despise separation; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. 主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。

凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。

{"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers tremble in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts while the guest boards the boat;
We raise our cups, but there is no music to accompany us.
Drunkenness brings no joy as we face parting,
And when we part, the vast river reflects the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, comes the sound of a pipa,
Making the host forget to go home and the guest delay departure.
Following the sound, I ask in the dark who plays,
The pipa stops, hesitant to speak.
I move my boat closer and invite her out,
Refilling the wine and relighting the lamp to resume the feast.
After countless calls, she finally appears,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turns the tuning pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before any melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs, each note carries thought,
As if telling of lifelong frustration.
With downcast eyes, she plays casually on,
Expressing all the boundless sorrow within.
She sweeps lightly, twists slowly, strums then picks,
First playing 'Rainbow Robes,' then 'Six Strings.'
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like secret talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Now sweetly rolling like orioles singing under flowers,
Now sobbing softly like springs struggling beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seem to cease,
When ceasing completely, the sound halts briefly.
Hidden sorrows and unspoken resentments arise,
At this moment, silence speaks louder than song.
Then, suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water spurts forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clashing loudly.
At the end of the piece, she draws the pick across the center,
The four strings snap once, tearing silk apart.
East boats and west ships fall silent,
Only seeing the white autumn moon in the river's heart.
Pensive, she puts away the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes and rises with composed demeanor.
She says herself that she was originally a girl of the capital,
Living near the Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first among the imperial academy dancers.
After finishing songs, even skilled musicians admired,
After dressing up, she made beauty queens jealous.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to give her gifts,
For one song, red silk scarves piled high unnoticed.
Gold-ornamented combs broke beating time,
Crimson skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and mirth,
Autumn moons and spring breezes taken for granted.
Her brother went off to war, her aunt died,
Days turn to nights, and beauty fades away.
Her door grows cold, horse carriages rare,
In old age, she married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit over separation,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, she waits alone at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, she dreams of youthful days,
Waking weeping, tears staining her rouge-laden cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I already sighed,
Hearing these words, my grief deepens further.
We are both wanderers fallen far from home,
Meeting here, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and bedridden in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote and lacks music,
All year round, no strings or flutes are heard.
Near the Pen River lives lowland and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, monkeys howling mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there not mountain songs and village pipes?
Their crude sounds are unbearable to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music, ears suddenly clear.
Please don't refuse; sit again and play another tune,
For you, I shall compose the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood long,
Then sat back, tightening strings played faster now.
Mournful notes unlike those before,
The whole audience hearing again wiped their tears.
Who shed the most tears among them?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked."}

{"translation":"The Ballad of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi
At night I saw a guest off by the Xunyang River's head,
Where maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn wind.
I dismounted, my guest on board; we raised our cups to drink,
But no strings or pipes were there to fill the air with sound.
Drunk yet joyless, gloom hung heavy as parting drew near;
We bade adieu amid vast waters where the moon lay submerged.
Suddenly, from out upon the water came pipa music sweet;
I forgot my homecoming, and my friend delayed his start.
Seeking the source, I asked softly who might be playing so;
The pipa ceased, but she seemed reluctant, slow to speak her name.
We moved our boats close together and invited her to meet us;
More wine was poured, lamps refilled, and the banquet resumed.
After thousands of calls and pleas, at last she came forth,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face shyly.
She turned the pegs and tested the strings two or three notes;
Before the melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string choked back sorrow, each note carried longing,
As if telling aloud of ambitions thwarted in life.
Head lowered, moving casually through continuous strokes,
She sang all the endless things buried deep in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking—
First "Rainbow Garment," then "Six Strings" followed next.
Thick strings rumbled like sudden rainstorm’s fury,
Thin strings whispered like private murmurs’ tender tone.
Rumbling, whispering—notes mixed intricately together,
Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate.
Smoothly gliding like warblers singing beneath blossoms,
Muffled groaning like spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold springs grew sluggish; strings froze, cut short—
Silence fell when they could not flow; sounds paused briefly.
Yet hidden sorrows and secret resentments stirred anew;
In that moment, silence surpassed even speech itself.
Then suddenly silver bottles burst open, water spurted;
Iron cavalry charged forth with clashing swords and spears.
The song ended; she swept the plectrum across the center—
One final chord rang sharp like tearing silk apart.
Boats east and west stood silent, no word spoken;
Only seen: autumn moon bright upon river's heart.
Lost in thought, she set down her plectrum between strings;
Adjusting clothes, rising, composing her solemn countenance.
She said she had once been a girl from the capital city,
Her home nestled below Shrimp Hill Lane's old ground.
By age thirteen she mastered the pipa fully trained;
Her name listed first among Imperial Academy girls.
After songs, masters praised; after makeup, courtesans envied.
Noble youths of Five Tombs vied lavishing gifts upon her;
For one piece, endless bolts of crimson silk poured forth.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke tapping rhythm’s beat;
Blood-red skirts stained overturned wine during revelry.
This year laughing, next again, idle months slipped away—
Autumn moons and spring winds passed without regard.
Then brother joined army; aunt died; days fled swiftly on;
Beauty faded as morning turned into evening light.
Front door neglected; horses rare; growing older now,
A merchant’s wife became. He prized profit over love.
Last month he left for Fuliang to trade tea; gone long.
Left alone guarding empty boat at river mouth’s cold spot.
Moonlight wrapped round vessel; river chill seeped bone-deep.
Late at night dreams returned youth memories vividly;
Crying in dream, tears streaked painted cheeks red.
Hearing pipas makes me sigh deeply already enough;
Now hearing such words brings repeated lamentations still more.
Both lost souls drifting far from world’s familiar shores—
Why must strangers need prior acquaintance before meeting?
Since last year left Emperor’s City exiled sick here too,
Xunyang remote land void music entire years never heard.
Near Penjiang dwelling low damp yellow reeds bitter bamboo.
What heard dusk dawn cuckoo blood crying apes mournful scream.
Spring rivers flower mornings autumn moons nights often took wine pour lonely self.
Mountain songs village flutes exist rough harsh unbearable listen tonight hear your pipa language fairy music ear temporarily clear please sit play another piece compose ballad pipa for you moved by these words stand long time return seat tighten strings tempo faster melancholy unlike previous sound everyone present covering faces weeping whose tears most plentiful Jiangzhou Sima blue robe wet."}

{"translation":"At dusk by the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell; maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.
I dismount my horse, while he stands on his boat; we raise our cups to drink, but lack for music’s note.
Though drunk, joy remains elusive as parting nears; the vast river holds the moon in its gleaming spheres.
Suddenly, sounds of a pipa drift over the water; the host forgets to return, the guest delays departure.
We seek the source, whispering who plays so fine; the pipa pauses, the player hesitant to speak mine.
We move our boats close, inviting her to appear; adding wine, relighting lamps, resuming the cheer.
After many calls, she finally emerges shyly, holding the pipa to half-hide her face modestly.
She tightens the pegs and plucks a few stray strings; before the melody forms, emotion already brings.
Each string suppressed conveys deep longing’s sigh, telling of a life where ambitions failed to rise.
Brows lowered, fingers move with ease and grace, pouring out endless sorrows hidden in this place.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, brushing then picking, first 'The Rainbow Feather', then 'The Six Strings' flicking.
Big strings rumble loud like sudden rain’s descent; small strings whisper soft like private sentiments.
Loud and soft notes mingle in intricate dance, like pearls, large and small, falling into jade trays’ glance.
Clear bird-song glides smooth beneath floral boughs; muffled streams choke hard beneath icy flows.
When ice-cold springs stagnate, strings freeze and cease; though silence reigns, it speaks more than voices release.
Hidden grief and dark resentment start to breed; this silent moment surpasses sound indeed.
Then silver bottles burst, water spurts in spray; iron cavalry charges, swords clash in array.
The piece concludes; she strikes the center with care; four strings snap once, like tearing silk from air.
East boats and west cabins fall silent, speechless all; only the autumn moon shines bright upon the hall.
Pensive, she puts away the pick among the strands, straightens her clothes, assumes a dignified stance.
She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital city, living near Shama Mausoleum, rich and pretty.'
By thirteen I mastered the pipa’s skillful art, listed first among the Imperial Music Department’s heart.
After playing songs, even great masters would admire; when dressed up, beautiful women felt envy fired.
Young nobles of Five Tombs competed to give gifts; one song earned bolts of red silk beyond counts and shifts.
Ornated hairpins snapped keeping time’s beat; blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine’s heat.
Year after year passed in laughter and delight; autumn moons and spring winds treated lightly quite.
But brothers joined armies, aunties died away; youth faded daily with changing day and night display.
My door grew cold, horses rare at the entrance; growing old, I married a merchant’s wife in penance.
The merchant values profit above all else, leaving me behind last month to buy tea elsewhere.
He comes and goes; I guard an empty boat alone; around us bright moonlight chills the river’s tone.
Late at night I dreamt of youthful days past; waking tears streaked rouge down my cheeks fast.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply in sorrow; hearing these words, my grief added to tomorrow.
Both are wanderers fallen from heaven’s favor; meeting now, why need prior acquaintance saver?
Since last year, I left the imperial city’s throne, demoted and sick, residing in Xunyang alone.
This remote land offers no musical pleasure; throughout the year, silk and bamboo sounds never measure.
Living near Pen River, low and damp ground holds; yellow reeds and bitter bamboos surround my folds.
What do I hear morning and evening in between? Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing keen.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights, often I take wine and drink alone in sights.
Are there mountain songs or village flutes nearby? Their harsh, grating tones make listening difficult, sigh.
Tonight hearing your pipa language divine, like celestial music clarifies ears in line.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune; I will compose for you this Song of the Pipa Lagoon.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence deep; then sat down quickly, tightening strings to weep.
Her mournful tones unlike those played before; everyone present heard them, masking sobs evermore.
Who shed most tears among those seated here? The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet."}

message.content:
{"translation":"At the head of Xunyang River, seeing off a guest at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is already on the boat.
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no strings or pipes.
Drunk, we cannot find joy; sad, we part soon.
In the moment of farewell, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa.
The host forgets to go home; the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I quietly ask: who plays?
The pipa stops. The player wishes to speak, but hesitates.
I move my boat closer and invite her to meet me.
We add wine, bring back the lamp, and reopen the feast.
After ten thousand calls, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half covering her face.
She turns the pegs and twangs a string or two,
Before the melody forms, emotion is already present.
Every note is suppressed, every sound full of longing,
As if telling a life of frustration.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely, playing on and on,
Telling all the infinite matters in her heart.
Light touches, slow twists, sweeps and plucks—
First the "Rainbow Garment," then the "Six Strings." 
The big strings boom like sudden rain;
The small strings whisper like private talk.
Booming and whispering, they tangle together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as birdsong under flowers, clear and flowing;
Choked as spring water running beneath ice, difficult and low.
The cold, sticky ice-water halts the strings, frozen stiff;
Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceases.
Then arise hidden sorrows and secret hates:
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
As if a silver vase suddenly breaks, water bursts forth;
As if iron cavalry surges out, swords and spears clanging.
When the song ends, she draws the plectrum across the center,
All four strings strike once, tearing like silk.
East boats and west barges fall silent, wordless;
Only visible is the white autumn moon in the middle of the river.
Lost in thought, she puts the plectrum among the strings.
She straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling (Shrimp Hill).
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, great musicians would admire her;
Once made up, even courtesans would envy her beauty.
Young aristocrats competed to wrap her in brocade;
One piece of red gauze cost countless bolts of silk.
Jeweled combs broke keeping time with the beat;
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilling wine.
Joyful laughter this year, again next year;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
Her brother joined the army; her aunt died.
Evenings came, mornings went; her youth faded.
Before her door, guests grew few; horses sparse.
Older now, she married a merchant for wife.
The merchant values profit, disregards separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left her alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat;
Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Late at night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days,
Crying in her dream, tears staining her rouge makeup.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed;
Hearing these words, I sigh deeply again.
Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace at the edge of the world;
Meeting here, what need has there been for prior acquaintance?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted, ill, lying low in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, I hear no strings or pipes.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Dusky cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring nights with flowers, on autumn nights with the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their harsh, noisy sounds are unbearable to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more tune.
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time.
Then she sat down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Melancholy, unlike the previous sounds;
The whole room heard it again and covered their faces, weeping.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou’s blue robe was wet."}

{
 "translation": "At the Xunyang River bank, I bid my guest farewell at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; his guest remains aboard the boat,
We raise our cups to drink, yet lack the strings and pipes.
Drunk but not joyful, grief awaits our parting soon,
Parting time: vast waters drown the moon's reflection.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa sounds arise,
The host forgets to go; the guest delays departure.
Seeking the source, I whisper, asking who is playing;
The pipa music stops, the player seems slow to speak.
I move my boat close by, inviting her to meet me,
Add more wine, trim the lamps, resume the feast anew.
Called again and again, she finally comes out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings,
Before a tune forms, emotion already flows.
String after string, muted notes convey longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled and thwarted.
Brow lowered, fingers moving with ease, playing on,
Expressing endless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping, then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Robe," then "Six Strings" melodies.
The thick strings rush like heavy rain falling,
The thin strings murmur as private whispers do.
Rushing and whispering, mixed together they play,
Like big and small pearls dropping onto a jade plate.
Clear and smooth as an oriole singing under flowers,
Choked and low as a spring flowing beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seem to stop,
Stopped and blocked, the sound briefly rests.
Hidden sorrows and secret grievances arise,
This silence speaks louder than any sound could.
Suddenly, a silver vase bursts, water splashing out,
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clashing loudly.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
One final note from four strings, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west are silent, speechless all around,
Only seeing the white autumn moon upon the river center.
Lost in thought, she puts her plectrum between the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises, composing her demeanor.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Her home lived near Xiama Ridge below.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa art,
Her name listed first among the imperial instructors.
After songs, even skilled masters would admire her skill,
When made up, courtesans like Qiuniang often envied her.
Young men from Five Mausoleums competed to give gifts,
For one song, bolts of red silk received beyond count.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine during revelry.
Joy this year, joy next year passed casually away,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent without care.
Her brother joined the army; her aunt died; time flew by,
Day and night changed, her beauty faded.
Before her door grew cold, horsemen rarely came,
Aging, she married a merchant who valued profit over love.
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, leaving her alone.
She waits at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Around the ship, bright moonlight; the river water is cold.
Deep in night, she suddenly dreams of youth's events,
Waking weeping, her makeup tears streak red down her cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply already,
Now hearing these words, I sigh again heavily.
Both of us are fallen souls drifting far from home,
Meeting now—why must we have known each other before?
I left the Imperial Capital since last year,
Exiled and sick, lying idle in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music entirely,
All year round, no sound of strings or flutes is heard.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here from dawn to dusk? Cuckoos bleeding their cries,
Monkeys howling mournfully in the depths.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights under the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone for myself.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? Their crude noise
Is discordant and harsh, impossible to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's language,
It's like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly clear.
Please don't refuse to sit again and play one more piece,
For you, I shall compose the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then resumed sitting, tightening strings, playing urgently.
The melody was sorrowful, unlike the previous sounds,
The whole room listened again, covering faces and weeping.
Who in the audience shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou is soaked through."
}

Before a melody formed, emotion was already present.
Each string muffled, each note laden with thought,

Brow lowered, fingers moving freely, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly rolling, sweeping then plucking,
First the "Rainbow Garment," then the "Six Strings."

The thin strings whispered like secrets shared.
Rumbling and whispering, intertwined and strung together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth and clear like the warbling of an oriole beneath flowers,
Choked and sobbing like spring water clogging under ice.
Ice-like springs, cold and stagnant; the strings froze and stopped,
Stopped and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.
But another hidden sorrow, dark resentment, arose—
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking, water burst forth,
Like armored cavalry charging, the clash of swords and spears.
The music ended; she drew the pick across the center of the strings.
A single cry from the four strings, like silk tearing.
Boats to the east and ships to the west fell silent.
All that remained was the white autumn moon in the middle of the river.
Lost in thought, she placed the pick between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, composing her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl of the capital,
Living by the Shrimp Hill Mound.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name entered the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When I finished a tune, even the finest musicians admired me;
When I completed my makeup, even the most beautiful women envied me.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer me gifts,
For one song, they gave me red silk beyond counting.
Gold-inlay hairpins and silver combs were broken keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year’s laughter repeated next year’s,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
My brother went to join the army; my aunt died.
Evenings pass, mornings come; my beauty faded.
The gate became desolate; horses and carriages grew scarce.
Getting old, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit above all, cares little for parting.
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
After he left, I guarded the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth,
In the dream I wept, tears staining my rouge.
I heard the pipa and sighed,
Heard these words and lamented anew.
We are both wandering souls cast down to the edge of the world—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital,
Demoted and bedridden in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the sound of silk strings or bamboo pipes.
Living near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers and flower mornings, on autumn nights and full moons,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, difficult to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece;
For you, I will compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time.
Then she returned to her seat, tightened the strings, playing faster.
The melancholy sounds differed from those before.
Hearing them again, the whole company covered their faces, weeping.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Assistant Governor was soaked."
}

{"translation":"Ballad of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

Night at the Xunyang River, seeing off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn wind.
The host dismounts by the boat; the guest is on board,
We raise our cups to drink, but there is no music or song.
Drunk yet unable to find joy, grief weighs heavy as we part;
At parting, the vast river soaks the moonlight.
Suddenly I hear pipa sounds upon the water;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I quietly ask who plays;
The pipa stops, hesitating before speaking.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Add more wine, relight the lamps, resume the banquet.
After many calls and entreaties she finally comes,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks two or three strings,
Before the tune forms, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs with suppressed feeling,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled.
Head bowed, fingers moving continuously,
She speaks all the boundless matters of her heart.
Light touches, slow twists, sweeps and picks,
First the 'Rainbow Robe', then the 'Six Strings'.
Big strings thunder like sudden rain,
Small strings whisper like private talk.
Thunder and whisper intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Birdsong slides smoothly beneath flowers,
Spring water chokes, frozen under ice.
Ice-cold streams stiffen, strings cease to resonate,
Stagnation cuts off flow, sound temporarily halts.
A new hidden sorrow, a dark regret arises;
In this silence, there is more than sound.
Silver vase bursts, water spurts forth,
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clang.
The tune ends, she draws the plectrum across the center,
Four strings strike once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent,
Only the white moon over the river is seen.
She pauses thoughtfully, inserts the pick among strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with composed dignity.
She says: "Originally I was a girl from the capital,
My home lived below Shama Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name belonged to the first rank of the Imperial Academy.
When I finished playing, even great masters admired me;
When made up, other beauties envied me.
Young men of Five Tombs competed for my favors,
One song earned bolts of red silk beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Brother went to army, aunt died,
Dusk passes, dawn comes, beauty fades.
Front gate desolate, horses sparse,
Aged, I married as a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit, disregards separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, I guard the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounding the boat, bright moon, cold river waters.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
Tears wet makeup, running down red cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
Hearing these words, I mourned anew.
Both we are fallen people at world's end;
Meeting now, why must we have known each other?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year round, no string or bamboo sounds heard.
Living near Pen River, low and damp ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there mountain songs and village flutes?
Ugly clatter, hard to bear hearing.
Tonight I hear your pipa speech,
Like listening to immortal music, ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more piece;
For you, I will compose 'The Ballad of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stands long,
Sits back, speeds up strings, notes become urgent.
Desolate, unlike previous sounds,
The whole audience hears again, all cover faces weeping.
Who sheds most tears among those seated?
The Blue-robed Official of Jiangzhou."}

{"translation":"At the head of Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night; Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted my horse while my guest remained on his boat; We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we prepared for a sorrowful parting; As we parted, the vast river was immersed in moonlight.
Suddenly I heard the sound of a pipa from over the water; The host forgot to return home, and the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing; The pipa music stopped, as if hesitant to speak.
I moved my closer to invite her to meet us; Added more wine, trimmed the lamp, and resumed the banquet.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally came out, Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times; Before the melody formed, emotion was already present.
Every string seemed suppressed, every note laden with longing, As if telling of a life unfulfilled in ambition.
With lowered brow, she played on unconsciously, Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twirling, brushing then plucking again; First she played "Rainbow Garment," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings crashed loudly like sudden rain; The thin strings whispered softly like private talk.
Loud and soft notes mingling and crossing; Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth and flowing, like orioles singing under blossoms; Muffled and choking, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When the cold spring froze stiff, the strings became silent; In that silence where nothing passed through, the sound paused briefly.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose anew; At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting and water spraying; Like iron cavalry charging forth, swords and spears clanging.
At the end of the tune, she drew the plectrum across the center; A single strike on four strings sounded like tearing silk.
Boats to east and west fell silent, no word spoken; Only seeing the white autumn moon in the heart of the river.
Pausing in thought, she placed the plectrum among the strings; Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said herself: "Originally a girl from the capital city, My home lies below Hama Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa; My name belonged to the first rank of the imperial academy.
After finishing a song, even skilled masters admired me; After applying makeup, the famous courtesans envied my beauty.
The young men of Five Tombs competed to give me scarves; For one song alone, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Hairpins with gold inlay broke tapping the rhythm; Blood-red silk skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter and joy, next year too; Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
My brother went off to join the army, my aunt died; Days went by, mornings came, and my looks faded.
Before my door, coldness reigned, horses and carriages scarce; Growing old, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above separation and reunion; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I stayed guarding an empty boat by the river mouth; Around the boat, bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful events; Waking weeping, tears staining my makeup, running down my cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed deeply; Hearing these words, I felt again heavy-hearted.
We are both people fallen upon hard times at the edge of heaven; Meeting each other, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital, Banished and lying ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, without music; All year long, no sounds of silk or bamboo are heard.
Living near Pen River, low and damp land surrounds my home; Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around it.
What do I hear here morning and evening? Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing sadly.
On spring rivers amidst flowers, on autumn nights under the moon; Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes here? Their crude noises are unbearable to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa's speech, It is like hearing immortal music, my ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece; For you, I will compose a new "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time; Then sat back down, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Melancholy sounds unlike those before; Everyone present wept, covering their faces.
Who shed the most tears in the room? The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet."}

{"translation":"The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers trembled in autumn's chill.
My horse had stepped down; my guests aboard their boat,
We raised our cups, yet lacked the music to fill the air.
Though tipsy, joy was scarce as parting loomed ahead,
The moon hung low, drowned in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa’s voice arose—
I forgot to go home; they delayed their departure.
Tracing the sound, I asked softly: who plays?
The pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
We drew our boats close, inviting her to meet us,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamps, resumed the feast.
After ten thousand calls, she finally appeared,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings—
Before any melody formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string sighed, each note conveyed longing,
As if telling of a life denied its due respect.
Brows lowered, fingers moved with casual grace,
Pouring out the endless sorrows of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First came 'Rainbow Garments,' then 'Six-Strand Elegy.'
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain;
The thin ones whispered like lovers’ private talk.
Thick and thin intertwined, complex and rich—
Large pearls and small falling onto a jade plate.
Birdsongs slid through flowers, clear and sweet;
Spring streams choked under ice, muffled and slow.
Ice-cold waters stalled the strings into silence,
In that stillness, hidden grief began to bloom.
At this moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Like a silver vase bursting, water spraying high;
Like armored cavalry charging, blades clashing loud.
The song ended as the plectrum swept across the center strings,
One final crash like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats fell silent, no word exchanged;
Only the autumn moon shone white on the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her robes, composed her solemn face.
She said: "Born in the capital, near Shrimp Hill I lived;
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, joined the top troupe.
Even masters praised when my songs concluded,
And rivals envied my beauty upon dressing.
Young nobles vied to scatter brocade gifts for me,
For one tune alone, countless red silks flowed.
Silver combs broke keeping time with drums,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter carried me along,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Then brothers left for war, aunties died away,
Days turned to nights, fading my youthful charm.
Once bustling gates grew cold, horses rare,
Now married, I live as a merchant’s wife.
He cares more for profit than for parting pains,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He leaves; I guard our empty boat at the dock,
Moonlight circling the ship, river cold beneath.
Late at night, dreams of youth return unbidden,
Tears soak my makeup, streaming down in red.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply already,
Hearing these words, I wept anew, broken.
We are both wanderers lost beyond the horizon,
Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year, leaving the imperial capital behind,
Exiled sick, I lay in Xunyang City’s gloom.
Remote lands here know no music’s touch,
All year long, not a flute or zither sounds.
Near Pen River’s banks, damp earth surrounds me,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo choke my home.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes mourning aloud.
On spring river mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it to myself alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their hoarse, jarring tones are unbearable.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speak,
It is like celestial music clearing my ears.
Do not refuse; sit again, play one more tune,
I will write this ballad for you: The Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened strings, playing faster now.
Sorrowful notes unlike those heard before,
The whole audience wept, faces hidden in tears.
Who among them shed most tears tonight?
The Blue-Clad Magistrate of Jiangzhou, soaked through."}

On the banks of Xunyang River, I bade my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn's chill.

Raised cups for wine, yet lacked the music of flute and string.
Drunkenness failed to bring joy; sorrow hung before parting,

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}
</原诗>

message.content:
{"translation":"The Song of the Pipa

At night by the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed blossoms shiver in autumn's chill.
I dismounted, my guest was already on his boat,
We raised our wine, but no flutes or strings made music float.
Drunk yet joyless, sorrow weighed upon our parting,
As we left, the vast river drowned the moon in its darkling.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa notes drifted near,
Forgetting home, I paused; my friend held back from fear.
We traced the sound, asking softly who played so well,
The pipa ceased; she hesitated before breaking her spell.
We moved our boats closer to invite her sight,
Added wine, relit lamps, renewed the feast tonight.
After countless calls, at last she emerged to view,
Still holding her pipa, half-hiding her face from us.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings true,
Before the tune began, emotion poured anew.
Each note suppressed, each sound heavy with longing,
As if telling of a life where hope failed belonging.
Brows lowered, fingers moving with easy grace,
She spoke all the sorrows hidden deep in place.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing and picking fast,
First "Rainbow Robes," then "Six-String Whirl" were cast.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain showers,
The thin ones whispered like private, tender powers.
Rumbling whispers intertwined, complex and deep,
Like large and small pearls into a jade plate they sweep.
Clear as orioles singing smooth beneath flowers bright,
Choked as spring water struggling through ice in the night.
When cold icy springs stalled the strings' flow,
The music paused, suspended in the glow.
A new kind of hidden sorrow started to rise,
In that silence, more was heard than in cries.
Then like a silver jar bursting, water spurts out,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clash and shout.
The song ended; she drew her pick across the center string,
One sharp tear like silk ripping, making hearts ring.
East and west boats fell silent, words unspoken,
Only the white autumn moon over the river was broken.
She pondered, placed her pick between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, composed herself with rings.
She said: "I was a girl from the capital city born,
My home lay below Shrimp Frog Hill, in old times worn.
By thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
Named first among the Imperial Music Department.
Once I finished playing, even masters bowed low,
When I dressed up, courtesans watched me glow.
Young nobles fought with treasures to win my favor,
For one song, red silk bolts beyond measure.
Gold-inlaid combs broke keeping time with beats,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine's sweets.
Year after year of laughter, carefree days,
Autumn moons and spring winds passed in lazy ways.
But when my brother joined the army and aunt died,
Time stole my beauty, fading pride.
My door grew cold, horses rare, visitors few,
Aged now, I married a merchant, true.
He values profit more than love's embrace,
Last month he went to Fuliang for tea's chase.
Leaving me alone at the river mouth, guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, cold water floats.
Deep in the night, I dreamed of youth's delight,
Woke crying, makeup tears streaming down right.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed with grief,
Hearing her words, my sorrow grew brief.
Both are wanderers fallen far from home,
Why need we have known each other to roam?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to Jiujiang, sick and pitiful.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music's charm,
All year long, no string or wind plays warm.
I live near the Pen River, land damp and low,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my abode.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk? Cuckoos bleed,
Gibbons wail, filling air with need.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
I often take wine, drinking alone in sights.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
Their harsh sounds grate against these ears alike.
Tonight I heard your pipa's language pure,
Like celestial music, my ears regained cure.
Do not refuse; sit again, play another song,
I will compose this 'Pipa Ballad,' strong.
Touched by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down quickly, plucking with fierce style.
Melancholy now, unlike earlier sweet,
The whole audience listened, weeping at feet.
Who shed the most tears in the crowd? I ask,
The Sima of Jiangzhou's blue robe is soaked with task."}

{"translation":"Ballad of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

At Xunyang River's head, I bid a guest goodbye at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; his guest is on the boat.
We raise our wine to drink, but lack the pipes and strings.
Though drunk, no joy remains; sad parting looms ahead.
At separation time, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa notes are heard.
The host forgets to go; the guest delays his start.
Following the sound, we ask who plays: the music stops,
And she hesitates, afraid to speak her name.
We move our boats close by and invite her forth.
More wine is poured; lamps turned up; the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls, ten thousand cries, she comes.
Pipa held close, half her face still veiled.
She turns the pegs and flicks three or two strings.
Before the tune begins, emotion fills the air.
Each string suppresses sigh; each note conveys deep thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Brows lowered, fingers moving continuously,
She speaks all boundless matters in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking—
First 'Rainbow Garment', then 'Six Strings' follows.
The thick strings rumble like a sudden rainstorm;
The thin strings whisper soft as private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle:
Large and small pearls falling into jade plates.
Flowers beneath, the warbling oriole flows smooth.
Deeply choked, the spring under ice struggles hard.
The ice-cold spring turns sluggish; strings freeze solid.
Frozen, blocked—the sound pauses briefly.
A different sorrow, hidden hate arises here.
This silence surpasses any spoken word.
Like silver vases bursting, water gushes out;
Like iron cavalry charging, blades clash loudly.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center.
One final strum sounds like tearing silk.
East and west boats fall silent, speechless all.
Only the white moon shines upon the river's heart.
Thoughtfully, she puts the plectrum between the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises, composing her face.
She says herself once was a city girl,
Home lived below Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen, learned to master the pipa well;
Her name listed first among imperial schools.
When songs were done, skilled masters praised her art.
When dressed, rivals envied beauty and charm.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums fought for gifts;
One song earned countless bolts of red gauze.
Jeweled combs broke keeping rhythm;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year too;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed lightly away.
Brother went to army; aunt died. Day and night pass.
Beauty fades; door grows cold, few horses come.
In old age, married to a merchant wife.
Merchants prize profit, treat partings lightly.
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Left me alone at river mouth guarding empty boat.
Moonlight surrounds ship; river water cold.
Late at night, dream suddenly of youth's affairs.
Tears stain makeup red down cheeks.
Hearing this pipa, I already sighed.
Hearing these words, my grief doubles again.
Both we are wanderers lost at world's end.
Meeting now, need not have known before.
Since last year I left Emperor's Capital City,
Banished to live sick in Xunyang Town.
Xunyang remote, no music exists.
All year long never hear pipes or strings.
Dwelling near Fen River, land low and damp.
Yellow reeds, bitter bamboo grow around house.
What do we hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos bleed tears; gibbons cry in agony.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine, pour alone.
Are there none mountain songs and village flutes?
Hoarse noises harsh, difficult to listen to.
Tonight hearing you play pipa language,
Like listening to fairy music, ears clear momentarily.
Do not refuse to sit further, play one more song.
For you, I will compose Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stands long time.
Sits back, tightens strings; playing becomes urgent.
Mournful tones unlike earlier ones.
Full room hears again, wipes tears openly.
Who weeps most heavily in the audience?
The blue robe of Jiangzhou Prefect is wet."}
