{
"translation": "At night by the Xunyang River I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest was on boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we turned sadly to part;
As we parted, the moon was drowned in the vast river's gleam.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked softly: who plays?
The pipa notes ceased; she wished to speak, then hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her to meet,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before the tune took shape, emotion was already present.
Each string murmured low, each note carried longing,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled in its ambitions.
With lowered brows, she played freely and continuously,
Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking again,
First playing "Rainbow Robe," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings buzzed like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like intimate talk.
Buzzing and whispering, intermingled in play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing among flowers, clear and flowing,
Choked like springs running beneath ice, hard and constrained.
Cold and sluggish as icy springs, the strings seemed to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound paused for a moment.
Then arose a hidden sorrow, a dark resentment;
At this moment, silence surpassed even sound.
Suddenly, as if a silver vase burst with splashing liquid,
Like iron cavalry rushing forth with clashing swords and spears.
The song ended; she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings;
One final chord rang out, like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and west fell silent, none spoke;
Only the white autumn moon was seen in the middle of the river.
She pondered deeply, put away her plectrum among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said that she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near the Xiama Ridge.
By thirteen she had mastered the pipa;
Her name belonged to the first rank of the imperial music bureau.
When she finished a piece, even skilled masters were impressed;
Once made up, she was often envied by beautiful women.
The young men of the Five Mausoleums competed to give her gifts;
For one song, red silk scraps numbered beyond count.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke against the beat;
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year more laughter;
Autumn moons and spring winds passed casually by.
Brothers left for military service, aunts died;
Dusk came, dawn went, and beauty faded.
Before her door grew cold, horses and riders became rare;
Older now, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit above separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth;
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, suddenly dreaming of youthful things,
She wakes crying, makeup tears staining her face red.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words again, I sighed anew.
Both are wanderers fallen to fate's ends;
Meeting here, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished and bedridden in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year round, I hear no sounds of silk and bamboo.
Living near the Pen River where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my home.
What do I hear here at dawn and dusk?
Blood-crying cuckoos and apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine to pour alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their rough, discordant sounds are difficult to bear.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing immortal music; my ears are temporarily cleared.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune;
For you, I will compose a new Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then returned to her seat, tightened the strings, and played them faster.
The melancholy sound differed from the earlier tunes;
Everyone seated heard it again, all covering their faces to weep.
Who among the audience shed the most tears?
The Jiangzhou Sima's blue robe was wet."
}

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}
</原诗>

{
  "translation": "Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, at night, I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts; his guest is by the boat awaiting;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack both flute and string.
Drunkenness fails to bring joy; sad is parting's sting,
And when we leave, vast moonlight bathes the river's flow.
Suddenly, music from the water strikes my ear;
The host forgets to go; the guest delays departure.
We seek the sound, asking softly: who plays here?
The pipa pauses, hesitant to speak aloud.
We move our boats close in, invite her out to show;
Add wine, relight lamps, resume the banquet now.
After much calling, she comes forth at last,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks strings, two or three notes,
Before the melody begins, emotion springs.
Each string suppresses sighs; each note conveys grief,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled, thwarted.
Lowering brows, fingers dance on, playing on,
Expressing all the endless sorrows deep inside.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept, then picked,
First 'Rainbow Garments', then 'Six Strings' follow next.
The thick strings thunder like a sudden rainstorm;
The thin strings whisper like private conversation.
Thunders and whispers intertwine, mixed play,
Like pearls large and small falling into jade plates.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blooming flowers;
Choked as spring ice flowing under frozen streams.
Ice-cold, sluggish, strings freeze, sound stops midway;
Blocked, silent, yet feeling grows within.
Hidden sorrow, secret hate are born anew;
At this moment, silence surpasses speech.
A silver vase bursts, water splashes forth;
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clash loud.
The song ends; she lifts the pick, strikes centrally,
One final note from four strings, like silk tearing.
East ships and west boats fall silent, no one speaks;
Only the white autumn moon shines in midstream.
Lost in thought, she puts down the plectrum, adjusts dress,
Stands up, composed, with solemn countenance shown.
She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Xiama Ridge. At thirteen years old,
I mastered the pipa, joining the top tier of teaching.
When songs ended, skilled masters would admire me;
When made up, the beautiful Qiuniang envied me.
The young men of Wuling vied to give gifts;
One song earned countless bolts of red silk cloth.
Jeweled combs broke keeping time; blood-red dresses stained
With spilled wine. One year of laughter followed another;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed lightly away.
My brother joined the army; my aunt died; days went by,
Age dimmed my beauty. Few horses came to my door.
Getting older, I married a merchant wife. He values profit, cares little for separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. Left alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
The bright moon circles, cold river waters surround.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful affairs,
I cry in dreams, tears staining makeup on cheeks.'
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I sigh again heavily.
Both of us are drifters at the edge of the world;
Meeting now, why need we have known before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and sick, living in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, not heard string or bamboo sounds.
Near Pengjiang River, land low and damp around home,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild nearby.
What do we hear morning and evening? Only cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring river flowers mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine, pour it alone. Are there no mountain songs and village flutes? They are harsh, discordant, hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa words, it seems celestial music clearing deafened ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another piece;
For you, I compose 'Song of the Pipa'.
Touched by my words, she stood for a long while;
Sat back down, tightened strings, tempo sped up.
Mournful, unlike previous tunes, full of sadness;
Everyone present listened again, covering faces weeping.
Who shed most tears among those seated here?
The green robe of the Jiazhou Prefect was wet."
}

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

{
  "translation": "At night by the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest; Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest aboard the boat; Raising wine to drink, yet lacking music's voice.
Drunk but not joyful, parting grew sorrowful; At farewell, vast mist soaked the Jiangmoon.
Suddenly, from the water, came pipi sounds; The host forgot to return, the guest set sail no more.
Seeking the sound, I asked who played; The music paused, she wished to speak but hesitated.
We moved our boats close, inviting her to join us; Added wine, lit the lamps again, resumed the feast.
After many calls, she finally emerged, Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
Turning pegs, plucking strings two or three times, Before a tune formed, emotion was already present.
Each string suppressed, each sound full of thought, As if telling of life's unfulfilled ambitions.
Head lowered, casually she continued playing, Expressing all the endless matters of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, brushing and picking, First "Rainbow Garment," then "Six Whispers."
The thick strings chattered like sudden rain, The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Chattering and whispering intertwined, Large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Sweet as orioles singing under flowers, Hushed as spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold springs choked the strings, stopping their flow, When stopped and unconnected, the sound briefly ceased.
But hidden sorrow and buried resentment arose, In this silence, louder than any sound.
As if a silver bottle burst, water spurting out, Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
The piece ended, the plectrum drawn across the center, Four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
East and west boats fell silent, No one spoke—only the white autumn moon over the river's heart.
Pondering, she placed the plectrum among the strings, Straightened her clothes, rising with composed demeanor.
She said she originally was a girl from the capital, Living near the Shama Ling.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa, Her name ranked first in the imperial music academy.
After performing, even skilled players admired her skill, Once made up, every beauty envied her charm.
Young nobles of Wuling competed to give her gifts, One song earned red silk beyond counting.
Hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time, Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year laughter repeated, Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly.
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died, Days went by, her beauty faded.
Before her door, coldness settled, carriages rare, Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit, lightly regarded separation, Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving her at the river mouth guarding an empty boat, Moonlight circled the vessel, river water cold.
Late at night she dreamed of her youth, Weeping in dreams, tears staining her makeup red down to the rails.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed, And hearing these words, my sighs grew heavier.
Both are fallen souls at the world's end, Meeting now—why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital, Demoted and ill, living in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, without music, All year I hear no zither or flute sounds.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp, Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear morning and evening? Cuckoos crying blood, apes howling sadly.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights, Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes? Their harsh, noisy tones are hard to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa speech, Like celestial music, my ears suddenly clear.
Please don't refuse to sit again and play another tune, For you, I shall compose the Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while, Then sat back, tightened strings, playing faster.
Mournful, unlike the previous sound, Everyone present, hearing again, covered faces and wept.
Whose tears fell most abundantly? The blue robe of the Ssiama of Jiangzhou was wet."
}

{"translation":"By the Yan River at dusk, I bid a guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, his guest remains aboard the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music’s note.
In drunkenness no joy; we part with heavy hearts,
As moonlight spreads across the misty river’s waters.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa sounds arise,
And both my host forgets to go, my guest delays.
I seek the source, ask softly who is playing there,
The pipa stops, the player hesitates to speak or stare.
I move my boat closer, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight the lamp, refresh the banquet here.
After ten thousand calls, she finally comes forth,
Still holding her pipa half-covering her face.
She tightens strings and plucks two, three notes so faint,
Before the tune begins, emotion fills the air.
Each string suppresses sorrow, each sound holds deep thought,
Seeming to tell of life’s disappointments wrought.
With lowered brows, she casually continues play,
Expressing endless things that weigh upon her day.
Light touches, slow twists, sweeps, and picks again,
First 'Nishang Yuyi', then 'Liuyao'’s refrain.
The thick strings thunder like a sudden rainstorm’s roar,
The thin strings whisper soft as private words before.
Loud and soft intertwined, they clash and blend anew,
Like pearls great and small on jade plates falling through.
Smooth as orioles singing under blooming flowers,
Muffled as spring streams struggling beneath ice showers.
When icy springs turn cold and strings seem frozen still,
That silence speaks more than any sound could fill.
Then suddenly, as silver bottles burst apart,
Water sprays out, iron cavalry charges, blades and spears.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum down the center line,
The four strings snap once, tearing silk with sharp design.
Boats east and west fall silent, hushed in awe,
Only the white moon over middle river saw.
She pauses long, inserts her pick among the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, stands up, composing dignity it brings.
She says herself: 'I was born a girl of capital fame,
My home lay near Xiamaoling, though now it’s not the same.'
At thirteen, I mastered pipa art so well,
Named first in teaching quarters, known for excellence.
When tunes were done, even skilled masters bowed their heads,
My makeup made rivals jealous, causing bitter deeds.
Young nobles from Five Tombs fought to give me gold,
One song earned bolts of red silk beyond control.
Jeweled hairpins snapped keeping time to rhythm’s beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine, careless sweet.
Year after year, laughter filled our days and nights,
Autumn moons and spring winds passed without our sights.
Brother joined the army; auntie died away,
Evening came, morning left, beauty faded gray.
Front gate grew quiet, horses rare and few,
So when old, I married a merchant’s wife, new.
Merchant values profit high, loves little care,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea there.
He leaves, I guard empty boat at river mouth,
Moonlight circles ship, cold river flows south.
Deep night, I dream of youthful times gone by,
Tears stain rouge cheeks, waking with a sigh.
Hearing pipa, I already sighed in grief,
Now hearing words, my sorrow grows beyond belief.
We are souls lost alike, drifting far from home,
Why need we have met before to understand our doom?
Since last year, I left the imperial city’s glow,
Exiled sick in Xunyang town, where sorrows grow.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of musical cheer,
All year long, no strings or flutes reach my ear.
Near Pen River, land is low and wet with damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my camp.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk within this place?
Cuckoo blood-crying and apes in mournful chase.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often take wine alone, drowning thoughts in flights.
Are there no mountain songs and village pipes to hear?
They’re rough and harsh, too jarring for the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech, I feel reborn,
Like celestial music clearing ears torn.
Do not refuse to sit and play another song,
For you, I’ll write this Ballad of the Pipa strong.
Moved by my words, she stood for moments long,
Then sat, tightened strings, playing fast and strong.
Sad sounds unlike before pervaded all the hall,
Everyone covered faces, tears began to fall.
Who shed most tears among those seated there?
The blue-shirted Magistrate of Jiangzhou, soaked by despair."}

{
  "translation": "At night by the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell; Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts his horse while the guest remains aboard; We raise our cups to drink, but have no music to accord.
Drunk yet joyless, we face a sorrowful parting soon, When suddenly, on the misty river, moonlight bathes the lagoon.
Then from across the water comes the pipa's sudden song; The host forgets to return, the guest delays his throng.
Following the sound, I ask who plays there in the dark; The pipa pauses, hesitant to speak its subtle mark.
I move my boat closer to invite this player out; More wine is poured, lamps trimmed, the feast resumes without doubt.
After many calls and pleas, she finally appears, Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face through tears.
She tunes the pegs and plucks three or two strings in succession; Before the melody forms, emotion flows with precision.
Each string is suppressed, each note full of longing thought, As if telling of a life where ambitions were not caught.
With lowered brow, she plays on with effortless grace, Expressing all the boundless sorrows within her embrace.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, then sweeping and picking, She starts with 'Rainbow Skirts,' then shifts to 'Six Strings' tricking.
Large strings roar like a sudden downpour of rain; Small strings whisper like private lovers in pain.
Loud and soft notes mingle in complex harmony, Like large and small pearls falling onto jade tray.
Chirping birds sing smoothly beneath the flowers' shade; Sobbing springs flow sluggish under ice laid.
The cold spring freezes stiff, the strings seem to cease; Blocked and silent, the sound takes a brief release.
Yet hidden sorrow and secret恨 arise anew; In this silence, more speaks than words ever could do.
Like a silver vase bursting, water spurts forth loud; Like iron cavalry charging, swords clash in crowd.
The tune ends as she draws the plectrum across strings; One sharp tear like silk ripping echoes among things.
East and west boats fall silent, no voice can be heard; Only the white autumn moon shines upon the river's word.
She hesitates, puts her plectrum between the strings once more; Adjusts her clothes, rises up, composing her spirit before.
She says herself: "I was originally a girl from the capital, Living my home near Harajima陵's footfall.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa skillfully done, Enrolled in the Imperial Music Bureau's first rank one.
After finishing tunes, great masters would bow in awe; After makeup, other beauties envied me with flaw.
Young men from Five Tombs vied to give gifts with haste; For one song, countless red silks were paid with taste.
Gold-broidered combs broke beating time in delight; Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine at every night.
Year after year laughter continued in vain; Autumn moons and spring winds passed without refrain.
My brother went to join the army, aunt died away; Days turned old, beauty faded as years did decay.
Before my door, visitors sparse, horses rare indeed; In late age, I married a merchant to meet my need.
The merchant values profit, cares little for goodbye; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea nearby.
He left me here guarding empty boat at river mouth; Moonlight circles the vessel, cold waters to south.
Deep in night, I dreamt of youth's joyful affair; Dreamt crying, makeup tears stained red everywhere.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply already so; Hearing these words, again sighs come forth in woe.
"We are both drifters cast far from home," I say; "Meeting now, why need prior acquaintance day?"
Since last year I left the imperial city behind, Banished to live sick in Xunyang town confined.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of musical art; All year long, strings and flutes never touch heart.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp and wet; Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos around home set.
What do I hear morning and evening amidst this place? Cuckoos bleeding cries, monkeys mourning embrace.
Spring river, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights; Often take wine alone, pouring it in delights.
Are there mountain songs and village pipes to hear? Yes, but harsh and jarring, difficult to cheer.
Tonight hearing your pipa's language divine, It seems celestial music, ears clear, soul fine.
Please do not refuse; sit again, play one more song; For you, I shall compose the 'Ballad of the Pipa' strong.
Touched by my words, she stood long in silence deep; Then sat back, tightened strings, tempo fast to keep.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those played just before; Full audience hears again, tears flowing more.
Who among them sheds most tears in grief's control? The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is wet whole."
}

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}
</原诗>

message.content:
{"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest in the night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn wind.
The host dismounts from his horse, the guest boards his boat;
We raise our cups for wine, yet there are no pipes or strings to play.
Though drunk, joy is incomplete; sorrow looms as we part,
At the moment of leaving, only the vast river and its moonlight are seen.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa floats over the water,
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays setting sail.
Following the sound, I quietly ask who plays,
The music stops, and someone hesitates to speak.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Add more wine, relight the lanterns, and restart the banquet.
After many calls, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times,
Before the melody forms, emotion is already present.
Each string is suppressed, each note full of longing,
As if telling of lifelong frustrations.
With downcast eyes, she casually continues to play,
Expressing all the boundless matters in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Garment," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumble like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whisper softly like private conversation.
Rumbling and whispering mixed together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Occasionally smooth as a warbler singing among flowers,
Sometimes choked like spring water flowing under ice.
The cold, sluggish spring makes the strings freeze and stop,
When frozen and blocked, the sound briefly ceases.
Then arises hidden sorrow and secret grief,
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting out,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords clashing.
The song ends; she sweeps her plectrum across the center of the strings,
The four strings emit one sharp sound, like tearing silk.
The boats on the east and west fall silent,
Only the white autumn moon is reflected in the middle of the river.
Lost in thought, she places her plectrum between the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, stands up, composing her expression.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shama Ridge.
By age thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first among the imperial music staff.
After finishing a tune, even master musicians admired her,
Once made up, every courtesan envied her beauty.
The young nobles of Five Mausoleums competed to give her gifts,
For one piece of music, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent carelessly.
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, her beauty fades.
Her door becomes desolate, few horses come now,
Getting old, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit over parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He leaves, and she guards an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Late at night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days,
Crying in her dream, tears staining her makeup.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed,
And hearing these words, I sigh deeply again.
Both of us are fallen people wandering far from home,
When meeting, why does it matter if we knew each other before?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and sick, living in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, no sound of silk and bamboo is heard.
My home is near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos bleeding cries, gibbons wailing sadly.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant sounds are unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa music,
It is like listening to celestial melodies; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play another piece,
For you, I will compose the "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightening the strings, which played faster.
Melancholy, unlike the previous sounds,
Everyone present listened again and covered their faces in tears.
Who in the audience shed the most tears?
The Blue-robed Sima of Jiangzhou."}

{"translation":"Ballad of the Pipa

By the Xun River at night I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn's chill.
I dismounted, my guest was boarding his boat,
We raised our cups but had no music to drink to.
Drunkenness brought no joy; sad was parting soon,
When we bade farewell, only moonlight soaked the vast river.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
Forgetting to return, neither host nor guest set sail.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa paused, as if hesitant to speak.
We moved our boats close by and invited her out,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast.
Called many times, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings;
Before the tune began, feelings were already there.
Each string suppressed, each note full of thought,
As if telling a life of thwarted ambition.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely on and on,
Expressing endless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, brushing then picking,
First "Rainbow Feather," then later "Six Strings."
The big strings thunder like sudden rain;
The small strings whisper like private talk.
Thundering and whispering mingled together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Bird calls, smooth beneath blossoms;
A sobbing stream struggling under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings seem frozen still;
Frozen still, unconnected, the sound briefly ceases.
Then arise hidden sorrows and secret regrets;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
As if a silver vase suddenly bursts, liquid spraying;
As if iron cavalry charge forth, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
All four strings strike once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent without word,
Only seeing the white autumn moon in the river's heart.
She hesitates, puts down the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with composed grace.
She says: "Originally I was a girl from the capital,
My home near Shama Ling below.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed in the first troupe of the Music Bureau.
After finishing songs, even master players admired me;
When dressed up, I was often envied by beautiful women.
Young nobles from the Five Tombs competed to give gifts,
One song earned countless scarlet silks.
Inlaid combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Laughing year after year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Brothers went off to war, aunties died;
Evenings depart, mornings come, beauty fades.
Front door grown cold, horse riders rare;
Getting older, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit over separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moon, cold river water.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of youthful days,
Waking crying, makeup tears run red down my face.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed,
Hearing these words, I lamented further.
Both are people lost far from home;
Meeting now, what need has passed acquaintance?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Exiled, bedridden in Xunyang City.
This place is remote, devoid of music;
All year long I hear no strings or pipes.
Living near Pen River where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, gibbons wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their hoarse, discordant notes are hard to bear hearing.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to immortal music; ears clear momentarily.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I shall write this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Returned to sit, tightened the strings, which grew urgent.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those before,
The whole audience heard again and wiped their tears.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Blue-robed Sima of Jiangzhou."}

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。

别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

{"translation":"On the banks of Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts while the guest is on his boat;
We raise our wine cups, but there are no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we mourn our parting soon to come;
As we leave, the vast river is bathed in moonlight.
Suddenly, over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
I search for the source, asking softly who plays;
The pipa stops, and she hesitates before speaking.
I move my boat closer and invite her to appear;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After many calls and cries, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She adjusts the tuning pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before even forming a melody, emotion is already present.
Each note is suppressed, full of thought and longing,
Seeming to tell of a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
She lowers her brows and lets her fingers wander freely,
Expressing all the boundless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First playing "Feathered Robes," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like intimate talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle as they play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade platter.
Clear and sweet, like orioles singing among flowers;
Low and choked, like spring water struggling under ice.
The cold ice-sealed spring makes the strings freeze and stop;
When blocked and unable to flow, the sound momentarily ceases.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arise;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water spurts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging out, with the crash of swords and spears.
The song ends; she draws her plectrum across the center string,
And all four strings ring out once, like tearing silk.
The boats to the east and west fall silent;
All that remains is the white autumn moon at the center of the river.
She pauses, inserts her plectrum into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital,
Her home near Shama Ling.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
And her name was registered in the first division of the Imperial Music Academy.
After finishing a piece, even skilled musicians would admire her;
Once made up, every beauty would envy her.
The young men of the Five Mausoleums competed to give her gifts;
For one song, she received countless red silks.
Jeweled hairpins broken keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year's laughter followed by next year's,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent lightly.
Then her brother joined the army, and her aunt died;
Days pass, nights come, and her looks fade.
The door becomes desolate, horses and carriages rare;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant values profit, cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and she stayed alone guarding the empty boat at the river mouth;
The bright moon surrounds the boat, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of events from youth,
Weeping in her dream, tears ruining her rouge, streaking down her cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Hearing her words, I sigh again deeply.
We are both people cast away to the ends of the earth;
Now that we have met, what does it matter if we were strangers?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
Throughout the year, I hear no sounds of strings or pipes.
My dwelling is near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood and gibbons mourning.
In spring days and flower mornings, in autumn nights under the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their harsh, jarring notes are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speak,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune;
For you, I will rewrite the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat down and played faster, the strings turning urgent.
The sad tones differed from those before;
The whole audience listened again, all covering their faces and weeping.
Who shed the most tears among the guests?
The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou was wet."}

message.content: {"translation":"On the banks of Xunyang River, I see off a guest at night; Autumn rustles in maple leaves and reed flowers. The host dismounts while his guest is aboard the ship; Raising wine to drink, we find no pipes or strings. Drunk but joyless, bitterly about to part; At parting, the moon sinks into the vast river. Suddenly from the water comes the sound of pipa; The host forgets to return, the guest does not set sail. Following the sound, I quietly ask who plays; The pipa stops, as if wanting to speak but hesitating. We move our boats close and invite her to meet us; Adding wine, turning up the lamps, we resume the banquet. After many calls she finally emerges, Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face. Turning the pegs, plucking two or three strings; Before forming a melody, feeling already arises. Each string muffled, each note full of longing; As if telling of a life unfulfilled. Brow lowered, fingers moving freely one after another; Expressing all the boundless matters of the heart. Light gathering, slow rubbing, brushing then picking; First playing 'Rainbow Skirt', then 'Six Strings'. The thick string booms like sudden rain; The thin string whispers like private talk. Booming and whispering, mixed together; Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate. Bird-like sounds slide smoothly under flowers; Muffled streams struggle beneath ice. Ice-cold springs stagnate, strings seem frozen; Frozen and blocked, the sound pauses briefly. Hidden sorrow and secret resentment arise anew; In this moment, silence surpasses sound. A silver vase suddenly bursts, water splashes out; Iron cavalry charges with swords clashing. When the song ends, she draws the plectrum across the center; The four strings give one sharp tear like silk ripping. East ships and west boats fall silent; Only the white autumn moon remains on the river’s heart. She pauses, places the plectrum among the strings; Straightens her clothes, stands with composed demeanor. She says herself: originally a girl from the capital; Her home was below Xiama Ridge. Mastering the pipa by thirteen, registered in the top troupe of the Academy; Her songs made great masters admire; Her makeup drew jealousy from beautiful women. Young nobles of Five Tombs competed to offer red silk; For one song, countless bolts were given. Gold-inlaid combs broken keeping time; Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine. This year laughing, next year again; Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away. Brother joined the army, auntie died; Days go by, beauty fades. Before her door desolate, few carriages come; Aging, she married a merchant wife. Merchants value profit over farewell; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. He left, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth; Moonlight surrounds it, river water cold. Deep at night, suddenly dreaming of youth; Waking crying, tears staining rouge down cheeks. Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply; Hearing these words, my grief doubles. We are both fallen souls at world's edge; Why must we have met before to understand? Since last year leaving the imperial capital, Banished sick to live in Xunyang city. Xunyang remote, lacking music; All year round, no strings or pipes heard. Living near Pen River, land low and wet; Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house. What do I hear morning and evening? Cuckoos cry blood, apes howl mournfully. Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights; Often take wine, pour alone. Are there no mountain songs and village flutes? Hoarse and harsh, too painful to listen. Tonight hearing your pipa speech; It’s like celestial music, ears instantly clear. Please don’t refuse, sit again for one more tune; For you, I compose the Ballad of the Pipa. Moved by my words, she stands long; Then sits back, pressing strings faster. Sorrowful tones unlike those before; The whole room hears, covering faces weeping. Who sheds most tears in the room? The Jiangzhou Sima, whose blue robe is soaked."}

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

{"translation":"On the banks of Xunyang, at night, I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest was on his boat;
Raised our cups to drink, but lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced our sorrowful parting,
When all we saw was the vast river steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I softly asked who played;
The pipa stopped, as if she hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer and invited her out,
Refilled the wine, relit the lamp, and resumed the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half-hiding her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Though no melody had begun, feeling already flowed.
Each string suppressed, each note deep with thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Head bowed, fingers moving freely, she continued playing,
Voicing the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking;
First 'Rainbow Skirts', then 'Six Melodies'.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, notes intermingled;
Large and small pearls fell upon a jade plate.
Clear and smooth as orioles singing among flowers,
Muffled and choked as springs flowing under ice.
Cold and sluggish, the spring froze; the strings seemed to stop;
Blocked and silent, the sound paused for a moment.
A hidden sorrow, a quiet resentment arose—
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water splashing out;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clashing.
The piece ended; she placed her pick at the center and swept;
All four strings rang out together, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fell into hush;
Only the white moon in the river’s heart remained visible.
She pondered, put down her pick between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: "I am originally a girl from the capital,
My home is near Shama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
And was listed among the first of the Imperial Music Academy.
After playing, even skilled masters admired me;
Once made up, courtesans grew jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs vied to give me red silk;
One song earned more bolts than could be counted.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and merriment,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
But my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Evenings come, mornings pass, and my beauty faded.
Before my door it became cold; horses and carriages rare;
In my old age, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit over parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I guarded the empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful days;
Waking crying, my tear-streaked makeup ran down.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed;
Hearing these words, again I murmured sympathetically.
We are both lost souls adrift at the edge of the world;
Since we meet now, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and ill, I lie low in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year round, no sound of silk and bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes howling in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights under moon—
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Clashing noise, hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, which played faster.
Sorrowful tones, unlike those before;
Everyone present listened anew, covering their faces in tears.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

{"translation":"On the bank of the Xun River, I bid a friend farewell by night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill of autumn.
I dismounted; my guest was already on the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Tipsy, we could not find joy, and parting seemed bitter;
At the moment of farewell, the vast river was soaked with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked quietly who was playing.
The pipa stopped, as if the player wished to speak but hesitated.
We moved our boats closer, inviting her to meet us.
More wine was poured, lamps were brought back, and the feast resumed.
After many calls and pleas, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before the melody took shape, emotion was already present.
Each string muffled and restrained, each note filled with thought,
As if telling a life story of unfulfilled ambition.
Eyes lowered, she played casually, continuing without pause,
Expressing infinite matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping, then picking—
First playing "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like secret talk.
Rumbling whispers mixed together in complex strumming,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Clear and smooth like orioles singing under flowers,
Choked and difficult like springs flowing beneath ice.
When the cold spring froze stiff, the strings paused in silence.
In that stillness, hidden sorrows and dark resentments arose;
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then, suddenly, a silver bottle burst, water spurting out,
Iron cavalry surged forth, the clash of swords and spears ringing.
At the end of the piece, she drew the plectrum across the center,
Four strings sounded once, sharp as tearing silk.
Boats to the east and west fell silent,
Only the white autumn moon remained visible in the river’s heart.
Pausing, she put down the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and composed her face.
She spoke: "Originally a girl from the capital city,
My home lay below Shrimp Mound.
At thirteen, my pipa skills were complete;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the Imperial Academy.
After finishing a tune, even master musicians would admire me;
When fully made up, often the finest courtesans envied me.
The young dukes of Five Tombs vied to give gifts for my songs;
For one performance, red silk bolts counted beyond number.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes lived through at leisure.
Brothers went off to war, aunties died;
Day and night passed, beauty faded.
The door became desolate, horses rare;
Aging, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit more than separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moon and cold river waters.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
Waking in tears, makeup running red down cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I lamented anew.
Both of us are wanderers fallen to earth’s ends;
Meeting here, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Demoted, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year long, no sounds of strings or pipes were heard.
Living near the Pen River, the land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grew around my house.
What is heard here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights—

Then sat down and tightened the strings, which turned urgent.

{"translation":"On the banks of Xunyang River at night, I bid a guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest stays in his boat;
I raise my cup to drink, but no music is there.
Drunk yet joyless, we part in sorrow;
As we part, the moonlight sinks deep into the vast river.
Suddenly I hear pipa strings upon the water;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I ask quietly: who plays?
The pipa stops, as if she hesitates to speak.
I move my boat close to invite her out,
Add wine, trim lamps, restart the banquet.
After a thousand calls, ten thousand pleas, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks three or two strings;
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string suppressed, each note full of thought,
Seems to tell of a life unfulfilled.
Head bowed, she plays continuously by heart,
Saying all the boundless things within her soul.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First playing 'Rainbow Garment', then 'Six Melodies'.
The thick strings roar like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Roaring and whispering mixed together,
Large pearls, small pearls falling on jade plates.
Birdsong chirps smoothly beneath flowers;
Hidden sobs struggle under icy springs.
Ice-cold, stiff strings freeze completely;
Frozen silent, the song pauses briefly.
Secret sorrows and hidden resentments arise;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
A silver bottle bursts, water splashes out;
Iron cavalry charges, swords clash loudly.
The tune ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
Four strings snap once like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall utterly silent;
Only seeing the autumn moon white in mid-river.
She ponders, puts down the plectrum amid the strings,
Straightens her dress and rises with composed grace.
She says herself: originally a girl from the capital city,
My home was below Shrimp Mound Street.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Named in the First Troupe of the Imperial Academy.
After finishing songs, even great masters were impressed;
Upon completing makeup, often envied by beauty Qiu Niang.
Young men of five tombs competed to give scarves;
One song earned countless red silks.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter again next year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Brother went off to war, aunt died;
Evenings pass, mornings come, beauty fades.
Before my door desolate, few horsemen arrive;
Getting old, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit over separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Going and returning, guarding empty boats at the river mouth,
Around the ship bright moon, cold river waters.
Late at night suddenly dreaming youthful events,
Dreaming weeping, tears staining rouge dry.
Hearing the pipa, I sigh deeply;
Hearing these words, again lamentations rise.
Both of us drift far from home;
Meeting now—why need we have known before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and sick, lying low in Xunyang city.
Xunyang remote without music;
All year not heard string nor pipe sounds.
Near Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, monkeys moan sadly.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine and pour alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Ugly discordant noises hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
Like listening to fairy music, ears clear momentarily.
Don’t refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I’ll compose new verses for Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by these words, she stood long;
Then sat back, tightened strings, tempo quickened.
Grief-stricken unlike previous sounds,
Full audience again heard, all wiped tears.
Who among them shed most tears?
The Blue-robed Prefect of Jiangzhou had wet sleeves."}

{"translation":"Song of the Pipa

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid a guest farewell by night,
Maple leaves and reed blossoms rustled in autumn’s chill.
The host dismounted; the guest sat aboard his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, yet lacked the sound of pipa strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy—sorrow loomed before parting;
At the moment of goodbye, vast mist lay upon the river moon.
Suddenly, across the water, we heard the voice of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home; the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I whispered: “Who is playing?”
The pipa stopped; she hesitated, wanting to speak but slow.
I moved my boat close and invited her to appear;
We poured fresh wine, relit the lamps, and began the feast anew.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally came out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face in shy reserve.
She turned the pegs, touched the strings two or three times;
Before the melody formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string sighed low with deep suppressed thought,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Eyes downcast, fingers moving freely without break,
She voiced all the boundless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking again,
First she played 'The Rainbow Skirt,' then later 'Six Strings.'
On the big strings, notes thundered like sudden rain;
On the small strings, whispers murmured like private talk.
Thundering and whispering, interwoven together in complex play,
Like large pearls and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Sweet as an oriole singing through flowers in spring's flow,
Then choked like a spring beneath ice struggling to move.
When icy coldness stiffened the strings until they ceased,
And silence fell because sound could no longer be made,
There arose a hidden sorrow and secret resentment:
In that silence, words spoke more eloquently than sound.
Then like silver bottles bursting, water gushed forth violently;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clashed and spears rang.
At the song's end, she drew her plectrum sharply down;
With one strike on the four strings, the sound tore like silk cloth.
Boats to east and west fell silent, speechless still,
All we saw was the white autumn moon over midstream.
Lost in thought, she tucked the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, composing her features.
She said herself: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My home located near Xiama Ling."
"At thirteen I mastered the pipa skill completely,
My name enrolled among the finest players in the Imperial Conservatory."
"After finishing pieces, even great masters would bow to my art;
Once dressed, other beauties always grew envious of me."
"Young men of power and wealth vied to give lavish gifts;
For one song, bolts of red silk were given beyond counting."
"Jeweled hairpins snapped when beating time to music,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine during revelry."
"Year after year passed in laughter and pleasure,
Autumn moons and spring winds spent carelessly away."
"My brother went off to join the army; auntie died;
Days came and days went, beauty faded with age."
"Before the door became desolate; horses rarely visited anymore;
Too old for romance, I married a traveling merchant wife."
"The merchant cares only for profit, disregards separation pains;
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea leaves."
"While he is gone, I guard this empty boat at the river mouth;
Moonlight surrounds the vessel; river waters bite cold."
"Deep in the night, suddenly dreaming things of youth long past;
Waking crying, makeup tears stain cheeks crimson lines."  
Listening to her pipa, I had already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words now, I felt profound grief once more.
"We are both people lost along distant horizons;
Meeting tonight, why must we have known each other before?"
Since last year, I left the imperial capital behind,
Demoted to live sick here in quiet Xunyang City.
Xunyang lies remote with little music around us;
Throughout the whole year, no silk-and-bamboo sounds reach ears.
Near Pen River, ground sits damp below elevation level;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow surrounding house walls.
What do I hear morning and evening amidst those places?
Gu-cuckoos cry blood; gibbons wail mournfully.
Spring rivers flower mornings, autumn moon nights arrive often;
Usually take wine alone pour drink solitary self-consumption.
Is there truly no mountain folk songs village flutes present?
Clumsy discordant rough noise hard listen pleasant taste.
Tonight hearing your pipa language so clear bright melody,
Like listening immortal celestial music ears temporarily clear vision.
Do not refuse sit further play one another piece please;
For you compose new poem Ballad Song Of The Pipa.
Pleased my words she stood long time reflect inward feelings;
Returned seated tightened strings faster tempo urgent pace.
Mournful unlike previous earlier performance tone style;
Full audience hearing again covered faces hide sobs cries.
Among seats whose tears fall most numerous abundant amount?
Prefect Jiangzhou Sima Blue Shirt Wet Soaked Through."}

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}
</原诗>

message.content:
{"translation":"At the head of Xunyang River, I bid a guest goodnight in autumn's chill; Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the breeze.
I dismount from my horse while he remains on his boat; We raise our cups to drink, but there are no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we part with heavy hearts; At the moment of farewell, the river is vast, soaked in moonlight.
Suddenly, over the water, comes the sound of a pipa; The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Seeking the source, I ask softly who plays; The pipa stops, as if she hesitates to speak.
We move our boats closer, inviting her to meet us; More wine is poured, lamps are turned up, the feast resumes.
After calling a thousand times, ten thousand times, she finally emerges, Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks two or three strings; Before the tune forms, emotion already spills forth.
Every string veils sorrow, every note carries longing, As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on, Expressing all the endless troubles in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking, First she plays "Rainbow Feathers," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings thunder like sudden rain; The thin strings whisper like private conversation.
Thundering and whispering intertwine, A cascade of pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as birdsong beneath flowers, choked as water flowing under ice.
When the cold spring freezes, the strings seem to stop entirely; When they cease, the music falls momentarily silent.
But hidden grief and secret resentment arise anew; In this silence, words speak louder than sound.
Then suddenly, as if a silver vase bursts, water splashing out; Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
The piece ends as she draws her pick across the center, One sweep of four strings sounds like tearing silk.
East and west boats fall silent, hearing nothing more; Only the white moon of autumn shines upon the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she puts her pick away among the strings, Straightens her clothes and rises with a composed manner.
She says she was originally a girl of the capital city, Living near Shama Mound.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa, Her name appearing first in the Imperial Music Bureau's roster.
Her songs won praise even from skilled masters; Her makeup made the beautiful women jealous.
The young nobles from Five Tombs vied to give her gifts; For one song, countless red silks were thrown to her.
Gold-inlaid combs shattered keeping time; Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and delight, Autumn moons and spring winds spent casually.
Then her brother went off to war, her aunt died, Days and nights wore on, beauty faded.
Her door grew desolate, carriages rare, So she married an old merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit above separation; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, she guards her empty boat at the river mouth, Moonlit and cold surrounding the vessel, the river waters chill.
Late at night she dreams abruptly of youthful days, Waking with tears streaming down her painted face.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply; Hearing her story, I lamented again.
We are both people fallen far from home, What does it matter that we had not known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital, Banished and ill, residing in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music; All year round I hear no strings nor pipes.
My home near Pen River is low and damp, Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my dwelling.
What do I hear here morning and evening? Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers and flower mornings, on autumn moonlit nights, Often I take wine and pour it alone for myself.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? But their harsh, jarring sounds are hard to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa music, It is like celestial sound, clearing my ears briefly.
Do not refuse; sit again and play one more piece, I will compose for you a ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time; Returning to sit, she hurriedly strung faster notes.
Melancholy sounds unlike those before, The whole audience hears and covers faces in weeping.
Who sheds the most tears among them? The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is soaked."}

message.content: {"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night; Maple leaves and reed flowers trembled in the autumn chill. The host dismounted, his guest remained on the boat; We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings. Though drunken, joy was lacking as we prepared to part; At departure, the vast river was soaked with moonlight. Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of the pipa; The host forgot to return home, the guest did not set sail. Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing; The pipa music stopped, the player hesitated, slow to speak. Moving my boat closer, I invited her to meet me; More wine was added, lamps trimmed, and the banquet resumed. After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerged, Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face. She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times; Before a melody formed, emotion was already present. Each string muffled, each note filled with longing, As if telling of a life where ambitions went unfulfilled. With lowered brows, she played continuously by instinct, Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart. Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking, First playing \"Rainbow Feather,\" then \"Six Strings.\" The thick strings rumbled like a sudden heavy rain; The thin strings whispered softly like private confidences. Rumbling and whispering intertwined in complex play— Large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate. Melodious, like yellow birds singing smoothly under flowers; Muffled, like a spring flowing beneath ice, struggling to move. Cold as icy springs, sluggish as the strings seemed to freeze; Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceased. A hidden sorrow, an unspoken resentment arose; In this silence, it surpassed even sound. Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water gushing out; Or iron cavalry charging forth, the clash of swords and spears. When the tune ended, she drew the pick across the center; One crack from the four strings sounded like tearing silk. East boats and west barges fell silent, no one spoke; Only the white autumn moon shone on the heart of the river. Lost in thought, she put the pick between the strings, Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression. She said she was originally a girl from the capital city, Living in a house below Xiama Ling (Toad Mound). By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa, Her name listed among the top tier of the Imperial Music Academy. When she finished a piece, even master musicians admired her; When made up, every beauty grew jealous of her charms. Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to offer red silk headbands; For one song, they gave her piles of red gauze unknown number. Ornate hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time; Blood-red skirts stained by overturned wine. Year after year, laughter followed laughter; Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away. Her brother joined the army, her aunt died; Days passed, nights came, and her youth faded. Fewer horses and carriages visited her gate; Growing older, she married a merchant’s wife. The merchant valued profit over separation; Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea. He was gone; she guarded the empty boat at the river mouth; Moonlight circled the boat, the river water cold. Deep in the night, she suddenly dreamed of her youthful days; Waking weeping, makeup tears streaked her face crimson. Hearing the pipa, I sighed in sympathy; Hearing her words, I lamented anew deeply. Both of us are fallen souls drifting at heaven’s edge; Meeting here, why must we have known each other before? Since leaving the imperial capital last year, I have been banished, Sick and bedridden in Xunyang City. Xunyang is remote, devoid of music; All year long, I hear no sounds of silk and bamboo. My dwelling near Pen River is low and damp; Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house. What do I hear from dawn to dusk there? Cuckoos crying blood, apes howling mournfully. On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights, Often I take wine and pour it alone. Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? Their rough, harsh tones are difficult to listen to. Tonight I hear your pipa’s language, Like hearing celestial music, my ears momentarily clear. Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune; For you, I will compose the \"Song of the Pipa.\" Moved by my words, she stood for a long while; Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster. Sorrowful, unlike the previous sounds; Everyone present listened again, covering their faces in tears. Who wept the most among those seated? The Bai Juyi, Sima of Jiangzhou, in his blue robe wet."}

{
"translation": "At dusk by the Xunyang River I see off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.
My horse dismounts; my guest stays aboard his boat,
We raise our wine but have no music to play.
Drunk with sorrow at parting, we gaze at the river
Where the moon floats upon the vast, misty water.
Then suddenly from the waters comes the sound of pipa,
Forgetting home, I stop; my guest halts his departure.
I follow the sound, asking softly who plays it,
The pipa stops; someone hesitates, about to speak.
I move my boat close to invite them ashore,
Add more wine, trim the lamp, and begin again.
After many calls she finally appears,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before the tune is formed, emotion already flows.
Each string suppressed, each note full of thought,
As if telling tales of life unfulfilled.
Her head lowered, she plays casually on,
Revealing the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly rubbing, then sweeping and picking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six One." (Note: 'Rainbow Skirt' refers to Nishang Yuqu, 'Six One' refers to Liuyao)
The thick strings roar like heavy rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Roaring and whispering mix together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
The melody glides like orioles singing under blossoms,
Sobs like a spring trapped beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound briefly pauses.
New hidden sorrows and resentments arise;
Now silence speaks louder than sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting, water sprays,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clang.
When the song ends, she draws the plectrum across the center,
Four strings snap once, like silk tearing.
Boats east and west fall silent;
Only in the river's heart does the autumn moon shine white.
She sighs, places the plectrum between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with composed grace.
She says she was originally a woman of the capital,
Living near Shama Ridge.
By thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first among the imperial musicians.
Her songs left skilled masters amazed,
Her makeup made even the beautiful Qiuniang jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs vied to give her gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Gold-ornamented combs snapped as she kept time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilling wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died,
Day and night went by, her beauty faded.
Fewer horses came before her door,
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant values profit over farewell;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving her to guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold water.
Late at night she dreams of her youth,
Waking weeps, tears staining her rouge.
Hearing her pipa, I already sighed,
And hearing her story, I am deeply moved.
Both lost souls wandering the ends of the earth,
Meeting now—why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the Imperial City,
Banished and ill, living in Xunyang Town.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long I hear no strings or pipes.
My home near Pen River is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around.
What do I hear day and night here?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing sadly.
In spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights,
I often take wine and drink alone.
Are there mountain songs and village flutes?
Crude and discordant, hard to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa words,
Like heavenly music, my ears are cleared.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits again, playing faster, strings urgent.
The melancholy differs from earlier sounds;
Everyone present listens anew, covering faces in tears.
Who sheds the most tears in this gathering?
The司马 (magistrate) of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."
}

冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

Suddenly, from over the water came the sound of a pipa; host forgot to return home, guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing; the pipa paused, hesitant to speak.
We moved our boats close together and invited her to join us; we added more wine, relit lamps, and began the feast anew.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times; before the melody formed, emotion spoke first.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with thought, seeming to tell of a lifetime’s unfulfilled ambition.
With downcast brow, she casually continued to play, expressing all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking, she first played "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings crashed like sudden rain; the thin strings whispered like private talk.
Crashing and whispering intertwined, like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Now clear and sweet like orioles singing under blossoms, now choked and muffled like springs flowing beneath ice.
The cold spring froze, the strings stiffened and stopped; the halt in flow silenced the song for a moment.
Then arose a hidden melancholy and secret resentment; in that silence, sound was surpassed by quietude.
Then, suddenly, as if a silver vase burst and water sprayed forth, or iron cavalry charged with swords clashing.

Eastward boats and westward ships fell silent in awe; only the white autumn moon gleamed upon the river’s heart.
She pondered, set aside the plectrum among the strings, straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her demeanor.
She said herself born a girl of the capital city, dwelling near Shrimp Hill.
By thirteen she had mastered the pipa, listed among the top performers of the Imperial Music Academy.
After finishing a piece, even master musicians admired her; when made-up, courtesans often envied her beauty.
Young men from Five Tombs vied to give her gifts; for one song, bolts of red silk were countless.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time; blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.

Her brother went off to war, her aunt died; days and nights wore on, fading her charm.

The merchant valued profit, thinking little of separation; last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, guarding an empty boat at the river mouth; around the ship shone bright moon, chilling the river waters.
Late at night she suddenly dreamed of youthful times, waking weeping, makeup tears staining the railings red.
Hearing her pipa, I already sighed; hearing these words, I grieved deeply again.
Both are wanderers lost at heaven’s edge; meeting now, why need former acquaintance?

On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights, I often take wine and pour it alone.

Tonight I hear your pipa speech, like listening to celestial music, ears momentarily cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece; for you, I shall compose "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by these words, she stood long; returning to sit, she tightened strings, which sounded swifter.
Mournful, unlike previous tones; everyone seated heard anew, covering faces in tears.
Who among them shed most tears? The Blue-robed Prefect of Jiangzhou, shirt soaked through."}
