{
"translation": "Song of the Pipa

By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest remains aboard the boat;
We raise our wine cups to drink, but find no music for it.
Drunk yet unjoyful, sorrow fills this parting scene;
When we depart, the vast river soaks the moon's pale sheen.
Suddenly, pipa strings sound upon the water’s flow,
The host forgets his home; the guest delays his row.
I seek the source, asking softly: "Who plays thus?"
The pipa stops, as if the player lingers over us.
I move my boat closer and invite her to appear;
We add more wine, relight lamps, resume the feast here.
After many calls and cries, she finally comes forth,
Still holding her pipa, half shielding her face from north.
She turns the tuning pegs, plucks strings a few times through,
Before the tune begins, emotion already breaks through.
Each string is muffled low, each note full of thought and sigh,
As if telling of a life where ambition had to die.
With downcast eyes, fingers glide on smoothly without haste,
Expressing all the endless sorrows time has wasted.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, then sliding and picking,
First 'Rainbow Skirt', then 'Six Strings'—the melodies are striking.
The thick strings rumble loud like sudden rainstorm’s roar;
The thin strings whisper soft like lovers’ secret lore.
Rumbling and whispering interweave in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto jade trays.
Birdsong flows smooth beneath flowers, sweet and clear,
Then chokes like spring water trapped by ice severe.
Cold ice blocks the stream, the strings freeze tight and stop,
Silence reigns when notes can no longer hop.
A hidden grief and silent hate now start to grow,
This silence speaks louder than any sound could show.
Silver bottles burst, water splashes out in spray,
Iron cavalry charges, swords clash in battle fray.
The tune ends; she draws her pick across the heart-strings tight,
One final chord tears silk with sharp and startling might.
East and west, boats fall silent, no word is spoken there,
Only the white autumn moon sees the river bare.
She muses long, places her pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises up, composed and serious things.
"I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My home was near Xiama Ling, where memories linger."
"At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s every art,
And belonged to the first troupe of the imperial court."
"Even great masters praised my tunes when they were done,
And beauty rivals envied me when makeup was won."
"Rich youths of Wuling fought to give me red silk scarves,
For one song alone, countless bolts filled their drawers."
"Gold hairpins broke keeping time, silver combs shattered too,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine, revelry ran through."
"Year after year, laughter echoed, seasons passed away,
Moonlight and breeze consumed my youth in idle play."
"My brother joined the army; my aunt died young and frail,
Days turned to nights, and my youthful beauty grew pale."
"The door stood cold and empty; horses rarely came,
So in old age, I wed a merchant, lost in trade’s game."
"He values profit high, cares little for our parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, heart hardening."
"While he was gone, I guarded the empty boat at the mouth,
Moonlight encircled the ship; river waters flowed south."
"Late at night, I dreamed of events in my younger days,
Woke crying, tears mixed with rouge running in hazy ways."

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply at its pain,
Then heard her words, and lamented twice again.
Both of us are wanderers stranded far from home,
Meeting need not require that we have known before.
Since last year I left the imperial capital behind,
Demoted to Xunyang, lying ill, confined and blind.
This place is remote, devoid of music’s charm,
All year long, no sounds of silk or bamboo alarm.
My house stands near Peng River, low and damp and wet,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo set.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk within these walls?
Cuckoos bleeding their voices; apes calling mournful calls.
On spring river mornings, flower-dawn and autumn moon,
Often I take my wine and pour it, lonely soon.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes to hear?
Their harsh and jarring noise is impossible to cheer.
Tonight I hear your pipa speak its eloquent tongue,
Like fairy music making my ears bright and sung.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more refrain;
For you, I will compose this Song of the Pipa vein.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while in thought,
Then sat again, tightening strings, emotions caught.
The melody sounded sad, unlike what played before,
The whole audience listened, tears streaming down the floor.
Who in the room shed most tears, soaking through their shirts?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe holds its hurts."
}

冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。

message.content:
{"translation":"One night by the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest.
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted my horse; my guest was already on his boat.
We raised our cups, wishing to drink, but lacked music.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced a sorrowful parting;
At the moment of farewell, only moonlight filled the vast river.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa.
My guest forgot to depart; I forgot to go home.
Following the sound, I softly asked who played.
The pipa stopped, and though she wished to speak, she hesitated.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to meet me.
More wine was brought, lamps were turned up, and the feast resumed.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-hiding her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked a few strings.
Before a melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each string suppressed a sigh; each note carried thought.
It seemed to tell of a life’s unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, she casually continued to play,
Pouring out infinitely many things in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing, then picking—
First playing the "Rainbow Garment," then the "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, mingled together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing among flowers;
Choked as spring water flowing under ice.
When the cold, hard ice made the strings freeze and stall,
The flow was blocked, and the sound paused for a moment.
Then arose a hidden sorrow and secret resentment.
At that moment, silence surpassed sound.
Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water splashed forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashed.
As the song ended, she gathered the plectrum with a final stroke;
All four strings rang out once, like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and ships to the west fell silent;
Only the white moon in the center of the river remained visible.
She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum into the strings,
Arranged her clothes, rose, and composed her countenance.
She said she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living at the foot of the Xiama Ling mound.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
And belonged to the first troupe of the Imperial Music Academy.
When her pieces ended, even famous masters admired her skill;
When her makeup was done, even the beautiful Qiuniang envied her.
The young men of the Five Tombs vied to pay her
With bolts of red silk for a single tune, beyond counting.
Jeweled combs broke when keeping time;
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter returned next year;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
Her brother went to join the army; her aunt died.
Evenings came, mornings went, and her beauty faded.
The door before her grew desolate; horses became rare.
Getting old, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant cares only for profit, not for parting.
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left her alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and the cold river waters.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreamed of youthful days,
Crying in her sleep, her makeup tears staining her face red.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words, I again felt deep sorrow.
We are both fallen people drifting at the ends of the earth;
Why do we need prior acquaintance when we meet?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
I have been exiled and bedridden in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and lacks music;
All year round, one hears no silk or bamboo instruments.
I live near the Peng River, where the land is low and damp,
With yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Ducks bleeding cries and apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers with flowers in bloom, on autumn nights with full moons,
Often I take wine to pour for myself alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes here?
But they are harsh and ugly, hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is as if hearing celestial music, my ears briefly clear.
Do not refuse to sit down again and play another piece.
For you, I will compose the Song of the Pipa.
Touched by my words, she stood for a long time.
Then she sat back, tightened the strings, and played more urgently.
The melancholy notes differed from those before;
The whole audience heard them again and covered their faces in tears.
Among those seated, who shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou was soaked wet."}

message.content:
{"translation":"One night by the Xunyang River, I saw a guest depart,
Amid autumn's rustling maple leaves and reed flowers.
The host dismounted; his guest remained on the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, yet heard no music play.
Though drunk, joy was absent; sorrow marked our parting,
As we separated, vast moonlight soaked the river.
Suddenly, above the water, a pipa sounded;
The host forgot to go home, the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I asked who played in the dark,
The pipa paused, hesitant before speaking.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Replenished wine, relit lamps, and reopened the feast.
After countless calls, she finally emerged,
Holding her pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked a few strings,
Before the melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each string suppressed deep thoughts in every note,
Seeming to tell of lifelong unfulfilled ambitions.
With downcast eyes and casual fingers, she continued playing,
Expressing all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked,
First playing "Rainbow Garment," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings thrummed like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversation.
Thrumming and whispering crossed in a mixture,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Clear as orioles singing smoothly beneath flowers,
Choked as spring water struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold and stagnant, strings frozen silent,
Silence blocked all flow, sound temporarily ceased.
Secret sorrows and hidden hatreds arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed any sound.
Then, like a silver bottle suddenly bursting with splashing water,
Or iron cavalry charging with clashing blades.
The song ended; she drew her plectrum across the center,
All four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west stood silently in awe,
Seeing only white autumn moon in the river's heart.
She pondered, placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She spoke: "Originally from the capital city,
My home lived near Xiama Tomb.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau.
After performances, even great masters admired me;
When dressed up, other courtesans were envious.
Young nobles of Five Tombs competed to offer gifts,
For one song, they gave countless red silks.
Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent casually.
My brother went off to war; my aunt died;
Evenings came, mornings passed, my beauty faded.
My gate grew desolate, horses rarely came,
Getting older, I married a merchant's wife.
Merchants value profit over partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I've guarded this empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moon and cold river waters.
Deep in the night I dreamt of youth's events,
Crying in dreams, makeup tears streaked red.
I sighed hearing the pipa,
And again, listening to these words, deeply grieved.
We are both lost souls drifting far from home,
Why should meeting require prior acquaintance?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and ill, living in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year long, no strings or pipes are heard.
Living near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here day and night?
Blood-crying cuckoos and mourning apes' cries.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are rough, harsh, and hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa language,
It is like celestial music; ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune;
For you, I will write this 'Ballad of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Returned to seat, quickened strings growing urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike sounds before,
The whole audience listened again, all covering faces weeping.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Jiangzhou Prefect's blue robe was wet."}

银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。

{
  "translation": "Song of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest was on his boat.
We raised our cups, wishing to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk yet joyless, sorrowful at parting,
As we bid farewell, the vast river held the moon in its depths.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, and the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing;
The pipa stopped, as if about to speak, then hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out for tea,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and renewed the feast.
Called a thousand times, urged ten thousand, she finally came out,
Still holding the pipa, half covering her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before the melody formed, emotion was already present.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with thoughts,
As if telling of a lifetime's unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, she played casually on,
Expressing all the boundless matters of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, strumming and picking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six One."
The bass strings boomed like heavy rain,
The treble strings whispered like private talk.
Booming and whispering, mixed together they rang,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Clear and sweet, like orioles singing under flowers,
Muffled and choked, like springs flowing beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seemed to freeze and stop;
Blocked and silent, the sound momentarily ceased.
Then arose hidden sorrows and dark grudges;
At this moment, silence surpassed speech.
Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water gushed forth;
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashed.
When the song ended, she swept the plectrum across the center;
All four strings sounded once, like silk tearing.
East boats and west ships were quiet, no one spoke;
Only the white autumn moon in the river's center was seen.
She pondered, put away the plectrum, tucked it among the strings;
Straightened her clothes, rose up, and adopted a solemn countenance.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near the Shama Ling district.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name belonging to the first branch of the Imperial Academy.
When I finished a piece, even skilled masters would admire;
Once made up, every beauty would envy me.
The young men of Five Tombs vied to give me red silk scarves;
For a single song, countless pieces of crimson gauze were given.
Silver combs adorned with jewelry shattered keeping time;
Red-dyed skirts stained by overturned wine.
This year laughing and rejoicing, next year the same;
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed idly by.
My brother went off to join the army; my aunt died;
Evenings came and mornings went, and my beauty faded.
The door became desolate; carriages and horses grew rare;
Getting old, I married the wife of a merchant.
The merchant values profit over love of companionship;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat;
Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of youthful days;
In the dream I wept, makeup tears staining red the railing.
Having heard the pipa, I already sighed;
Hearing these words added further lamentation.
"We are both lost souls drifting at the edge of the world;
Meeting now, why does it matter that we knew each other before?"
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and living sick in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote and lacks music;
All year long, I do not hear the sound of strings and flutes.
Living near the Fen River, where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights, full moons—
Often taking wine, I pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village pipes?
Their harsh, grating sounds are difficult to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa play,
It is like listening to immortal music; my ears are temporarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit down again and play another piece;
For you, I will compose the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Sitting back down, she tightened the strings, which turned urgent.
The melancholy sound was unlike the previous one;
The whole audience, hearing again, covered their faces and wept.
Who in the room shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou was wet."
}

{
  "translation": "Song of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River I bid a guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, the guest is on his boat,
We raise our cups but lack music to lift our throats.
Drunk yet joyless, grief hangs at parting,
The river vast, moonlight submerged in water.
Suddenly pipa sounds rise from the water,
The host forgets homecoming, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I ask in the dark who plays,
The pipa pauses; hesitation before speech.
I move my ship close to invite her out,
Add wine, return lantern light, reopen the feast.
After countless calls she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
Turning pegs, plucking strings, a few notes first,
Before melody forms, emotion already breathes.
Each string suppressed, each note a sigh,
As if telling a life of thwarted dreams.
Eyes lowered, fingers casually continue playing,
Telling all the boundless thoughts within.
Light pinches, slow twists, sweeps then picks,
First 'Rainbow Skirt', then 'Six Strings'.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumble and whisper intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Chirping like orioles sliding beneath blossoms,
Sobbing like springs blocked under ice.
Ice-cold streams stagnant, strings freeze to silence,
Silence where no sound passes, music briefly stops.
Yet hidden sorrow and secret regret arise;
This silence speaks louder than any sound.
A silver vase suddenly bursts, water spurts forth,
Iron cavalry charges, swords clash and ring.
The song ends; the plectrum strikes the center,
One final cry like tearing silk.
East ships and west boats fall silent,
Only seeing white moonlight on the river's heart.
She hesitates, puts the plectrum among strings,
Straightens her clothes, assumes a composed face.
She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home near Shama Ridge below the city.'
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Named in the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After each piece even master musicians admired me,
When dressed up, even famed beauties were envious.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to give gifts,
For one song, red silk received beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year laughter continued,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly away.
Then brother went to army, aunt died,
Days fade, nights pass, beauty fades.
Before my door desolate, horses rare,
Old age forced marriage to a merchant wife.
The merchant values profit over separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me alone guarding an empty ship at the river mouth,
Moonlight circles the ship, river water cold.
Late at night I dream of youthful days,
Wake crying, makeup tears streaming down red cheeks.
Hearing the pipa I already sighed,
Hearing these words I sigh again deeply.
'Though strangers meeting now, we share fate:
Both are wanderers fallen from grace beyond the sky's edge!'
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, sick in bed in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music,
All year round no sound of strings or bamboo flutes.
Living near Pen River, low land damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine, drink it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
Crude, discordant sounds hard to bear listening to.
Tonight hearing your pipa language,
Like hearing celestial music, ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit again, play one more piece,
For you I shall write this 'Song of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words she stood long,
Then sat back, tightened strings, tempo faster.
Mournful tones unlike those played before,
The whole audience listened anew, covering faces weeping.
Who shed most tears in the room?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet."
}

{"translation":"The Song of the Pipa

By the Qanshui River, I saw my friend off at night; Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill of autumn.
My horse dismounted, my guest remained on his boat; I raised my wine to drink, but found no music to accompany it.
Though drunk, joy was absent as we faced our sad parting; When we parted, a vast moon floated upon the river's surface.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa; The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who played; The pipa paused, the player hesitated before speaking.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to meet me; We added more wine, relit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally appeared, Yet still held her pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times; Before the melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed sorrow, each note carried longing; As if telling of a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, she played casually yet skillfully, Expressing all the boundless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking, First playing 'Rainbow Garments,' then 'Six-String Melody.'
The thick strings sounded like heavy raindrops rushing down; The thin strings whispered like intimate secrets shared.
Thick and thin sounds mingled intricately together; Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate.
Then came the chirping of orioles sliding beneath blossoms; And the choked sobbing of springs trapped under ice.
The cold spring froze, the strings stopped dead; Stuck and silent, the music ceased for a moment.
But hidden sorrows and secret regrets arose anew; At that moment, silence surpassed speech.
Like a silver vase suddenly bursting with water splashing out; Or armored cavalry charging forth with swords clashing loudly.
When the piece ended, she swept the plectrum across the center; Four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
To the east and west boats fell into quiet awe; Only the white autumn moon shone in the middle of the river.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between the strings; Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city; My family lived near Shama Hill.""At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name ranked first among the Imperial Music Academy's troupe.
After finishing a tune, even skilled masters would admire me; After putting on makeup, the famous courtesan Qiuniang envied me.
The young nobles of Wuling vied to offer me gifts; For one song, countless pieces of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs broke keeping time to the rhythm; Blood-red skirts stained by spilt wine during revelry.
This year laughter continued into next; Autumn moons and spring winds passed casually away.
But then my brother joined the army, my aunt died; Days faded into nights, and my beauty withered.
Before my door grew lonely, horses few; Aging, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant valued profit over farewell; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat; Around the ship bright moonlight, cold river waters lap.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of youthful days; In dreams I wept, make-up tears staining my red cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply; Hearing these words, I groaned again with grief.
We are both lost souls drifting at heaven's edge; Having met now, why should it matter if we knew each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital; Banished and ill, lying idle in Qanshui City.
Qanshui is remote and lacks music; All year long I never hear stringed instruments.
Living near Penjiang where land is low and damp; Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there morning and evening? Cuckoos bleeding with cries, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights; Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there truly no mountain songs or village flutes? Yes, but their harsh cacophony is unbearable to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa song, It is like hearing celestial music, ears suddenly clear.
Please don't refuse to sit longer and play another piece; For you, I will compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while; Then sat back down, tightened strings, speed increasing.
The melancholy tone differed from earlier notes; The whole audience listened again, covering faces and weeping.
Who shed the most tears among those present? The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。

轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。

冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

The host dismounted, his guest was on the boat; We raised our cups but had no music to play. East and west boats fell quiet; Only the white autumn moon reflected on the river's heart remained. Hesitating, she placed her pick among the strings; Straightened her clothes, rising with composed dignity. She said: 'Originally I was a girl from the capital city; My family lived near Xiama Ling. Young nobles from Five Tombs competed to give her gifts; For one performance, countless lengths of red silk were given. Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time; Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine. Year after year, laughter continued; Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually. Her brother went off to war, her aunt died; Morning turned to evening, beauty faded away. Fewer horses stopped at her door, solitude grew cold; Too old now, she married a merchant's wife. Deep in night dreams, memories of youth returned; Crying in sleep, tears blurred her makeup. Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply; Listening further to these words, my sighs grew heavier. We are both wanderers lost at heaven’s edge; What need is there to have known each other before? Since last year, I departed the imperial capital; Banished here to live sickly in Xunyang city. This remote place has no music; Throughout the year, not a single string instrument is heard. Living near Penjiang, where land lies low and damp; Yellow rushes and bitter bamboo surround my house. Between dawn and dusk, what sounds do I hear? Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing mournfully. In spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights; Often alone, lifting cups to pour drinks myself. Aren’t there folk songs and village flutes too? But their harsh tones are unbearable to listen to tonight. Tonight hearing your pipa’s voice, it feels like celestial music clearing my ears. Do not refuse to sit down and play one more piece; I will write for you this Ballad of the Pipa. Moved by my words, she stood long in contemplation; Returning to sit, she tightened strings, playing faster still. The melancholy notes differed greatly from those earlier; Everyone present covered their faces, tears flowing anew. Who shed the most tears among them? It was me, Jiangzhou Prefect, my blue robe soaked through."}

{"translation":"Ballad of the Pipa

At night by the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn wind.
I dismounted from my horse while he waited on his boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but found no music to delight.
Drunk yet joyless, grief hung heavy at our parting hour;
The moon shimmered pale upon the vast, mist-covered river.
Suddenly, drifting over water, came the pipa's song;
My guest forgot to sail, and I forgot to go home.
Following the sound, I whispered: "Who plays so well?"
The music paused; she hesitated, loath to speak her tale.
I moved our boats close by, inviting her to join us here,
Adding fresh wine, lighting lamps, resuming the feast anew.
Though called ten thousand times, she shyly came at last,
Still hiding half her face behind the pipa as she passed.
She twisted pegs and plucked the strings a few tentative notes,
Before the melody began, emotion filled the throats.
Each string sighed low with deep suppressed sorrow and thought,
As if telling tales of ambitions forever thwart.
Head bowed, she played with ease, letting fingers roam,
Pouring out endless stories hidden in her soul's home.
Light touches, slow twists, sweeps, and plucks intertwined,
First 'Rainbow Feather', then 'Six Strings' melodies refined.
Thick strings crashed like sudden rain pouring fast and loud,
Thin strings whispered soft secrets, tender, gentle, proud.
Loud and soft intertwining, mixed in complex play—
Large and small pearls dropping into a jade tray.
Smooth as orioles singing under blossoms bright,
Then choked like spring water struggling through ice at night.
Cold and stiff, the strings seemed frozen, sound grew faint and still,
Silence held more meaning than any note could fill.
A hidden grief awakened, bitter resentment stirred,
In this quiet moment, silence spoke louder than heard.
Like silver vases bursting, water spraying high and clear,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords clashing near.
The tune ended; she drew the plectrum across the center,
Four strings snapped once, like tearing silk, sharp and tender.
East and west ships lay silent, hushed in wonderment,
Only the white autumn moon watched on the river bent.
Lost in thought, she put down her pick amid the strings,
Adjusted clothes, composed herself with quiet things.
"I was once a girl from the capital's grand halls," she said,
"My home stood beneath Xiama Ling's shaded beds."
"At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, skilled and fine,
Among the first in the Imperial Music Academy's line."
"Famous musicians envied me after every performance;
Even beauty queens felt jealousy at my adornments."
"Young nobles fought for favor, tossing bundles of silk red,
For one song, countless lengths of scarlet cloth were spread."
"Gold-inlaid combs broke rhythm’s beat in joyful dance;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine in wild romance."
"Year after year of laughter, careless and free-flowing;
Autumn moons and spring winds passed, life brightly glowing."
"But brothers joined the army, aunties died away;
Days and nights turned, youth faded, colors lost their sway."
"The front gate fell silent, horses rare, visitors gone;
In old age, I married a merchant, cold and alone."
"Merchants value profit over love, care little for goodbyes;
Last month he left to Liang to buy tea, no more ties."
"He's gone, and I stay guarding an empty ship by the port;
Moonlight wraps around it, river water cold support."
"Deep in night, dreams of youthful days come flooding back;
Tears stain makeup red as pillowcases soak.""
Hearing the pipa made me sigh deeply in sympathy,
And her words brought renewed tears, drowning dignity.
"We are both drifters far from home, fallen alike;
Why must we have known each other before tonight?"
"Since last year, leaving the Emperor's city behind,
Exiled to Xunyang, sick and weary-minded."
"Here lies isolation, lacking all musical charm;
No silk or bamboo sounds ever reach my calm."
"Near the Pen River lives lowland marshy ground;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos surround my abode bound."
"What do I hear morning and evening in this place?
杜鹃 cry blood, monkeys wail in mournful embrace."
"Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often take wine alone, pouring solitary delights."
"Are there no mountain songs or village flutes nearby?
Harsh noises clash discordantly, difficult to enjoy."
"Tonight hearing your pipa language, pure and divine,
It feels like celestial music making ears shine."
"Do not leave; sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Ballad of the Pipa'."
Moved by my words, she stood long in thoughtful mood,
Then sat, tightening strings, playing urgent, swift, and rude.
Melancholy tones unlike those earlier sung,
The whole audience wept, listening, hearts wrung.
Whose tears flowed most among those seated round?
The Blue-robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou, soaked to the ground."}

{"translation":"The Song of the Pipa
by Bai Juyi

By night I saw off a guest at the mouth of the Xunyang River;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; his guest was already on the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Though drunk, we found no joy; sorrow hung over the parting.
As we parted, the vast river soaked up the moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return; the guest delayed departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa stopped, and she wished to speak yet hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her to come out;
More wine was poured, the lamps were brought back, and the feast resumed.
Amid countless calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the tuning pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before the tune formed, feeling was already present.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing,
Seeming to tell of a life unable to fulfill its ambitions.
With lowered brows, she played casually, continuously,
Telling fully of boundless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly rolling, sweeping then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Sixth Mode."
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like hushed secrets.
Rumbling and whispering mixed together in playing,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as an oriole’s song beneath blossoms;
Choked as a spring flowing under ice.
When the cold ice made the strings stiff and silent,
And silence blocked all sound for a pause,
There arose elsewhere hidden sorrows and unspoken resentments.
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then, suddenly, silver jars burst and water sprayed out;
Iron cavalry charged forth, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ended: she drew the pick across the center,
A single cry from four strings, like silk tearing.
Boats to the east and west fell silently quiet,
All that remained visible was the white autumn moon mid-river.
Ponderous, she put down the pick into the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her features.
She said herself: "Originally I was a girl of the capital,
My home lay below Shrimp蟆陵 (Xiamaling).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name was listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire her skill;
When adorned, often rival beauties would envy her grace.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to offer gifts;
For one song, bolts of red silk counted beyond measure.
Inlaid hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
This year laughter followed next year’s mirth;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Her brother went off to soldier; her aunt died;

{"translation":"The Song of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

On the bank of the Xunyang River, I bid a friend farewell at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat;
We raise our cups, but there is no music to hear.
Drunken yet joyless, we face the sorrow of parting,
As the vast river holds the moon in its immersion.
Suddenly, from across the water, comes the sound of a pipa,
The host forgets to return home; the guest delays departure.
Following the melody, I ask who plays it, but the strings cease,
And the player hesitates, reluctant to speak.
I move my boat close by and invite her out,
Replenish the wine, relight the lamps, and resume the feast.
After much calling and urging, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few preliminary notes,
Before the tune begins, emotion already fills the air.
Each string muffled, each note sighing, as if telling
Of lifelong frustration and unfulfilled dreams.
With lowered brows, she plays continuously, expressing
The boundless matters hidden within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking again,
First playing 'Rainbow Skirt,' then later 'Six Strings.'
The thick strings thunder loudly like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper softly like private conversation.
Loud and soft intermingle in complex strumming,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smoothly flowing like orioles singing beneath flowers,
Choked and sobbing like spring water freezing under ice.
The cold, sluggish flow stops, the strings seem broken off,
In this silence where nothing passes through, the sound temporarily halts.
A different kind of deep sorrow and secret resentment arises,
At this moment, silence speaks louder than any sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting with splashing water,
Or iron cavalry charging with clashing swords and spears.
The song ends; she places her pick in the center of the strings,
One final stroke sounds like ripping silk.
Boats on the east and ships on the west fall silent,
All that is seen is the white autumn moon in the river's heart.
She pauses thoughtfully, inserts her pick among the strings,
Arranges her clothes, stands up, and assumes a composed demeanor.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near the Shrimp-Toad Mound.
Mastering the pipa at thirteen years old,
Her name listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau musicians.
After finishing a piece, even skilled masters admired her craft;
When made up, every beauty envied her grace.
The young nobles of Five Tombs vied to give her red silk scarves;
For one song, they gave so many pieces that none could count them.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs snapped from beating time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent casually.
Then her brother joined the army, and her aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and her youth faded away.
Visitors became scarce before her door, horse and carriage rare,
So, aging, she married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit above all else and cares little for separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me here alone guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days,
Waking with tears streaming down her painted cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply already,
But hearing these words, my sighs grow even heavier.
We are both lost wanderers at the edge of heaven,
Why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and sick, dwelling in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year round, I hear not the sound of strings or pipes.
My home lies near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround the house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, and autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant noises are hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears clear momentarily.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I shall compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, which sounded more urgent.
The melancholy notes differed from those played before;
The whole audience listened again, covering their faces and weeping.
Who among the guests shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked wet."}

{"translation":"Ballad of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

Beyond the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is aboard his boat,
We raise our cups to drink, but lack strings and pipes.
Drunken mirth turns to gloom as parting draws near,
When we say goodbye, the vast river holds the moon submerged.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa sounds arise,
The host forgets to return; the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I quietly ask: who plays?
The pipa stops, the player wishes to speak, yet hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her sight,
Add wine, relight the lamps, and reopen the feast.
Amid countless calls and pleas, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks two or three strings,
Though no melody forms, emotion already fills the air.
Each string restrains, each note speaks longing,
Seeming to tell of a life thwarted by fate.
With lowered brow and free hand, she plays on continuously,
Voicing all the infinite affairs within her heart.
Her fingers lightly gather, slowly twist, then strum and pick,
First playing "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Strings"
Of the Great Tang.

The thick strings roar like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Roaring and whispering intermingle and blend,
Like pearls, large and small, falling onto a jade plate.
Birdsong slides fluently through blossoms below,
A spring chokes sullenly beneath ice, hard to flow.
Cold springs stagnate, the strings freeze and cease,
Ceasing without passage, the sound pauses briefly.
But hidden sorrow and dark resentment are born anew—
At this moment, silence surpasses sound itself.
Then silver vases burst with spraying water,
Iron cavalry charges, clanging blades and spears.
The song ends; she gathers the plectrum for a final stroke,
All four strings strike once, tearing silk in loud rending.
East boats and west barges fall silent, speechless,
Only seeing the moon-white heart of the river.
She contemplates deeply, inserts the plectrum among strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her demeanor.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home lay beneath Shrimp Hill (Xiama Ling).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first in the Imperial Conservatory.
After songs, even great masters admired me;
When made up, courtesans envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Tombs fought to offer red silk,
One song worth thousands of bolts unknown.
Gold-temple hairpins broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year again;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
Brother went off to war; aunt died;
Evenings came, mornings left, fading my beauty.
The door stands desolate, horsemen rare;
Getting old, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit, cares little for separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He leaves; here I watch an empty boat at the river mouth,
Bright moon circling the boat, cold river waters.
Late at night I suddenly dream of youthful days,
Wake crying, makeup tears running down my red cheeks.

Hearing the pipa, I have already sighed,
And hearing these words, sigh again deeply.
Both of us are drifted souls at the world's end;
Meeting now, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled to live sick in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music,
All year long I hear no silk-and-bamboo tunes.
Living near Penal River where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my home.
What do I hear there morning and evening?
Bleeding cuckoos cry; apes wail mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower-morning nights, autumn moonlight,
Often take wine alone to pour myself.
Are there not mountain songs and village pipes?
They groan and chatter, harsh to listen.
Tonight I hear your pipa language,
It sounds like celestial music; my ears clear momentarily.
Please don't refuse to sit and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this Ballad of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long while,
Then sat back quickly, tightening strings that played more urgently.

{"translation":"Song of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

On the banks of the Xunyang River at night, I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn breeze.
The host dismounted, while the guest remained on the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but had no music.
Though drunk, there was no joy, sorrowing over our parting;
At the moment of farewell, the vast river reflected the moon.
Suddenly, over the water, we heard the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, and the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa music stopped, as if the player wished to speak but hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out;
Refilled the wine, relit the lanterns, and reopened the feast.
After many calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa before her face, half hiding it.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the melody took form, emotion was already present.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing,
As if telling of a life of frustration.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless affairs within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and plucking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like private conversation.
Roaring and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath flowers, clear and flowing,
Choked and sobbing like springs trapped under ice.
As the cold spring froze and the strings stalled,
The silence lingered, unable to break through.
A hidden melancholy and silent resentment arose;
In that moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then suddenly, a silver vase burst, water splashing forth,
Iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clanging.
The song ended; she drew the plectric across the center of the strings;
All four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and west fell silent;
Only the white autumn moon shone on the heart of the river.
She pondered, placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shama Ling.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name belonging to the first department of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even skilled musicians admired her;
When dressed, every beauty felt envy.
The young men of Wuling vied to give her gifts,
For one song, red silk went uncounted.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red satin skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter continued,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died,
Day by day, her youth faded.
Her door grew cold, visitors rare;
Growing older, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant valued profit over separation,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He came and went, leaving me alone on the boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my youthful days,
Waking crying, makeup tears staining my face red.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply;
Hearing her words, I lamented again.
Both of us are wanderers fallen in the world;
Meeting now, why does it matter if we knew each other before?
I too, since last year, left the imperial capital,
Banished to live ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, no stringed instruments are heard.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear there morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing sadly.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh cacophony is painful to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa song,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit down and play another tune;
I will compose a poem, "Song of the Pipa," for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, plucking faster and more urgently.
The mournful sound unlike the previous performance;
Everyone in the room, hearing it again, covered their faces weeping.
Who among us shed the most tears?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe became wet."}

{"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted from my horse while he waited on his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, yet found no music there.
Drunkenness failed to bring joy before our bitter parting,
As we left, the vast river bathed the moon in its depths.
Suddenly, pipa notes drifted across the water;
I forgot to return home, and my guest halted his departure.
Following the sound, I whispered asking who was playing;
The pipa paused, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boats closer, inviting her to come out;
We added wine, trimmed the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she emerged,
Still holding her pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before the melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string’s restrained note carried deep thought,
Seeming to tell of talents wasted in life.
With lowered brows, she played casually and continuously,
Expressing the infinite sorrows within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and plucking,
First she played “Rainbow Skirts,” then “Six Strings.”
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Thunders and whispers intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdsong chirping smoothly beneath blossoms,
Buried sobs struggling through ice-bound springs.
When cold springs froze and strings choked off,
The silence held more meaning than any sound.
A silver bottle burst, water spraying forth;
Iron cavalry charged, swords clashing loud.
At the song’s end, she swept the plectrum across the center,
And all four strings sounded once, ripping silk apart.
Boats east and west fell silent, speechless;
Only the white autumn moon shone upon the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between strings,
Straightened her clothes and composed her face.
She said: “Originally I was a girl of the capital,
My home near Shama Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
And my name ranked first among the imperial musicians.
After performing, even great masters admired me;
When made up, every beauty envied me.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to give gifts;
For one tune, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Hairpins with gold inlays broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year brought laughter and joy,
While moonlit autumns and spring breezes passed idly away.
Then my brother went into the army, my aunt died;
Morning turned to evening, and my beauty faded.
The door grew lonely, horses rare;
In old age I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit above all else,
He had gone last month to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Deep in the night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
I woke crying, tears staining my makeup red."""
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I lamented again and again.
We are both fallen souls wandering the ends of the earth;
Given this meeting, why should it matter if we knew each other?
Since last year I bade farewell to the Imperial Capital,
Banished, sick at heart in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long I hear not the sound of strings or pipes.
Living near Pen River in low, damp land,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
In spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
I often take wine and pour it for myself alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their rough, grating sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight hearing your pipa’s voice,
It is like celestial music; my ears clear anew.
Do not refuse to sit and play another piece;
For you, I will compose the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down, tightening strings which played faster.
The melancholy did not resemble earlier sounds;
The whole audience listened again, covering faces in tears.
Who among those seated shed the most tears?
The Blue-Robed Prefect of Jiangzhou saw his sleeves wet."}

Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa!
The host forgets his return; the guest delays his departure.

We follow the sound, whispering queries: 'Who is playing?' The pipa halts, its player hesitates to speak.

We move our boat closer, inviting her to meet us; More wine is poured, lamps are turned up, and the banquet resumes.

Still holding the pipa before her face, half-concealed.

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings, two or three notes;

As if telling of a life where ambitions went unfulfilled.

Expressing all the endless things within her heart.

With gentle pinches, slow twists, strokes, then picks,
First "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Strings" she plays.

The thick strings rumble loudly like sudden rainstorms;
The thin strings murmur softly like private whispers.

Loud and soft sounds intermingle in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now clear as orioles singing beneath the flowers,
Now choked as springs flowing under ice, struggling.

Ice-cold springs stagnate; the strings seem to freeze solid;
Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceases.

But hidden sorrows and dark resentments arise anew;
At this moment, silence surpasses even sound.

Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting and water spurting out,
Or armored cavalry charging forth, swords and spears clashing loud.

When the tune ends, she draws her plectrum across the center;
One final stroke of four strings, like tearing silk cloth.

East boats and west barges fall silently quiet;
Only the mid-river autumn moon shines pale.

Pausing thoughtfully, she puts her plectrum back between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her face.

She says herself: 'I was originally a girl of the capital,
My home lived by the hill known as Shrimp Frog Ridge.'

My name entered the first tier of the Imperial Music Bureau.

After finishing a piece, even skilled musicians bowed to me;
Once made up, every beauty grew envious of my looks.

Young men of Five Tombs competed to offer gifts of brocade;
For one song, red silk received could not be counted.

Gold-inlaid hairpins broke while keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.

Year after year of laughter repeated itself;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.

My brother joined the army; my aunt died;
Days pass, nights come, and my beauty fades.

Before my door, visitors have grown sparse, horses few;
Growing old, I married into a merchant's family.

Merchants value profit more than farewells;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left; here at the river mouth, I guard an empty boat;
Around it, bright moonlight, cold river waters flow.

Crying in dreams, tears stain my makeup, running down like railings.

{"translation":"At the mouth of the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; his friend remained aboard the ship;
We raised our wine cups to drink, but had no music to fill the air.
Drunk, yet joyless, we faced the bitter parting,
When we parted, the vast river soaked the moon's reflection.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa,
So that the host forgot to return home, and the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who played it;
The pipa’s notes ceased, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer and invited her out,
Refilled our wine, and turned up the lamps to reopen the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She twisted the pegs and plucked a string or two,
Before any melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each chord sighed with suppressed longing, each note full of thought,
As if recounting a life spent frustrated and unfulfilled.
Head lowered, she played confidently and continuously,
Pouring out every endless matter of her heart.
With light gatherings, slow twists, strokes, and picks,
She began with "Rainbow Robe," then followed with "Six Melodies."
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering intertwined as she played,
Like large pearls and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Chattering birds sang smoothly among the blossoms,
Then sobbed like a spring struggling beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seemed to freeze and stop,
Stopped and blocked, the sound paused for a moment.
But hidden sorrows and secret resentments were born there,
Where silence spoke more powerfully than sound ever could.
Then, suddenly, a silver vase burst, and water splashed forth,
Iron cavalry charged, with swords clashing and spears ringing.
The tune ended; she gathered the plectrum to strike four strings at once,
And they cracked like tearing silk.
The boats to the east and west fell into silent awe,
Only seeing the moon pale white upon the river’s heart.
Lost in deep thought, she put away the plectrum beside the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Her home near Shama Hill.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name belonging to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
After finishing a tune, even masters admired her skill,
Upon completing her makeup, the courtesans often envied her beauty.
The young men of the Five Tombs competed to gift her with silks,
For a single song, countless bolts of red gauze were thrown to her.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs shattered as they beat time on tables,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Through laughter this year and next,
They passed the autumn moons and spring breezes idly away.
But her brother joined the army, and her aunt died,
Days passed, and her beauty faded with them.
Her door stood cold, few carriages came,
Older now, she married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all, caring little for farewells;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and here I stay, guarding an empty boat at the river’s mouth,
The moonlight circles the vessel, making the river water seem cold.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of things in my youth,
Waking weeping, tears through my rouge ran down.
Hearing her pipa, I long since had sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief grew deeper still.
We are both wanderers fallen low beneath heaven’s edge;
Why need we have known each other before meeting here?
Since last year I bade the Imperial City farewell,
Exiled and sick, I lie in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year round, I hear no stringed wind-instruments’ sound.
My dwelling lies near Peng River, low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing around my house.
Morning and evening, what do I hear here?
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing in sorrow.
On spring nights by flower-filled rivers, under autumn moons,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there truly no folk songs or village flutes?
Their harsh jargon is too grating to listen to.
Tonight I heard your pipa language,
Like celestial music, briefly clearing my ears.
Please do not refuse; sit again and play one more piece,
For you, I shall rewrite the Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to her seat and tightened the strings, playing faster.
Mournful sounds unlike those before filled the air,
The whole audience listened anew, covering their faces in tears.
Who wept most among them?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe grew wet."}

{"translation":"Song of the Pipa
by Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a friend;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn wind.
The host dismounts; the guest is already on his boat,
We raise our cups but lack the strings and pipes to play.
Though drunk, joy fails us as parting draws near;
In that moment, the moon dips into the boundless river.
Suddenly, over the water, we hear pipa music rise;
The host forgets to return; the guest delays his start.
Following the sound, I ask who plays it in the dark;
The pipa pauses, hesitant, before speaking.
I move my close to invite the player out,
Add wine, relight the lamp, and begin the feast anew.
After many calls and pleas, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks two or three strings,
Before the melody forms, emotion flows first.
Each string suppresses, each note carries sorrow,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
With lowered brows, she plays freely, note after note,
Expressing all the endless affairs of the heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, brushing then picking,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Melodies" are played.
The thick strings roar like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, mixed together they sound
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Clear and flowing, like birdsong beneath flowers;
Choked and sobbing, like spring water under ice.
When the cold ice blocks the flow, the strings break off;
When blocked and stopped, the sound momentarily ceases.
Secret grief and hidden hatred arise within;
This silence speaks louder than sound ever could.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting with water,
Or iron cavalry charging with clashing swords.
The song ends; she sweeps the plectrum across the middle,
And all four strings snap once, like tearing silk.
East and west boats fall silent, no one speaks;
Only the white autumn moon shines upon the river.
Lost in thought, she puts down the plectrum between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
Living below Xiama Ling (Toad Hill).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked among the top troupe at the Music Bureau.
After playing, even the best masters bowed to me;
When dressed up, every beauty envied my grace.
The young men of Wuling fought to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless red gauze scarves.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy;
I took for granted the autumn moon and spring breeze.
But when my brother joined the army and my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded.
The gate became desolate, horse and carriage rare;
Growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit and treats partings lightly;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left me here guarding an empty boat at the river mouth;
The bright moon surrounds the boat, the river waters cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days;
I weep in my dreams, makeup running wet down my cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply already;
Hearing these words, I sigh again in distress.
Both of us are wanderers sunk at the edge of the world;
Why need we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished and lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, I hear no strings or pipes.
Living near the Pen River, where the land is low and wet,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there morning and evening?
杜鹃 crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring rivers with flowers, on autumn moons' nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
They are harsh and noisy, unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, which sounded urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous tunes;
Everyone present listened again and covered their faces, weeping.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Blue-robed Sima of Jiangzhou had his robe soaked."}

{"translation":"At the head of Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts his horse, while the guest waits in the boat;
We raise our wine cups to drink, but there are no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we face the sorrowful parting,
As we leave, the vast river is bathed in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa,
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, we ask softly who is playing;
The pipa music stops, hesitant, as if about to speak.
We move our boats closer and invite her to join us,
Add more wine, bring back the lanterns, and restart the feast.
After calling out many times, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times,
Before the melody forms, emotion is already present.
Each string suppresses its note, every sound carries longing,
As if telling of a lifetime unfulfilled.
With lowered brows, she plays freely and continuously,
Expressing all the endless matters within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing, then picking again—
First "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumble loudly like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper softly like private talk.
Loud rumbles and soft whispers intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Melodious like orioles singing beneath flowers, smooth and flowing,
Choked and sobbing like spring water struggling under ice.
The icy spring grows cold and stiff; the strings seem to break off,
Broken off and blocked, the sound pauses for a moment.
Then arise hidden sorrows and deep-seated resentments;
In this silence, sound is surpassed by quietness.
Suddenly, as if a silver vase bursts open, water spurts forth;
As if armored cavalry charge, swords and spears clash and ring.
When the piece ends, she draws the pick carefully across the strings,
One sharp snap from the four strings sounds like tearing silk.
Boats on the east and west fall silent,
Only the white autumn moon shines upon the center of the river.
Lost in thought, she places the pick among the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, straightens up, and composes her expression.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even skilled masters admired her,
And when made up, other beauties envied her.
Young men of power vied to give her gifts,
For one song, she received countless bolts of red silk.
Hairpins adorned with diamonds and silver combs were broken keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy passed,
Autumn moons and spring breezes idly spent.
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died,
Day after day, her beauty faded.
The door became desolate, visitors rare,
So she grew old and married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit above love and separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving and returning, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth,
The moonlight encircling the boat, the river water cold.
Late at night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days,
Wakes crying, makeup streaked with red tears.
I heard the pipa and sighed heavily,
Hearing her story, I moan again deeply.
Both of us are people adrift far from home,
Meeting now, does it matter that we knew each other before?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Relegated to illness in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long, no strings or flutes are heard.
My dwelling is near Pen River, low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
The blood-crying cuckoo and mournful gibbons.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, and autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine alone and pour it down my throat.
Are there not mountain songs and village pipes?
Crackling and jarring, they are hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing you play the pipa,
It is like listening to fairy music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece;
For you, I will write the "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits back down, tightens the strings, playing faster.
The melody becomes sorrowful, unlike the previous tunes,
The full audience hears it again and covers their faces weeping.
Who among them sheds the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is wet."}

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}
</原诗>

{
"translation": "Song of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

At night, by the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; the guest was aboard his boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but lacked music’s sweet sound.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced a sad parting;
When we said farewell, vast was the river, moonlight submerged.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of pipa strings;
The host forgot to return home, the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked quietly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, the player hesitating to speak.
I moved my boat close to invite her out,
Added wine, turned up the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After countless calls, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked three or four notes,
Before a melody formed, emotion already poured forth.
Each string suppressed, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely one after another,
Singing out all the boundless troubles of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Garments,” then the “Six Strings.”
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private murmurs.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in play,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath flowers,
Choked and sobbing as spring water froze underground.
Ice-cold water, stiffened strings, sound cut off abruptly,
Blocked and silent, the music paused for a moment.
Yet hidden sorrows and secret resentments arose,
In that silence, more than any voice could say.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking, water bursting forth,
Or armored cavalry charging, swords clashing loudly.
The song ended; she drew the plectrum across the center,
A sharp snap of the four strings, like tearing silk.
To the east boats and west ships stood silent, no word spoken,
Only seeing the autumn moon bright on the river’s heart.
She pondered a while, tucked the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose with a composed dignity.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My home near Shrimp Hill, under its foot."
"At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name belonged to the top tier of the Imperial Music Bureau."
"After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire me,
When dressed up, often envied by beautiful courtesans."
"Young men of the Five Tombs vied to give gifts,
One song earned bolts of red silk beyond counting."
"Jeweled hairpins broken keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine."
"This year laughing, next year still joking,
Casually passing through autumn moons and spring breezes."
"My brother went to war, my aunt died,
Evenings passed, mornings came, my beauty faded."
"Cold and deserted before my door, few carriages remained,
So when older, I married a merchant’s wife."
"Merchants value profit, disregard separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea."
"He left; here at the river mouth I guard an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, cold river waters."
"Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
Waking, tears flowing down my painted face, staining it crimson." 
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
And hearing these words, I sighed deeply again.
"Both of us are people adrift in the edge of heaven,
Meeting now—what need is there for having known each other before?"
"I myself, since last year, left the imperial capital,
Demoted, sick, lying low in Xunyang City."
"Xunyang is remote, without local music,
All year round, never hearing the sound of strings and flutes."
"Living near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house."
"What do I hear morning and evening there?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing sadly."

Often take wine, pouring alone for myself."

Hoarse and discordant, painful to listen to."

It is like listening to immortal music; my ears clear for a moment."
"Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I will rewrite this 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Then sat down again, plucking hurriedly, the strings growing faster.
Mournful sounds unlike those before,
The whole assembly heard again, all hiding their tears.
