message.content: {"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest at night; Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill of autumn. The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard; We raised our wine cups to drink, but there was no music, no sound of pipes or strings. Drunk yet unable to find joy, we faced the sorrow of parting; At the moment of farewell, the vast river lay submerged in moonlight. Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa; The host forgot to return home, and the guest delayed his departure. Following the sound, I asked discreetly who was playing; The pipa stopped, and she seemed hesitant to speak. I moved my boat close to invite her to meet us; We added more wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the banquet. After being called upon time and again, she finally emerged, Still holding her pipa to partly cover her face. She turned the pegs and plucked a few preliminary notes; Before the melody even formed, emotion was already present. Each string was suppressed, each note full of thought, As if telling of a life's unfulfilled ambitions. With lowered brows, she played on continuously, Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart. Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing then picking, First playing 'Rainbow Garments', then followed by 'Six Eves'. The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain; The thin strings whispered like private murmurs. Rumbling and whispering intermingled in complex play, Like large and small pearls falling onto jade plates. Birdsong slid smoothly beneath blossoms; A spring choked and sobbed as it struggled under ice. The cold, sluggish stream froze the strings into stillness; In this frozen blockage, the sound momentarily ceased. Hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose anew; In this silence, the quiet spoke louder than any sound. Then suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting open, water splashed out; Like iron cavalry charging forth, swords and spears clanged together. As the piece ended, she drew the plectrum across the center; One sharp stroke from four strings sounded like silk tearing. East boats and west barges fell silent without a word; All that was seen was the white autumn moon reflecting in the river's heart. She paused, placed the plectrum back among the strings, Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her expression. She said: \"I was originally a girl from the capital, Living near Shrimp Mound in the city.\" \"At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, And was listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau's finest.\" \"After finishing a tune, even master players would admire me; When fully made up, every courtesan envied my beauty.\" \"Young men of the Five Tombs vied to offer me gifts; For one song, countless pieces of red silk were tossed my way.\" \"Jeweled combs broke keeping time with the beat; Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.\" \"One year of laughter after another, Autumn moons and spring breezes passed in idle days.\" \"My brother joined the army, my aunt died; Evening went and morning came, my looks faded.\" \"The door before me grew cold, fewer horses came; Getting old, I married a merchant's wife.\" \"Merchants value profit above love, they do not mind separation; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.\" \"When he returns, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth; Moonlight surrounds the boat, the river waters are cold.\" \"Deep in the night, I often dream of my youth; Waking weeping, tears stain through my makeup, running red down my face.\" \"Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply; Hearing these words, I sighed again and again.\" \"We are both people adrift far from home; Since we meet now, why does it matter if we knew each other before!\" \"Since last year, I left the imperial capital, Banished here to lie ill in Xunyang City.\" \"Xunyang is remote, lacking music; Year-round, no sound of silk and bamboo is heard.\" \"Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp; Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.\" \"What do I hear here, morning and evening? Cuckoos crying blood and gibbons wailing in grief.\" \"Even on spring rivers, flower mornings, and autumn moon nights, Often I take wine and pour it alone.\" \"Are there no mountain songs and village flutes? They are harsh and noisy, unbearable to listen to.\" \"Tonight hearing your pipa language, It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are temporarily cleared.\" \"Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune; For you, I will compose a 'Song of the Pipa'.\" \"Moved by my words, she stood for a long while; Then sat back down and tightened the strings, playing faster.\" \"Sorrowful sounds, unlike those before; Everyone in the room listened again and covered their faces weeping.\" \"Who among them shed the most tears? The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked wet.\""}

The host dismounted while his guest waited on the boat; We raised our cups to drink but had no pipes or strings to play. Though drunk, joy was incomplete, sorrow looming before parting; At the moment of farewell, the vast river bathed the moon. Suddenly, from across the water, came the sound of a pipa; The host forgot to return, and the guest delayed departure. Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing; The pipa music paused, hesitant as if about to speak. I moved my boat closer, invited her to see us; More wine was poured, lamps turned up, and the banquet resumed. Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing then picking, First she played “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six Strings.” The great strings rumbled like sudden rain, The small strings whispered like secret talk. Rumbling and whispering intertwined in complex play, Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate. Sweet and clear as orioles singing beneath blossoms, Muffled and choked as springs flowing under ice. Cold and stagnant, the strings seemed to freeze, Frozen and blocked, the sound briefly ceased. Yet hidden sorrows and secret resentments arose— In that silence, there spoke more than any sound. Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, Water splashed forth; Like iron cavalry charging out, swords clash and spears ring. When the song ended, she swept the plectrum across the center, All four strings sounded once, like tearing silk. East boats and west ships fell silent, No one spoke; Only the white autumn moon reflected in the heart of the river. She pondered for a moment, inserted the plectrum into the strings, Straightened her clothes, stood up, composed her expression. She said she was originally a girl from the capital city, Her home located down by Shrimp Frog Hill. At thirteen, she mastered the pipa, Her name ranked first among those trained in the Imperial Music Bureau. After finishing a tune, even skilled masters would admire; Once made up, even famous courtesans felt envy. Young men from the Five Tombs competed to give her gifts, For one song, red silk scrolls amounted to countless pieces. Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs snapped against the beat, Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine. This year’s laughter followed next year’s, Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually. Her brother went to join the army, her aunt died; Days and nights passed, and her beauty faded. Few horses remained before her door, lonely and neglected; Growing old, she married a merchant as his wife. Merchants value profit lightly regarding separation; Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea. He goes and comes, leaving her alone guarding an empty boat at the river mouth; Moonlight circles the vessel, the river water cold. Deep in the night, she suddenly dreamed of youthful days, Waking weeping, makeup tears staining her face red. Hearing her pipa, I already sighed; Hearing these words, I lamented anew. How bear this lonely lodging, shut in springtime cold,
The setting sun, the cuckoo calling into dusk?
Plum blossoms sent by post, silk letters borne by fish,

message.content:
{"translation":"At the Xunyang River head at night I saw a guest off;
Maple leaves and reed flowers sighed in the autumn chill.
My horse had been dismounted, but the guest remained on his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, yet there was no music to hear.
The wine brought no joy; we parted in gloom,
As moonlight shimmered upon the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
I forgot my return, and my guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked softly who played it;
The pipa stopped, and she seemed hesitant to speak.
We moved our boats closer to invite her forth;
We added more wine and relit the lamp to restart the banquet.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before forming any melody, emotion already flowed.
Each string’s suppressed tone carried deep thought,
Seeming to tell of a life thwarted in its ambitions.
With lowered brows and casual hand, she played on,
Expressing all the infinite sorrow within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sliding then picking—
First playing “The Rainbow Feather Garment,” then “Six Strings.”
The thick strings rumbled loudly like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered low like private conversation.
The loud and soft intertwined as she played;
Large pearls and small pearls fell onto a jade plate.
Smooth as an oriole’s song beneath blossoms;
Choked as spring water under ice, hard to flow.
Cold and stagnant, the strings froze and ceased;
Stopped and blocked, the sound temporarily vanished.
Then arose hidden grief and secret resentment—
This silence surpassed even the previous sound.
Like a silver vase bursting with water gushing out,
Or armored cavalry charging with clashing swords.
The piece ended; she struck the center of the strings once;
All four chords rang together like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fell silent, no word spoken,
Only the white autumn moon seen on the river’s heart.
She paused, placed the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl of the capital,
Living by Shama Hill."
"At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name was listed first in the Teaching Bureau."
"After playing a tune, masters admired me;
Upon finishing makeup, other beauties envied me."
"Young men of the Five Tombs competed for my favors;
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given."
"Jeweled hairpins broke beating time;
Red skirts stained by spilled wine."
"Year after year passed in laughter and joy;
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent idly."
"My brother joined the army; my aunt died;
Time passed, and my beauty faded."
"My door grew cold, few horses came;
Aged, I married a merchant’s wife."
"Merchants value profit over parting sorrows;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea."
"He left me watching empty ships at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water."
"Late at night, I dreamed again of youthful days,
Crying in dreams, tears staining my rouged cheeks.""Listening to her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words, I sighed again deeply."
"We are both fallen souls wandering the ends of the earth;
Why must we have known each other before meeting?"
"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled, sick, lying in Xunyang City."
"Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long I heard no wind or string instruments."
"Near the Pen River, my home sits low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo."
"What do I hear morning and evening?"
"Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing sadly."
"On spring nights under flower moons,"
"I often take wine and drink alone."
"Are there mountain songs and village flutes here?"
"But their harsh noises are unbearable to listen to."
"Tonight hearing your pipa speech,"
"It is like celestial music enlightening my ears."
"Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;"
"For you, I will write this Song of the Pipa.""
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, playing faster."
"Her mournful tones differed from those before;"
"Everyone present listened again, covering faces in tears."
"Who among us shed the most tears?"
"The Sima of Jiangzhou, his green robe soaked through.""}

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}
</原诗>

{"translation":"By night I saw off a guest on the Yangtze of Xunyang, where maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted while my guest remained aboard his boat; we raised our cups to drink but lacked music for our wine.
Though drunk, joy eluded us as sorrow loomed before parting; at departure, vast waters were steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa. I forgot to return home, and he delayed his sailing.
Following the notes, I quietly asked who played; the music ceased, yet hesitation kept her speech slow.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to join us; more wine was poured, lamps trimmed, and the banquet reopened.
After thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties she finally emerged, still holding her pipa half-hidden before her face.
She turned the tuning pegs and plucked the strings two or three times; before a melody took shape, emotion already filled the air.
Each string seemed to sigh, each note tinged with melancholy, as if telling of a life thwarted by misfortune.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving freely, she continued playing, pouring out all the boundless events within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking; first she played "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings thundered loudly like sudden rain; the thin strings whispered softly like private murmurs.
The loud and soft sounds intermingled in complex play, like pearls large and small falling into a jade plate.
Now smooth as an oriole's song beneath blossoms, now choked like a spring flowing under ice.
As icy springs grew cold and sluggish, the strings froze and stopped; when they could not pass through, sound briefly paused.
In that silence, hidden sorrows and unspoken resentments arose; at this moment, no sound surpassed the power of sound.
Then, abruptly, like a silver vase bursting, water surged forth; like iron cavalry charging, swords clashed and spears rang.
At the tune's end, she drew her plectrum across the center strings; all four chords sounded once, sharp as tearing silk.
Boats east and west fell silent, utterly voiceless; only the white autumn moon shone upon the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she set aside her plectrum between the strings, straightened her clothes, and rose with composed dignity.
She declared herself originally a girl from the capital, living near the Shrimp Hill district.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa and was ranked among the finest in the Imperial Music Bureau.
Her performances earned the praise of master musicians; her beauty provoked envy even among renowned courtesans.
Young nobles from Five Tombs competed to offer gifts; one piece of music brought countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled headpieces and silver combs shattered keeping rhythm; blood-red skirts became stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter passed, spending autumn moons and spring breezes casually.
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died; time wore on, fading her beauty.
Before her door visitors dwindled, horsemen scarce; growing old, she married a merchant wife.
Merchants value profit above farewell; last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
Leaving behind, she guards an empty ship at the river mouth, surrounded by bright moonlight and cold waters.
Deep in the night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days, she wakes crying, tears staining her makeup red.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed; hearing these words, I groaned again deeply.
Both are wanderers fallen far from home; meeting now, why need we have known each other before?
Since leaving the imperial capital last year, I have been exiled and bedridden with illness in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote and devoid of music; all year long, I hear no string or wind instruments.
Living near the Pen River where land lies low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening? Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, and autumn nights, often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there none mountain songs or village flutes? Their hoarse, discordant sounds are hard to bear listening to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language, it is as if listening to celestial music, ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece; for you, I shall compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while, then returned to her seat and tightened the strings, which now sounded urgent.
Mournful tones unlike those before; everyone present heard anew and covered their faces weeping.
Who shed the most tears among us? The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked."}

message.content:
{"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid a friend farewell one night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest sat aboard his boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but lacked the strains of music.
Though tipsy, joy was absent as we parted in sorrow,
And at parting, the vast river held only the moon's reflection.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa,
Making the host forget to return home, and the guest delay departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa ceased, and she hesitated, reluctant to speak.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to join us,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-concealing her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the melody formed, emotion already spoke through them.
Each string sighed with suppressed longing,
As if telling of a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition.
Eyes downcast, she played on without pause,
Voicing all the endless matters within her heart.
With light touches, slow twists, sweeps, and flicks,
She began with 'Rainbow Garment' and ended with 'Six Flutes'.
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private murmurs.
Thick and thin intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Now smooth as orioles singing among flowers,
Now choked like spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold and stiff, the strings froze into silence,
Blocked and still, the sound briefly ceased.
Then arose new hidden sorrows and unspoken resentments,
This moment of silence surpassed any sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly bursting, water spraying forth,
Like armored cavalry charging out, swords clashing.
At the song’s end, she drew her plectrum across the center,
And one final sweep on four strings sounded like tearing silk.
East and west boats fell silent, no word was spoken,
Only the white autumn moon hung above the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between strings,
Straightened her clothes and rose with composed dignity.
She said she had originally been a girl of the capital,
Living near Prawn Mound Terrace.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name registered in the first troupe of the Imperial Music Bureau.
Her performances impressed even skilled masters,
Her beauty provoked envy from courtesans.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to offer gifts,
For one piece of red silk paid, they knew not how many times.
Hairpins and combs broke keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent casually.
Brothers went off to army service, aunties died,
Days turned to nights, and her looks faded.
Her doorway grew cold, visitors rare,
Aging, she married a merchant for security.
He valued profit over companionship,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving her alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Encircled by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
Waking in tears that reddened her makeup.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Hearing her words, I lamented anew.
We are both wanderers cast adrift at heaven’s edge,
Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year when I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and sick, I lay in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, no sound of strings or pipes reaches here.
My dwelling lies low and wet near the Pen River,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Cuckoos crying blood and gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring rivers amid blossoms, on autumn nights under moon,
I often take my cup and pour wine alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, harsh notes are unbearable to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa play,
It is like listening to celestial music, my ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune,
For you, I shall compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat and tightened the strings, which now sounded urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous melodies,
The whole audience listened again, wiping away tears.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou was soaked with weeping."}

message.content:
{"translation":"By the Xunyang River, I saw a guest off at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; the guest was on his boat.
We raised our wine to drink but had no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we parted bitterly,
While moonlight blended with the vast river.
Suddenly, from over the water, pipas sounded,
Making the host forget home and delaying the guest's departure.
Following the sound, I asked who played; the music paused, as if she wished to speak but hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Added more wine, relit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After calling many times, she finally came,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings,
And before the tune formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note carried thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Head lowered, fingers moving casually, she played on,
Saying all that lay hidden deep within.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Beats."
The thick strings clattered like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Clattering and whispering mingled in play,
Like large and small pearls bouncing onto a jade plate.
Clear bird-song slid through flowers below;
Under ice, springs choked, flowing with difficulty.
Cold, stiff, the strings seemed frozen and cut off;
Cut off, blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.
Then arose new secret sorrow, hidden resentment—
At this moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
A silver vase burst, water splashing forth!
Iron cavalry charged, swords and spears ringing!
When the song ended, the plectrum swept across the center,
All four strings rang once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fell silent, none speaking;
Only the white moon in the river center remained visible.
Pondering, she put down the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, composing her face.
"I myself," she said, "was originally a girl from the capital;
My home was near Shrimp Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name listed first among the Imperial Conservatory players.
After finishing a piece, even great musicians admired me;
When made up, every beauty grew jealous.
The young men of Five Tombs competed to give gifts;
For one song, red silk could not be counted.
Gold-adorned combs shattered keeping time;
Blood-colored skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter continued;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Days and nights wore on, fading my youth's color.
Before my door, loneliness settled; horses and carriages dwindled.
Growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit, lightly regarding parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I've waited alone by the river mouth in an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
I wept in sleep, tears ruining my painted face.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I groaned again.
Both of us are lost wanderers under heaven—
Meeting now, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted, sick, lying low in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year round, I hear not the sound of silk and bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp,
Around my house grow yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Poorly tuned, harsh sounds, hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa melodies,
It feels like listening to fairy music, making my ears clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Melancholy unlike the previous sound,
The whole audience listened again and hid their tears.
Who in the room shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou was wet."}

曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。

{"translation":"Ballad of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill autumn air.
The host dismounted; the guest remained on his boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to hear.
Drunkenness brought no joy; sorrow filled our parting,
At departure, only a vast moon hung over the river’s immersion.
Suddenly, from across the water, came the sound of pipa strings;
The host forgot to return home, and the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the sound, we asked quietly who might be playing,
But the pipa music stopped, as if hesitant to speak.
We moved our boats closer together and invited them to meet us,
Poured more wine and lit the lamps again to resume the feast.
After countless calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few preliminary notes,
Before the melody formed, emotion had already arisen.
Each string muffled, each note laden with thought,
As if telling of a lifetime of thwarted ambitions.
With lowered brow, she played casually yet continuously,
Expressing all the boundless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then later "Six Measures."
The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private confessions.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Sliding smoothly like orioles singing amidst flowers,
Then choked and sobbing like spring water struggling under ice.
The icy springs grew cold and sluggish, strings froze into silence,
In that frozen stillness, blocked pathways, sound momentarily ceased.
Yet another hidden grief and secret resentment arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed speech.
Then suddenly, as if a silver vase burst, splashing forth its contents,
Or iron cavalry charging out, blades clashing with spears.
When the song ended, she swept her pick across the center,
And one final chord from four strings sounded like tearing silk.
Ships to the east and west fell silent without word,
Only seeing the white autumn moon glowing on the river’s heart.
Pausing in deep thought, she placed her pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and stood up with composed countenance.
She said herself she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Her home located near Xiama Ling.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first among the Imperial Conservatory’s finest.
After finishing songs, even renowned masters admired her skill,
After adorning herself, she often aroused the envy of courtesans.
Young nobles from the Five Tombs competed to give her gifts,
For one song, she received red silk bolts too numerous to count.
Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.
Laughter and joy through this year and next,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly away.
Her brother went off to war, her aunt died,
Days and nights passed, and her beauty faded.
The door before her faced desolation, carriages and horses rare,
Growing older, she married a merchant for wife.
The merchant valued profit lightly regarding separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving and returning, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth,
Around the boat shines bright moonlight, the river water is cold.
Late at night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days,
Waking crying, makeup tears stain her red cheeks dry.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply,
Hearing these words, I again murmured complaints.
Both of us are wanderers fallen low beneath heaven's edge,
Since meeting here, why must we have known each other before?
I left the imperial capital since last year,
Banished and bedridden ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote and barren, devoid of music,
All year long, not heard any string or wind instrument sounds.
Living near Penjiang where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my dwelling.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries and gibbons wailing mournfully.
Spring river, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often taking wine alone to pour myself.
Are there no mountain songs or village flute melodies?
Ugly noises harsh to listen to indeed.
Tonight hearing your pipa language,
It is as if hearing celestial music, ears temporarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit further; play another tune,
For you, I will compose anew: Ballad of the Pipa.
Touched by my words, she stood long in contemplation,
Returned to seat, tightened strings which turned urgent again.
Sorrowful tones unlike those played before,
The entire audience heard anew and covered faces weeping.
Who in the assembly shed most tears?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is wet."}

{"translation":"At dusk by the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest; maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn's cold.
I dismounted, my guest sat aboard the boat; we raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Though drunk, joy eluded us as parting drew near; at farewell, vast mist veiled the moon reflecting on the river.
Suddenly, over the water, came the sound of a pipa; forgetting home, I lingered; my guest delayed departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who played. The pipa paused, hesitant to speak.
We moved our boats close and invited her out; wine was refilled, lamps trimmed, and the banquet resumed.
After countless calls, she finally emerged, yet still held the pipa before half her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings; before forming any melody, feeling already filled the air.
Each string mournful, every note laden with thought, seeming to tell of lifelong disappointments.
Head bowed, fingers moving naturally, she poured forth endless inner sorrows.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, strumming then picking again, first playing 'Rainbow Garment', then 'Six Strings'.
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain; the fine ones whispered like private talk.
Thick and thin intertwined, mixed melodies played—large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Sweet trilling like orioles gliding under blossoms; choked sobs like springs struggling under ice.
Ice-cold spring sluggish, strings frozen silent; blocked and unpassable, sound briefly ceased.
Then hidden grief and secret resentment arose; this silence spoke louder than words.
As if a silver vase burst, water surging forth; as if armored cavalry charged, swords clashing.
When the song ended, she swept the plectrum across the center; all four strings rang once, like silk tearing.
Boats east and west fell utterly silent; only the white autumn moon shone upon the heart of the river.
Pondering deeply, she set down the plectrum among the strings, straightened her dress, composed her countenance.
She said herself: "I was originally a girl from the capital; my home lay below Xia Ma Ling.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa; my name ranked first among the imperial music school.
After finishing a tune, even masters admired me; when made up, beauty rivals envied me.
Young men from Five Tombs vied to offer gifts; for one song, red silk bolts beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time; crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year laughter continued; autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
My brother went to war, my aunt died; days and nights wore away my youth.
Before my door, desolate now, horses rare; aged, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit, neglects separation; last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Left and right, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth; moonlight circles the vessel, river waters chill.
Deep in night, suddenly dreaming of boyhood affairs; waking tears wet my painted cheeks, streaming red.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed; hearing these words, I grieved anew.
Both of us drifted souls far from home; meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since leaving the imperial capital last year, I’ve been demoted, sickly, lodged in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music; all year long no strings or flutes are heard.
Living near the Pen River, land low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here? Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings, flower-filled dawns, autumn moonlit nights, I often take wine alone to drink.
Are there no folk songs and village whistles? They are harsh, discordant, difficult to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language, it feels like celestial music; my ears momentarily clear.
Please, sit again and play another piece; I will compose for you this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood a long while, then returned to her seat, tightening strings that grew urgent.
Melancholy tones unlike those before; everyone seated listened again, covering faces in tears.
Who shed most tears in the hall? The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

{
  "translation": "Title: Song of the Pipa
Author: Bai Juyi

By night I see off a friend on the Xunyang River shore,
Maple leaves and reeds rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is already aboard;
We raise our cups, yet there are no flutes or strings to cheer.
Drunkenness brings no joy as we face a sorrowful parting,
The river vast and moonlit at the moment of farewell.
Suddenly, from the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the music, I ask softly who plays.
The pipa stops, as if wanting to speak but hesitating.
I move my boat closer and invite her to come forth;
Fresh wine is poured, lamps turned up, the feast resumed.
Though called upon thousands of times, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half concealing her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before a tune forms, emotion is already present.
Each string suppressed, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Head bowed, fingers moving with ease, she continues playing,
Expressing all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly pinching, slowly twisting, brushing and picking again,
First playing 'Rainbow Skirt', then 'Six Strings'.
Thick strings boom like sudden rain, thin ones whisper like secret talk.
Boom and whisper interweave in complex play,
Like pearls large and small falling into a jade plate.
Birdsong trills smoothly beneath flowers, stream sobbs hard under ice.
Ice-cold spring slows the strings, sound seems to cease.
Ceasing, blocked, the music pauses for a moment.
New hidden sorrow and dark resentment arise;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Like a silver vase bursting, water spurts out;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clash and ring.
The piece ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
One final sound from four strings, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent, no words remain;
Only the white autumn moon shines over the river's heart.
In deep thought, she places the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and assumes a composed look.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Xiama Ling (Toad Hill).
By thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed in the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When her songs ended, even skilled masters admired her craft;
After makeup, courtesans envied her beauty.
Young nobles from Five Tombs competed to offer gifts;
For one song, red gauze rolls numbered beyond measure.
Gold-inlaid combs shattered keeping the rhythm;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy passed casually,
With autumn moons and spring breezes taken for granted.
Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died,
And day by day, morning by evening, her looks faded.
Lonely before her gate, horsemen few;
Aging, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit over love, caring little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, cold river waters.
Late at night she suddenly dreams of her youth,
Wakes crying, tears staining her rouge down her cheeks.
I heard the pipa and sighed already;
Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.
Both are wanderers fallen from grace in a far-off land;
What need to have known each other before meeting?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and ill, lying low in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year round, not a string or bamboo sound is heard.
Living near Pen River, the land is low and wet;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, gibbons wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, difficult to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech is like hearing celestial music;
My ears clear temporarily.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time;
Then sat back and played faster, strings urgent.
The melancholy differed from earlier sounds;
The whole audience listened again, wiping away tears.
Who in the seat shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Sima (Prefectural Secretary) of Jiangzhou is wet."
}

{"translation":"On a night by the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to my guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on the boat—
We raise our cups for wine, but there are no strings or pipes.
Drunkenness fails to bring joy; sorrow looms at parting,
And as we say goodbye, the vast river soaks the moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa,
Making the host forget his return and the guest delay his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa stops, and the player hesitates to speak.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Refill the wine, turn up the lamps, and resume the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand pleas, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa before half her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few strings;
Before a melody forms, emotion is already there.
Each string is suppressed, each note laden with thought,
As if lamenting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition.
Head lowered, she plays continuously with casual ease,
Voicing all the infinite matters within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First playing the 'Rainbow Garment,' then the 'Six Melodies.'
The thick strings rumble like urgent rain,
The thin strings whisper like secret confidences.
Rumbling and whispering mixed together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Cooing like an oriole gliding under flowers,
Muffled like a spring flowing beneath ice.
Cold, stagnant, the strings freeze and stop,
Blocked and unable to pass, the sound briefly ceases.
A hidden sorrow and dark resentment arise;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
As if a silver bottle suddenly bursts, splashing water,
Or iron cavalry charging forth, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends; she sweeps the pick across the center,
And four strings strike once, tearing like silk.
East boats and west barges fall silent without word,
Only seeing the white autumn moon in the middle of the river.
Pausing in contemplation, she inserts the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her expression.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living under the Shrimp Mound. At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed in the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When she finished a tune, even skilled masters were impressed;
Once made up, she often drew envy from beauty queens.
Young men of the Five Mausoleums competed to give her gifts;
One song would earn her countless rolls of red silk.
Hairpins with jeweled heads broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy repeated,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Then her brother went off to join the army, her aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and her youthful looks faded.
Her door became cold and desolate, visitors scarce,
So, growing old, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit above all, caring little for separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, she has guarded their empty boat at the river mouth,
The bright moon encircling the boat, the river water cold.
Late one night, she suddenly dreamed of events from her youth,
Waking from the dream crying, tears staining her makeup red.
Hearing the pipa, I had sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, I sigh anew.
Both are people fallen from grace at the ends of the earth—
What need is there that we must have known each other?
I, too, last year left the imperial capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year round, no sounds of strings or bamboo are heard.
My home is near the Pen River, low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear here from dawn to dusk?
Only cuckoos bleeding cries and gibbons wailing mournfully.
In spring, by flower-laden rivers, in autumn, under moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone for myself.
Are there truly no mountain songs or village pipes?
Their crude, grating sounds are painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are temporarily purified.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood there for a long while,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings into rapid notes.
The melancholy tone differed from the previous sound;
The full audience listened again and all covered their faces, weeping.
Among those present, who shed the most tears?
The Blue-shirted Official of Jiangzhou."}

{"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, at night I saw off a guest.
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest stood on his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, yet had no strings or pipes for music.
Drunk but not joyful, gloomy as parting drew near—
At the moment of farewell, vast was the river, soaked in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, the sound of a pipa drifted up;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boats close to invite her out,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the wicks, and reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, urged ten thousand, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before forming a melody, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed, each note laden with thought,
As if telling of a lifetime’s unfulfilled ambitions.
Brows lowered, fingers moving freely, she played on continuously,
Expressing all the boundless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then flicking,
First playing “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six Strings.”
The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain,
The thin ones whispered closely like private murmurs.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Chattering like an oriole sliding through flowers below,
Muffled sobs like a spring flowing under ice.
Then the icy spring grew cold and sluggish, strings frozen tight;
Frozen and blocked, the sound paused briefly.
Another sorrow took root in darkness and hidden resentment—
Now silence spoke louder than any sound could.
Then, suddenly, silver vases burst, water splashing out;
Iron cavalry charged forth, swords and spears clashing.
When the song ended, she swept her pick across the center;
All four strings rang together, tearing like silk.
Boats east and west fell silent, people hushed;
Only the white autumn moon remained reflected in the river’s heart.
She pondered deeply, placed her pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said, "I was originally a girl from the capital,
Living my home beneath Shrimp Mound Hill.
By thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name was listed among the finest in the Imperial Music Academy.
After finishing a tune, even great masters would admire;
Once made up, courtesans often envied me.
Young men of Five Tombs competed to gift me silks;
For one song, countless lengths of red gauze were bestowed.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine during revels.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes enjoyed carelessly.
Then my brother went to war, my aunt died;
Evenings came, mornings went, beauty faded away.
My door grew lonely, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above separation;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He departed; I stay guarding an empty boat at the river mouth;
Surrounding the boat, bright moonlight makes the river water cold.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful affairs;
In dreams, crying, tears washed rouge down my face.
Hearing this pipa song, I sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I felt fresh waves of grief once more.
We are both people lost at the ends of the earth;
Meeting now, what need to have known each other before?
Since last year when I left the imperial capital,
Banished and ill, I have lain low in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year round, no sounds of silk or bamboo reach us.
I live near the Pen River, land low and damp,
With yellow reeds and bitter bamboos growing around my house.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Duck-billing cuckoos bleeding cries, apes grieving loudly.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I take wine alone and pour it down.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
But their harsh, jarring noises are hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; ears momentarily clear.
Please do not refuse: sit again and play another tune;
For you, I shall rewrite a Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood still for a long while,
Then sat back, tightened strings—the tempo grew urgent.
Sorrowful notes unlike those from before;
The full audience heard again, all covering faces to weep.
Who in the room shed most tears?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou was wet."}

The boats to east and west fell silent, speechless,

She pondered for a moment, tucked the plectrum into the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: "Originally a girl from the capital city,
My home was below Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire;
When fully dressed, even courtesans would envy me.
The young men of the Five Tombs vied to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine."
"Year after year of laughter and joy,
Taking spring winds and autumn moons lightly for granted."
"But then my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded."
"The door grew desolate, few horses remained;
Getting old, I married a merchant’s wife."
"Merchants value profit above all, indifferent to parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea."
"Gone and come, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the boat shines the bright moon, the river waters are cold."
"Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of youthful days;
Waking, I cry, makeup tears streaming red down my cheeks."

Hearing these words, I sighed again deeply.

Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year, leaving the Imperial Capital,
Demoted, I lay ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year round, I hear not the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.

Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights under the moon,
Often I take wine, pouring it alone.

They are harsh, discordant, difficult to bear hearing.

It is like listening to fairy music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose 'The Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings—the tempo quickened.
Sorrowful, unlike the earlier tunes,
The whole company heard it again and wiped away tears.
Who among us shed the most tears?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet."

{"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest at night; 
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill. 
The host dismounted while the guest remained on his boat, 
We raised our wine cups, longing to drink, but lacked music. 
Drunkenness failed to bring joy as we faced a sorrowful parting, 
In that moment, only the vast river reflected the moon. 
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa (Chinese lute), 
The host forgot to return home, and the guest refused to depart. 
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing; 
The pipa stopped, and she seemed hesitant to speak. 
I moved my ship closer to invite her out, 
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and resumed the banquet. 
After countless calls and invitations, she finally emerged, 
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face. 
She turned the tuning pegs and plucked two or three strings, 
Before forming a melody, emotion already filled the air. 
Each string suppressed, each note laden with thought, 
As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition. 
With head bowed, fingers moving with practiced ease, 
She poured out all the endless matters of her heart. 
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking, 
First playing 'Rainbow Feather,' then 'Sixth Melody.' 
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain, 
The thin strings whispered like private talk. 
Rumbles and whispers intertwined in complex play, 
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate. 
Smooth and fluid, like orioles singing beneath flowers, 
Choked and low, like spring water struggling under ice. 
The cold spring slowed, the strings froze, cutting off the flow, 
When sound ceases and cannot pass through, silence takes hold. 
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose, 
At this moment, silence surpassed any sound. 
Then, like a silver bottle bursting open, water splashing forth, 
Or iron cavalry charging, the clash of swords ringing out. 
The piece ended; she drew the plectrum across the center, 
All four strings struck together, ripping like silk tearing. 
Boats to the east and west fell silent, no one spoke, 
Only the white autumn moon shone upon the river's heart. 
She pondered deeply, placed the plectrum among the strings, 
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression. 
She said she had originally been a girl of the capital city, 
Her home near Xiama Ling. 
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa, 
Listed among the first troupe of the imperial music academy. 
After performing, even master musicians admired her skill, 
Once made up, women of renown often envied her beauty. 
Young men of the Five Mausoleums competed to give her gifts, 
For each song, she received countless bolts of red silk. 
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time, 
Crimson skirts stained by spilled wine. 
Years of laughter followed years of merriment, 
Autumn moons and spring winds passed casually by. 
Her brother went to war, her aunt died, 
Days and nights wore on, her beauty faded. 
Few horses and carriages stopped at her door now, 
Past her prime, she married a merchant’s wife. 
Merchants value profit more than separation, 
Last month, he left for Fuliang to buy tea. 
Since leaving, she has guarded an empty boat at the river mouth, 
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters. 
Deep into the night, she suddenly dreamed of her youth, 
Waking, tears streaming down her painted cheeks. 
Hearing her pipa, I already sighed, 
And hearing these words, my sighs deepened further. 
Both of us are wanderers lost in the world, 
Meeting thus, why need we have known each other before? 
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital, 
Demoted and bedridden in Xunyang City. 
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music, 
All year long, no stringed instruments are heard. 
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp, 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround the house. 
What do I hear there, morning and evening? 
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully. 
On spring nights with blooming flowers, or autumn nights beneath the moon, 
Often I take wine and pour it alone. 
Are there truly no mountain songs or village flutes? 
Their harsh, discordant notes are hard to bear. 
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice, 
It is like celestial music, clearing my ears at once. 
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece, 
For you, I will compose a ballad of the Pipa. 
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time, 
Then sat back down, tightened the strings, and played faster. 
The melancholy tone differed from before, 
Upon hearing it anew, everyone present wiped away tears. 
Who among them shed the most tears? 
The Blue-robed Prefect of Jiangzhou, his shirt soaked."}

{"translation":"Ballad of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi (Tang Dynasty)

On the banks of Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell by night,
Amid rustling maple leaves and silver reeds in autumn's light.
The host alights; the guest remains upon his boat below,
We raise our cups, but lack the sound of pipes to help us go.
Intoxication brings no joy; sorrow clouds parting’s hour,
As moonlight sinks into vast, misty waters’ melancholy power.
Suddenly, from across the stream, a pipa’s voice is heard,
Forgetting home, delaying departure, we hang on every word.
I follow the sound, asking softly who plays this song,
The music stops, but she hesitates, holding back her tongue.
I bring my boat close by, inviting her to join us there,
Add wine, relight the lamps, and start again the banquet fair.
After countless calls, she finally emerges shyly so,
Half-hiding her face behind the pipa, delicate and slow.
She turns the tuning pegs and plucks the strings just two or three,
Before the melody forms, emotion flows spontaneously.
Each string sighs low, each note conveys a deep-seated grief,
As if recounting all her life’s frustration and belief.
Head bowed, fingers move with ease, playing ceaselessly along,
Pouring out the infinite sorrows within her soul’s song.
With gentle sweeps, slow twists, and flicks both soft and bold,
First she plays “Rainbow Feather,” then “Six Melodies” untold.
The thick strings thunder like sudden rain in heavy downpour,
The thin strings whisper like lovers sharing private lore.
Loud and soft intermingle, complex and sweet combined,
Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate, refined.
Now smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms, clear and bright,
Then choked as springs running under ice, struggling in flight.
When cold ice blocks the spring, the strings freeze, sounds cease,
But hidden sorrow blooms anew, bringing inner peace?
No, silence speaks louder than any note could say,
A profound melancholy fills the air that day.
Then suddenly, like silver vases bursting open wide,
Water spurts forth; iron cavalry charge, swords clash aside.
The song concludes with one last sweep across the center string,
Four notes ring sharp as tearing silk, making everything cling.
Boats east and west fall silent, no one dares to speak,
Only seeing the white autumn moon reflected on the creek.
She pauses, inserts her pick among the strings with care,
Adjusts her dress, rises up, with solemn dignity there.
She tells how she was born a girl in the imperial city,
Her home near Shrimp-Frog Hill, where music lessons giddy.
At thirteen, she mastered pipa, fame reached top ranks first,
In instruction bureau, her name stood highest, noblest, worst? No, best!
Her songs made master musicians bow in pure envy’s grip,
Her beauty caused courtesan Qiu Niang tears of jealous ship.
Young nobles from Five Hills scrambled for red silk gifts,
One tune earned countless bolts of fabric, rare and swift.
Hairpins of gold and silver broke keeping time’s beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained by spilled wine, wild and fleet.
Year after year, laughter rang, autumns and springs passed by,
Youthful days wasted lightly under moonlit sky.
Brother went to war, aunt died, time moved day to night,
Her beauty faded, age crept in, dimming her bright plight.
Door grew lonely, horses rare, visitors few came,
So she married a merchant, chasing profit, not flame.
He cares for wealth, neglects love, left last month for tea,
To Fuliang town, leaving her alone by river’s sea.
Coming and going, she guards empty boats at Xunyang’s mouth,
Moonlight surrounds the vessel, water cold south-to-north.
Late at night, dreams of youth return, waking cries stain cheeks,
Makeup mixed with tears runs down, past midnight peaks.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply, moved by pain,
Now hearing her story, sadness weighs me down again.
Both are wanderers lost at edge of world, far from home,
Why need prior acquaintance when hearts together roam?
Since last year, I left the capital, demoted here,
Sick and idle in Xunyang City, yearning, tearful fear.
Remote place lacks musical sound, whole year no strings play,
Living near Pen River, land damp, low, gray.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk? Cuckoo bleeding cry,
Gibbons wailing mournfully under starry sky.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often take wine alone, drinking bitter sights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flute tunes true?
They’re rough, harsh, grating, impossible for ears to view.
Tonight hearing your pipa words, like immortal music clear,
My ears awaken fresh, washed free of dull years.
Please don’t refuse; sit down, play another tune for me,
I’ll rewrite it into verse: Ballad of the Pipa, free.
Moved by my words, she stands long, then sits to play more fast,
Strings tight, tempo rapid, intensity surpassed.
The sound, unlike before, pierces with deeper sorrow’s cut,
Full audience hears again, tears flowing, hearts shut.
Who shed most tears in crowd? The Jiangzhou Prefect’s blue robe,
Wet with saltwater streams, grief beyond measure, hope.
"}

{"translation":"On the bank of Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest is on the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no tunes or strings to hear.
Drunk yet without joy, we part with sorrow deep,
As we say goodbye, vast mist covers the river, moon submerged.
Suddenly from over the water come the sounds of a pipa,
The host forgets to return home, and the guest does not set sail.
Following the music, I ask softly: who plays?
The pipa stops; she seems about to speak, then hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Add more wine, turn back the lanterns, and restart the feast.
After being called thousands of times, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Every string muffles sighs; every note speaks longing,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled and thwarted.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving with ease and grace,
Playing out the endless sorrows hidden in her heart.
With light pinches, slow twists, sweeps, and picks,
She first plays "Rainbow Robes," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings boom like sudden heavy rain,
The thin ones whisper like intimate secrets.
Booming and whispering intermingle freely,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Sweetly rolling like orioles singing beneath flowers,
Low and choked like spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold springs stagnate, strings seem frozen tight;
When sound ceases utterly, silence holds its breath.
A hidden grief and secret resentment arise anew—
At this moment, silence surpasses even sound.
Then suddenly, as if a silver vase bursts, water splashes forth;
Like armored cavalry charging out, swords clash and spears ring.
The tune ends; she drags the plectrum across the center strings,
One sharp cry from four strings, like tearing silk.
Ships to the east and west fall silent without word,
Only seeing the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she inserts the plectrum between the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises, and composes her face with dignity.
She says she was originally a girl of the capital city,
Her home near Shama Ridge in the old town.
By thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
Renowned among the First Troupe of the Imperial Music Academy.
After playing a piece, great masters would bow in admiration;
Once made up, courtesans would envy her beauty.
Young gallants from Five Tombs rushed to shower her with gifts,
For one song, bolts of red silk came by countless rolls.
Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped when beating time for rhythm;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine during revelry.
Year after year passed in laughter and merriment,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent carelessly away.
But her brother went off to army service, her aunt died,
Morning turned to evening, and her youth faded slowly.
The door grew cold, horse riders rare indeed;
In old age she married a merchant as his wife.
The merchant values profit, disregards separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; she waits alone at the river mouth by an empty ship,
Moonlight circles the vessel, river waters cold.
Deep in night, she dreams of youthful days once more,
Crying in dream, tears wetting powder down her cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply already;
Hearing her words, I groan again with heavy hearts.
Both are wanderers cast adrift at world’s end—
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled here, ill-prostrate in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music all year round;
Never do we hear strings or wind instruments play.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp surrounding,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo encircle my house.
What do I hear morning or evening there?
Ducks crying blood, gibbons wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights, full moon—
Often I take wine and pour it out, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? Yes, but
Their harsh clatter grates upon the ear unfittingly.
Tonight hearing your pipa speak these words,
It is like listening to divine music that clears my ears.
Please don’t refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I shall compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my speech, she stands long in reflection,
Sits back down, tightens strings, now faster they vibrate.
More desolate than earlier tones, the whole room listens—and many cover faces in weeping.
Who sheds most tears among us seated here?
The Blue-robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his shirt soaked through."}

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

{"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang, I bid a guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is already on the boat.
We raise our wine to drink, yet there are no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, no joy remains; grief weighs upon parting.
As we depart, the vast river floats beneath the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, comes the sound of a pipa.
The host forgets to return; the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask quietly: who is playing?
The music stops; she hesitations before speaking.
I move my boat closer, inviting her to meet us.
More wine is poured; the lamps are turned up; the feast resumes.
After countless calls, at last she comes forth,
Still holding her pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few strings;
Before the melody forms, emotion is already present.
Each string suppressed, each note full of longing,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled.
With lowered brows, she plays with casual grace,
Expressing all the infinite affairs within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing then picking,
First the 'Feathered Robe,' then the 'Six Strings' dance.
The thick strings roar like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, intertwined in play,
Large and small pearls fall onto a jade plate.
Like birdsong sliding through flowers, clear and sweet;
Like water chocking under ice, stifled and hard.
Then cold slowness seizes the strings until they cease;
Blocked and silent, the sound momentarily rests.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment arises;
At this moment, silence surpasses speech.
Then, like a silver bottle bursting, the liquid sprays;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clash and spears ring.
When the tune ends, she draws the pick across the center;
One final stroke sounds like tearing silk.
The boats east and west fall into quietude;
Only the white autumn moon shines on the river's heart.
After a long pause, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She says: "Once I was a girl of the capital,
My home lived below Xiama Ling (the Toad Hill).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first among the Imperial Academy's ensemble.
After finishing a piece, even great masters admired me;
In makeup, I often provoked the jealousy of Qiuniang.
The young nobles of Five Tombs vied to wrap my head with gifts;
For one song, bolts of red silk were given without count.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke as they beat time;
My blood-red skirt was stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and delight;
Autumn moons and spring breezes went unnoticed and unvalued.
Then my brother joined the army; my aunt died.
Evenings pass, mornings come; my beauty fades.
Before my door, visitors grow sparse; carriages are few.
Past my prime, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit more than separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left me to guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Bathed only in bright moonlight, surrounded by cold waters.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
I wake crying, makeup running down, tears staining red."""

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.
Both of us are those lost at the sky's edge;
Meeting, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, leaving the imperial capital,
I was demoted and lay ill in Xunyang City.
This remote place knows no music;
All year round, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos cry blood; gibbons wail in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant sounds are difficult to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speak,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit once more and play another piece;
For you, I will compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
The mournful tone differed from the previous voice;
The entire hall, hearing it again, covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

{
  "translation": "Ballad of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

On the banks of Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell by night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle through the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is in his boat;
We raise our wine cups, but no pipes or strings are near.
Drunk yet joyless, we face a gloomy parting;
As we depart, vast waters soak the moon’s reflection.
Suddenly, from over the water, pipa sounds arise—
The host forgets to return; the guest delays setting sail.
Following the sound, I whisper: 'Who plays?' 
The pipa stops; she hesitates, about to speak but slow.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
We add wine, trim the wicks, and restart the feast.
After thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she emerges at last,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks three or four strings,
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string restrained, each note laden with thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled, dreams denied.
Lowering her brow, she plays on without pause,
Unveiling all the boundless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, wiping and picking again,
First the 'Rainbow Garment,' then the 'Six Strings' tune follow.
Big strings drone like sudden raindrops falling fast,
Small strings whisper as if in secret talk.
Loud and soft notes mingle, complex and intertwined,
Like large and small pearls dropping onto a jade plate.
Smooth like an oriole singing among blossoms,
Choked like a spring flowing under ice, struggling hard.
Ice-cold streams stiffen, the strings seem frozen dead,
Frozen and blocked, the sound momentarily ceases.
Then hidden grief and silent resentment are born;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
A silver bottle bursts suddenly, water sprays forth;
Iron cavalry charges, swords clash and ring.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
Four strings strike together like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and west fall silent, wordless;
Only the white moon of autumn shines upon the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she puts down the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her face.
She says herself: 'I was once a girl of the capital,
My home near Shama Ling hill.'
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's skill,
My name ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After playing, even master musicians bowed in awe;
When made up, courtesans like Qiuniang grew envious.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to offer gifts;
One piece of red silk brought countless more.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs snapped with the beat;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year merriment returned;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
Brother joined the army; auntie died;
Evenings went, mornings came, beauty faded.
Doorway cold, horsemen rare;
Age came, I married as a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit, disregards farewell;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Around the boat bright moonlight, cold river water.
Deep at night, I suddenly dream of youthful days;
Crying in dreams, makeup tears flow down my cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed;
Hearing these words, I sigh heavily again.
Both wanderers lost at heaven’s edge;
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial city,
Banished, sick, dwelling in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, no sound of strings or pipes.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there, dawn till dusk? 
Cuckoos cry blood; apes howl mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights;
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there not mountain songs and village flutes? 
Cacophonous noise, painful to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is like celestial music; ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more song;
For you, I compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stands long;
Returns to seat, tightens strings, which turn urgent.
Sorrowful tone unlike previous voice;
The whole hall hears again, all wipe away tears.
Who shed most tears among those seated? 
Prefect of Jiangzhou, his green robe soaked."
}

At night I bid farewell to a guest by the Xunyang River bank,
Amidst maple leaves and reed flowers, autumn’s chill blows bleak.
The host dismounts; the guest remains on board his boat;
We raise our cups, but lack the music of strings and pipes.
Drunk yet joyless, we grieve at parting imminent;
As we part, vast is the river, moonlight soaking deep.
Suddenly, over the water, sounds of a pipa are heard;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, in darkness, I ask who plays so well;
The pipa pauses, as if the player hesitates to speak.
We move our boats closer, inviting her to meet us;
Wine is refilled, lamps brought back, the feast resumed.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half concealing her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few preliminary strings;
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string restrained, each sound laden with thought,
Seeming to recount a life of thwarted ambition.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Telling all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Softly gathered, slowly twisted, swept then picked anew:
First the "Rainbow Feather," then the "Six Strings" tune.
The thick strings roar like sudden heavy rain;
The thin strings whisper like quiet private talk.
Roaring and whispering intermingle in the playing,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Now smooth as orioles singing beneath the blossoms,
Now choked as spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold springs stagnate, the strings seem frozen tight;
Frozen and blocked, the sound briefly ceases.
But hidden grief and dark resentment arise anew—
At this moment, silence surpasses all sound.
Then, suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water sprays;
Or iron cavalry charging, swords clashing loudly.
The song ends; she draws her plectrum across the center;
One final strum from the four strings rips like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent, no words spoken;
Only the white autumn moon shines on the river’s heart.
Pondering, she inserts her plectrum between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, with composed countenance.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home located near Shama Mound.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name ranked first among the Imperial Music Academy.
After my songs finished, even skilled masters admired me;
When I made up my face, other beauties grew envious.
Young men from Five Vaults vied to offer me silks;
For one song, red gauze was given without counting.
Jeweled combs broke as time was beaten out;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter passed in vain,
Spending autumn moons and spring breezes carelessly.
My brother joined the army; my aunt died;
Days turned, nights came, and my beauty faded.
The door became desolate, horses rare;
Getting old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit above love of companionship;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.

Living near Pen River, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
