{
  "translation": "Ballad of the Pipa

By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, my guest was aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink but had no music.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced the sorrow of parting,
As the vast river submerged the moon in its depths.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the sound, I asked who played; the pipa paused,
The player hesitated, shy to speak. We moved our boats close,
Invited her to come out, added wine, relit the lamps,
And reopened the feast. After countless calls and pleas,
she finally emerged, still holding the pipa to half-conceal her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before forming a tune, melody already brimming with feeling.
Each string suppressed sighs, each note carried longing,
As if telling of a life thwarted by fate. Head bowed, fingers moving effortlessly,
she poured out endless tales within her heart. Lightly gathering, slowly twisting,
plucking and sweeping, she first played "Rainbow Robes," then "Six Strings." The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversation. Rumbling and whispering, confused together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birds chirping smoothly under blossoms, muffled waters struggling beneath ice.
When icy springs froze stiff, the strings ceased their flow,
Silence held sway, and sound briefly died away.
Yet another hidden sorrow, a dark resentment arose:
In such moments, silence speaks louder than sound.
Silver vials bursting, water splashing forth;
Iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
When the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center,
All four strings sounded once, tearing silk apart.
East and west boats fell silent, not a word spoken;
Only the white autumn moon remained in the river's heart.
She pondered for a moment, placed her plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression. She said herself: originally a girl from the capital city,
Her home lay below Xiama Ling (Toad Tomb).
At thirteen she mastered the pipa, named among the first rank of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After playing, even expert musicians admired her skill;
When adorned, other beauties grew envious. Young men from Wuling fought to give her gifts,
One song earned countless red silks. Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine. This year’s laughter gave way to next year’s;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
Her brother went to war, her aunt died; day after day, youth faded.
Visitors dwindled at her door, horse and carriage rare;
Aging, she married a merchant as his wife.
The merchant values profit above all else, cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. He left; she guarded an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold. Deep in the night she suddenly dreamed of her youthful days,
Waking from dreams, tears streaming, makeup running down flushed cheeks.
I heard the pipa and sighed; hearing these words made me groan anew.
Both are persons adrift far from home—what need to know each other before meeting?
I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished, ill, living in Xunyang City. A remote place, devoid of music;
All year long I hear no string or wind instruments. My dwelling near Pen River is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear there, morning and evening? Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone. Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
They are harsh, grating, unpleasant to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa speech; like celestial music, my ears brighten momentarily.
Please don’t refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I will compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while, then returned to sit,
Plucked the strings faster, growing urgent. Sorrowful sounds unlike those before;
The whole audience listened again and covered faces while crying.
Who among us shed most tears? The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked."
}

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

{"translation":"The Ballad of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

At Xunyang's bank, I bid a guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed blossoms rustle in autumn's chill.
I dismount from my horse; my guest awaits aboard;
We raise our cups to drink, yet lack the pipes and strings.
Though drunk, we find no joy, for sorrow marks our parting;
As we depart, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, comes the sound of pipa,
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his start.
Following the music, I softly ask who plays;
The pipa stops, the player hesitates to speak.
I move my boat close by and invite her to appear;
More wine is poured, lamps trimmed, the banquet starts anew.
Amidst calls both thousand and ten-thousand times she emerges,
Still holding her pipa half before her face.
She twists the pegs and plucks two or three notes;
Before the melody forms, emotion already stirs.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing,
As if recounting a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Her brows lowered, fingers moving freely on,
Telling all the endless stories in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, wiping then picking,
First 'Rainbow Skirt', then later 'Six Strings' she plays.
The great strings thunder like sudden rain,
The small strings whisper like private talk.
Thunder and whispers intermingle in play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Chirping orioles slide smoothly beneath flowers,
Muffled sobs as springs struggle through ice below.
Cold, sticky spring water halts the strings to silence,
Blocked and mute, the sound pauses momentarily.
Another hidden sorrow born of dark resentment arises,
In this moment of silence, sound speaks more than words.
Silver vases burst, water jets forth suddenly,
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clash loud.
The song ends; she draws her pick across the center,
One final strum from four strings tears like silk.
Boats to east and west fall silent, none speak,
Only the white autumn moon seen in the river's heart.
Pondering deeply, she places her pick among the strings,
Adjusts her dress, stands up, composing her face.
She says: "Originally I was a girl of the capital,
Living near Mound of the Toads."
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name enrolled in the First Section of the Imperial Academy.
After finishing songs, skilled masters praised me;
When made up, every courtesan envied my beauty.
Youths of Five Tombs competed to wrap their heads in scarlet,
For one song they gave countless bolts of red gauze.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter followed last year's merriment,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
Brothers went to war, aunties died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, beauty fades.
The door grows cold, horses rare,
Growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
Merchants value profit over love, care not for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left me guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Around us bright moonlight, icy river water.
Deep in night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
Weeping in sleep, makeup streaked red down cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
Hearing these words, I lament again and again.
Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Since meeting here, why need past acquaintance?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished to sickbed in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year round, never hear silk-and-bamboo sounds.
Living near Pen River where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my home.
What do I hear day and night there?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often take wine alone and pour it out.
Are there mountain songs and village flutes?
Hoarse noises, harsh tones difficult to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa language,
As if listening to celestial music, ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one tune;
For you, I will compose 'The Ballad of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stood long,
Then sat back, tightened strings, now faster played.
Sorrowful unlike previous sounds,
Full audience heard again, all covering faces weeping.
Who shed most tears? The Magistrate of Jiangzhou,
His blue robe wet."}

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}
只给英文译文正文。

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。

钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。

忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

{"translation":"The Ballad of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

One night by the Yangtze at Xunyang, I saw a guest off;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on the boat,
Raised wine to drink but heard no music.
Drunk yet unable to find joy, sorrow loomed as we parted;
At parting, the vast river was soaked in moonlight.
Suddenly, a pipa melody drifted across the water;
The host forgot to return, the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing;
The music stopped, hesitant to speak.
We moved our boats closer, inviting her to meet us,
Added more wine, lit the lamps again, and resumed the banquet.
Called thousands of times, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
Turning the pegs, plucking three or two strings,
Before the tune formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed with sighs in every note,
As if telling how life had frustrated its ambitions.
Lowering her brows, fingers strumming in succession,
She expressed all the endless matters within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Feathers," then "

主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

**Translation Strategy: *Pipa Xing* (Song of the Pipa)**

### 1. Handling Ambiguity & Indeterminacy
*   **Subject/Agent:** Preserve the fluid shift between narrator, listener, and performer without explicit pronoun insertion unless strictly necessary for grammatical cohesion in English. Retain the implicit "we" or generic subject where Bai Juyi omits it.
*   **Cultural Proper Nouns:** Keep *Xiayaling*, *Jiaofang*, *Qiuniang*, *Wuling*, *Hongxiao*, *Fuliang*, *Jiangzhou Sima* as transliterations with brief footnotes rather than domesticating them (e.g., do not translate "Tea Merchant" as "Businessman"). This preserves the specific socio-historical ambiguity of Tang dynasty references.
*   **Emotional Nuance:** Terms like *cǎn* (miserable/sad) and *jī jī* (sighing/repeatedly sighing) are rendered via contextual phrasing ("grief-laden," "heavy sighs") rather than single-word equivalents, acknowledging their layered classical connotations.

### 2. Imagery Relationships
*   **Sound-Visual Synesthesia:** Map auditory metaphors directly to visual/kinetic imagery without explanatory bridging.  
    *   *Example:* "Large strings roar like sudden rain / Small strings whisper like private talks."  
    *   *Example:* "Pearls large and small drop on a jade plate."  
*   **Nature-Mood Mirroring:** Maintain the tight coupling between natural elements (moon, water, autumn wind) and emotional states. Do not separate stanzas that blend landscape description with inner feeling (e.g., the transition from "autumn moon immersed in river" to "forgetting return").
*   **Color Palette:** Prioritize exact color terms (*hong* red, *qing* blue/green, *bai* white, *xue-se* blood-red). Retain the symbolic weight of "blue shirt" (low official rank) by translating literally but noting its social implication in paratext, not altering the image itself.

### 3. Structure & Rhythm Arrangement
*   **Line Length:** Use variable line lengths mimicking the original’s irregular meter (mostly seven-character lines but with shifts). Avoid strict rhyming couplets to prevent forced archaisms; instead, use internal rhyme, alliteration, and rhythmic cadence (e.g., trochaic substitutions) to echo musicality.
*   **Stanza Breaks:** Divide strictly according to narrative pivot points:
    1.  Farewell at night (setting scene)
    2.  Discovery of sound (transition)
    3.  Performance description (climax of music)
    4.  Biography of the player (shift to past/personal)
    5.  Poet’s parallel fate (shift to present/self-reflective)
    6.  Final reaction (emotional convergence)
*   **Pacing:** Slow down syntax during the pipa performance section using short, crisp phrases. Accelerate through biographical narration with longer, flowing clauses. End with abrupt, heavy silence ("wet blue shirt") to mirror the original’s concluding stillness.

### 4. Uncertainties Retained
*   The precise age implied by "thirteen years old" vs. later "grew older" is left ambiguous; no modern dating logic applied.
*   The exact nature of "Liu Yao" and "Ni Chang" dances is referenced by name only, retaining cultural opacity.
*   The temporal gap between "this year" and "next year" in the biography is kept vague to reflect the fleetingness of youth described in the poem.

**英译方案：琵琶行 (The Ballad of the Pipa)**

1.  **歧义处理 (Ambiguity Handling)**
    *   **叙事视角融合**：保留第一人称“我”（白居易）与第三人称叙述者之间的模糊界限，不强行统一为单一视角，以体现原作中听者、作者与弹者身份在情感共鸣中的流动。
    *   **“秋娘”指代**：译为 "the beauty" 或保留音译 "Qiunniang" 并加注说明其作为唐代名妓/美人的文化符号意义，避免直译为具体人名造成历史语境断裂。
    *   **“司马青衫”**：不直译官职细节，侧重意象 "blue robe" 与 "moisture"，暗示贬谪身份与泪痕，保留社会地位低微的隐含信息而非显性行政术语。

2.  **意象关系 (Imagery Relations)**
    *   **通感链条**：严格对应声音→视觉→触觉的转换路径。如 "big strings... like sudden rain" (声转视/触), "pearls falling on jade plate" (声转视/听), "ice under water" (冷涩触感), "silver bottle bursting" (视觉爆发)。
    *   **自然与人造物的互喻**：保持乐器部件（弦、柱）与自然物象（雨、珠、莺、泉、冰、银瓶、铁骑）之间的直接隐喻连接，不使用明喻词 "like/as" 过多破坏节奏，必要时用动词直接转化（e.g., "strings weep", "music cracks"）。
    *   **“月”之复现**：将开篇“江浸月”、中段“秋月白”、后段“绕船月明”作为贯穿全诗的情感锚点，保持其清冷、孤绝的色调一致性。

3.  **篇章及节奏安排 (Structure & Rhythm)**
    *   **段落功能划分**：
        *   Part I (Setting): 短促、静谧，铺垫离别氛围。
        *   Part II (The Music): 密集、多变，模拟琵琶曲的起伏（慢板-快板-停顿-高潮-戛然而止）。
        *   Part III (Her Story): 平缓、叙述性强，回忆往昔繁华与今日凄凉对比。
        *   Part IV (Our Shared Fate): 抒情、升华，从个体悲叹扩展至普遍的人生沦落感。
    *   **节奏控制**：
        *   音乐描写部分采用短句、断句和头韵/尾韵模仿拨弦的顿挫感。
        *   “此时无声胜有声”处留白，下一行立即切入强音，制造听觉上的突然冲击。
        *   结尾“青衫湿”单行独立，余音袅袅，不作额外解释。

4.  **不确定处保留 (Preserving Uncertainties)**
    *   **弹者年龄变化**：原文未明确交代“十三岁”到“老大”的具体时间跨度，译文不添加推测性时间状语，仅通过事件顺序暗示岁月流逝。
    *   **白居易与琵琶女的实际交流深度**：保留两人之间由音乐引发的精神契合，但不虚构对话内容或心理独白，维持原诗“同是天涯沦落人”的抽象共鸣状态。
    *   **“翻作”一词**：对“为君翻作琵琶行”中的“翻”字，若无法确定是“改编”、“新创”还是“谱写”，则选用具有多重含义的动词（如 "compose anew" 或 "turn into verse"），并在注释中标记此语义模糊性。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

message.content:
**1. 歧义处理 (Ambiguity Resolution)**
*   **“主人”与“客”**：保留原文视角模糊性。不强行指定主角为白居易，译文中以“The host”和“The guest”指代，直至后文“Jiangzhou Sima”出现前保持身份悬置。
*   **“秋色/瑟瑟”**：译为 *rustling* 或 *shivering*，兼顾风声与植物动态，避免单一感官锁定。
*   **“虾蟆陵”**：音译 *Hama Ling* 并加注（若允许）或意译为 *Toad Ridge*，强调地名而非生物实体，保留其作为长安繁华象征的隐喻张力。
*   **“青衫”**：直译 *blue robe*，保留唐代官服等级标识，不解释为悲伤色彩，让读者在语境中体会身份落差。

**2. 意象关系 (Imagery Relations)**
*   **声音-视觉通感**：将琵琶声描述转化为视觉/触觉意象时，严格遵循原作比喻链：急雨→私语→珠落玉盘→莺语→泉流→冰涩→银瓶破→铁骑鸣。重点在于“流动感”到“爆裂感”再到“凝固感”的物理状态变化，而非单纯情感宣泄。
*   **月-水-人三角**：强化“江浸月”、“江心秋月白”、“绕船月明”的循环结构。月光作为冷寂、旁观、见证的恒定背景，与人物情绪的波动形成对比。
*   **空船-满座**：商人妇的“守空船”与诗人/乐工的“满座重闻”形成空间对立，突出孤独与共鸣的二元性。

**3. 篇章及节奏安排 (Structure & Rhythm)**
*   **三段式镜像结构**：
    1.  **引子（环境）**：短句为主，模拟秋风萧瑟与酒宴冷清的顿挫感。
    2.  **高潮（音乐）**：使用密集拟声词（onomatopoeia）和快速音节转换，模仿琵琶曲的变速、强弱对比；在“无声胜有声”处故意留白或延长停顿。
    3.  **自述与共情（叙事）**：转为长句叙述，节奏放缓，体现回忆的绵延与现实的沉重。
*   **押韵策略**：放弃严格尾韵，采用内部韵律（inner rhyme）和头韵（alliteration）来重现中文叠字（如“嘈嘈”、“切切”、“幽幽”）的节奏感。例如用 /s/ 音表现丝弦之声，/k/ 音表现裂帛之脆。
*   **断句逻辑**：依据动作连续性断行，而非语法完整性。如“千呼万唤始出来”应作为一个呼吸单元，强调延迟感。

**4. 不确定处保留 (Preservation of Uncertainty)**
*   **演奏者性别**：虽暗示女性，但译文初期不显性标记性别，仅通过服饰、妆容描写间接呈现，保留“弹者谁”的神秘感至最后揭晓。
*   **具体曲目细节**：“霓裳”与“六幺”译为音译 *Nishang* and *Liuyao*，不展开舞蹈形式描述，假定这些符号本身携带的文化重量足以引发联想，否则即视为未知。
*   **时间跨度**：“今年欢笑复明年”中的年份虚化，译为 *year after year*，不锚定具体历史时刻，维持命运沧桑的非特定性。

{"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest at night; Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted from my horse, while my guest was on his boat; We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet unable to find joy, we faced a sorrowful parting; At the time of farewell, the vast river immersed the moon.
Suddenly, I heard the sound of a pipa over the water; The host forgot to return home, and the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing; The pipa music stopped, and the player wished to speak but hesitated.
We moved our boats closer and invited her to meet us; We added more wine, turned up the lamps, and resumed the banquet.
After being called upon thousands of times, she finally appeared; Still holding her pipa, she half-covered her face.
She twisted the pegs and plucked two or three strings; Before forming a melody, emotion was already present.
Each string suppressed its tone, each note full of thought, As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows and idle hands, she played continuously, Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly rolling, sweeping, and picking; First she played 'Feathered Garments,' then 'The Six Orders.'
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain; The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering mixed together in play, Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Chirping like an oriole sliding through flowers beneath; Muffled like spring water flowing with difficulty under ice.
The icy spring became cold and sluggish, the strings froze and ceased; Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily halted.
Another hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose; This silence surpassed any sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly bursting, water spurted forth; Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashed.
At the end of the tune, she drew the pick across the center; With one stroke from the four strings, it sounded like tearing silk.
The boats to the east and west fell silent; Only the white autumn moon in the middle of the river remained visible.
She paused, put down her pick among the strings, Smoothed her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital; My home was by the Shama Mausoleum.""
"At thirteen, I mastered the pipa; My name belonged to the top rank of the Imperial Music Bureau."
"After finishing a piece, great masters would be impressed; Once made up, even Autumn Lady would envy me."
"Young men of the Five Tombs vied to give me scarlet silk; For one song, countless lengths of red gauze were given."
"Ornate hairpins and silver combs broke as they tapped the beat; Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine."
"This year laughing and rejoicing, next year again; Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually."
"My brother went off to join the army, my aunt died; Day after day, my beauty faded."
"Before my door grew desolate, horses rare; Getting older, I married a merchant's wife."
"Merchants value profit heavily and scorn separation; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea."
"Since he left, I have guarded this empty boat at the river mouth; Around the boat, bright moonlight and cold river waters."
"Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of affairs from my youth; Waking from dreams with tears staining my rouge makeup."
"Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed; Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply."
"Both are people fallen from the ends of the earth; When we meet, why must we have known each other before?"
"I left the imperial capital last year; Demoted to stay sick in Xunyang City."
"Xunyang is remote and has no music; All year round, I do not hear the sounds of silk and bamboo."
"Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp; Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house."
"What do I hear here morning and evening? Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing mournfully."
"Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights: Often taking wine, I pour alone."
"Are there no mountain songs and village flutes? Their hoarse and chaotic noise is hard to listen to."
"Tonight hearing your pipa language, It is like hearing celestial music, ears momentarily clear."
"Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece; For you, I will rewrite this Ballad of the Pipa."
"Moved by my words, she stood for a long time; Then sat back down, tightened the strings, which grew urgent."
"Mournful unlike the previous sounds; Everyone seated again covered their faces and wept."
"Who shed the most tears among those seated? The Prefect of Jiangzhou: His blue robe was wet.""}

**英译方案：琵琶行 (Pipa Xing)**

**1. 歧义处理与不确定处保留**
*   **“瑟瑟” (Sese):** 译为 “rustling/shivering” 而非仅指颜色。保留听觉上的风声/叶声双关，暗示秋意寒凉与心境萧瑟的模糊界限。
*   **“霓裳后六幺” (Nishang/Yaozhong Qu):** 音译 *Nishang* 和 *Liuyao*（或 *Six Strings*），加注说明其为唐代著名舞曲。不强行解释其具体旋律特征，保留音乐专有名词的异域感与历史距离感。
*   **“虾蟆陵” (Hama Ling):** 直译为 “Toad Hill” 并保留地名音译。此名在中文语境中带有长安繁华与世俗气息的双重隐喻，英语中难以完全对应，故保留字面意象以维持原作的地缘特异性。
*   **“青衫” (Qing Shan):** 译为 “blue/green robe”。白居易当时官阶低微，服色为青绿。保留颜色的视觉冲击，不强加“低级官员”的解释性翻译，让读者通过上下文推断身份落差。

**2. 意象关系构建**
*   **自然与音乐的互文:** 强化“月”、“水”、“风”作为背景音轨的角色。前段江浸月、后段秋月白，形成冷色调闭环；中段将琵琶声直接映射为自然声响（急雨、私语、莺啼、泉流、崩瓶、骑鸣），建立通感体系。
*   **空间转换:** 突出从“开阔江面”到“封闭船舱”再到“回忆中的长安”最后回归“现实浔阳”的空间收缩与扩张节奏。强调“空船”与“满座”的对比。
*   **色彩与触觉:** 聚焦“红”（枫叶、罗裙、泪）与“白/冷”（荻花、月、江水、青衫）的对冲，象征热烈过往与凄清现状的张力。

**3. 篇章及节奏安排**
*   **序曲 (Stanzas 1-4):** 缓慢、叙事性。使用长句描绘环境，节奏沉郁，模拟送别的滞重感。“忽闻”二字需单独成行或加强停顿，制造转折。
*   **演奏 (Stanzas 5-16):** 动态、多变。前半段轻柔连贯（如珠落玉盘），中段凝滞压抑（冰泉冷涩），后半段爆发激烈（银瓶乍破）。译文句式长度应随乐势起伏：短句表现急促，长句表现绵延，断句表现休止。
*   **自述 (Stanzas 17-28):** 平稳、哀婉。转为第一人称叙述，节奏趋于平缓但情感浓度增加。今昔对比部分需保持平行结构，强化时间流逝的无情。
*   **共鸣 (Stanzas 29-End):** 紧凑、终结。由个人感慨升华为普遍命运。“同是天涯沦落人”一句需独立突出，具有格言般的重量。结尾“青衫湿”需简洁有力，留有余韵，避免过度修饰。

**4. 风格建议**
*   采用自由体诗 (Free Verse) 而非严格押韵，以避免为了韵脚牺牲意象准确性。
*   语言风格应兼具古典雅致与现代清晰度，避免维多利亚式的陈词滥调。
*   保留原文中数字的精确性（十三、五陵、四弦等），以体现纪实感与艺术细节的真实。

message.content:
### 英译方案：Pipa Xing (Song of the Pipa)

#### 1. 歧义处理 (Ambiguity Resolution)
*   **“瑟瑟” (Sese)**: 译为 *whispering rustle*。保留风声与秋叶摩擦的听觉意象，避免直译为“颤抖”或“寒冷”，以符合中文语境中常用来形容秋风拂过草木的声音特性。
*   **“霓裳后六幺” (Nishang, Liuyao)**: 采用音译加注释策略：*the Rainbow Feather and the Six-Beat*。保留专有名词的音乐指涉性，不强行意译为具体舞曲名称，以免丢失唐代宫廷音乐的特定文化符号。
*   **“青衫” (Qingshan)**: 译为 *blue robe*。保留白居易官职低微（江州司马为八品，服青色）的象征意义，不解释为“悲伤的衣服”或“普通百姓衣服”。
*   **“虾蟆陵” (Xiamaling)**: 译为 *Toad Hill*。保留地名原貌，不改为更文雅的“蟾宫”等，以维持叙事的地缘真实感。

#### 2. 意象关系 (Imagery Relations)
*   **月之贯穿**: “浸月”、“秋月白”、“绕船月明”、“梦啼”后的月色，构建从冷寂、澄澈到孤寂、凄清的视觉递进。译文需保持 *Moonlight* 作为静默见证者的角色，连接送别之景、演奏之高潮与身世之悲。
*   **声画通感**: 重点处理琵琶声与自然/战争意象的转换。急雨、私语、莺语、泉流、冰下难、银瓶破、铁骑鸣。译文需用动态动词 (*patter, murmur, glide, choke, burst, clash*) 强化声音的物理质感，形成从柔美到激越再到骤停的节奏闭环。
*   **空间对照**: “浔阳江头”（现实流放地）与“京城女/五陵年少”（记忆繁华地）的空间折叠。译文通过时态切换（过去完成时与现在进行时）区分回忆与当下，强化“天涯沦落”的心理距离。

#### 3. 篇章及节奏安排 (Structure & Rhythm)
*   **四段式结构**:
    1.  **序曲 (Lines 1-8)**: 七言节奏，舒缓压抑。译文使用长句与停顿，模拟秋夜送别的沉闷与期待。
    2.  **主奏 (Lines 9-24)**: 快速多变。译文采用短促、密集的节奏，模仿琵琶指法的变化（轻拢慢捻抹复挑），在“无声胜有声”处设置明显的排版留白或短句断行。
    3.  **自诉 (Lines 25-40)**: 叙事平稳。译文转为流畅的叙述语气，反映其身世浮沉，节奏趋于均匀但沉重。
    4.  **共鸣 (Lines 41-末)**: 情感爆发。译文在“同是天涯沦落人”处加强重音，结尾“青衫湿”用简短有力的收束，呼应开头的“惨将别”，形成环形结构。
*   **押韵策略**: 不强制尾韵，侧重内部音节的重叠与回响（如 *sibilance* 模拟琵琶弦音，*plosives* 模拟裂帛之声），以再现原作平仄起伏而非严格格律。

#### 4. 保留不确定处 (Retained Uncertainties)
*   **“呕哑嘲哳” (Ouya Zhaozha)**: 保留拟音词 *rough, grating sounds* 的模糊性，不具体化为某一种劣质乐器声，让读者自行感知其刺耳与不和谐，对应诗人对民间粗俗音乐的不适感。
*   **“颜色故” (Yanse gu)**: 译为 *her beauty faded* 或 *time darkened her looks*，保留衰老过程的自然性与无奈感，不指明具体年龄或外貌细节，维持“老大嫁作商人妇”的命运无常感。

住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。

{"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustling in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts while the guest is on the boat;
We raise our wine cups to drink, but have no strings or pipes to accompany us.
Drunken yet unable to be joyful, we face a sorrowful parting;
At the moment of departure, the vast river immerses the moon.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifts over the water;
I forget to return home, and my guest does not set sail.
Following the music, I quietly ask who is playing;
The pipa stops, as if she wishes to speak but hesitates.
We move our boats close together and invite her to see us;
We add more wine, trim the wicks, and resume the feast.
Though called thousands and tens of thousands of times, only then does she emerge,
Still holding the pipa halfway across her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings three or two times;
Before the melody forms, emotion already arises.
Each string suppresses its tone, each sound carries longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Lowering her brows, she plays casually and continuously,
Expressing the infinite matters within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking again,
First she played 'Rainbow Skirt,' then later 'Six Whims.'
The thick strings rumble loudly like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper softly like private conversation.
Rumbling and whispering, mingled in complex play,
Large and small pearls fall onto a jade plate.
Sweet and clear, like orioles singing smoothly beneath flowers,
Choked and sobbing, like springs flowing with difficulty under ice.
When the icy spring becomes cold and sluggish, the strings seem frozen;
Frozen and blocked, the sound momentarily ceases.
Then hidden sorrows and dark resentments arise anew—
In this silence, it surpasses the beauty of sound.
Like a silver bottle suddenly bursting, water spurts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clash and shout.
At the end of the song, she draws her plectrum across the center of the strings;
One sharp cry from the four strings sounds like silk tearing.
The boats to the east and west fall silent without a word;
All that remains is the white autumn moon in the middle of the river.
She contemplates deeply, puts down her plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her countenance.
She says she was originally a woman from the capital city,
Her home lived near Shama Hill.
By age thirteen, she had mastered the pipa;
Her name belonged to the first department of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, even the great masters would admire her skill;
Once dressed up, she often provoked jealousy even from Qiuniang.
The young men of Five Tombs competed to give her red silk headbands;
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were unknown.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broken keeping time,
Blood-red silk skirts stained by overturned wine.
This year laughing, next year also laughing;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed by idly.
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died;
Evenings pass, mornings come, and her beauty fades.
Before her door, the place grows desolate, horses and carriages rare;
In old age, she married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit highly and take parting lightly;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and she stayed guarding an empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the boat, bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, she suddenly dreams of events from her youth;
In the dream, she cries, tears staining her makeup red.
I heard the pipa and sighed;
Hearing these words, I sigh deeply once more.
We are both people lost on the road to Heaven's edge;
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since leaving the imperial capital last year,
I have been demoted and lie ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
Throughout the year, I hear no sound of silk and bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding calls and apes’ mournful cries.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights—
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their harsh and chaotic sounds are difficult to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music, and my ears temporarily become clear.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I will compose a new ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stands for a long time;
She returns to her seat, tightens the strings, which turn urgent.
Sad and mournful unlike the previous tones,
Everyone present hears them again and covers their faces, weeping.
Who among those seated sheds the most tears?
The Blue-robed Prefect of Jiangzhou has wet his robe."}

message.content:
**The Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest stepped onto his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no music played.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced the sorrow of parting;
As we said goodbye, the vast river bathed the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, came the sound of a pipa!
The host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, as if she hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to meet;
We added more wine, turned up the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before the melody formed, emotion already poured forth.
Each string suppressed, each note full of thought,
Seeming to tell of lifelong frustration and unfulfilled dreams.
Head lowered, fingers moving confidently, she continued to play,
Expressing endless affairs hidden within her heart.
Light gathering, slow twisting, wiping, then plucking—
First playing *Ni Shang*, then *Liu Yao*.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like intimate confidences.
Rumbling and whispering interwoven in chaotic play,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smoothly flowing like orioles singing among flowers,
Muffled and choked like spring water freezing under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings seemed to snap in silence;
Silence halted, no sound for a moment.
Then arose new dark sorrows and hidden resentments;
At this moment, silence surpassed even sound.
Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water splashed out;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashed and rang.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center;
The four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
Boats on the east and west fell silent, saying nothing;
Only the white autumn moon shone upon the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She spoke of herself: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home living near Shama Ling (Frog Mound).
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
And my name belonged to the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, even great masters would admire me;
When I put on makeup, every beautiful woman envied me.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to give me gifts,
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Gold hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Idly spending the autumn moons and spring breezes.
My brother went off to war, my aunt died;
Day by day, morning by evening, my beauty faded.
Before my door, life grew cold, horses and carriages rare;
Aging, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit over love, and care little for separation;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I waited alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat;
Around the boat, bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of youth’s affairs;
I woke crying, tears staining my rouge-covered cheeks red.
I listened to the pipa and sighed already deeply,
And hearing these words, I sobbed anew.
Both of us are wanderers lost at the end of the world;
Since we’ve met, why must we have known each other before?
I left the Imperial Capital last year,
Banished and bedridden with illness in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, I hear not the sounds of silk and bamboo.
Living near the Pen River where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleaking blood, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring river blooms’ mornings and autumn moon nights,
I often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh, discordant, and unbearable to listen to.
Tonight I heard your pipa’s language,
It was like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly clear.
Please, don’t refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For your sake, I shall compose *The Ballad of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, which now played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous sound,
Those seated again listened and all covered their faces, weeping.
Who among the guests shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked through.

message.content:
**The Song of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount to meet him on his boat; we raise our wine,
Yet no pipes or strings accompany this drink.
Drunk but not joyful, gloom hangs over parting;
At the moment of goodbye, the moon drowns in the vast river.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifts across the water;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The music stops, as if she hesitates to speak.
We move our boats closer, inviting her to appear;
More wine is poured, the lamps are turned up bright, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the melody forms, emotion already breathes.
Every string sighs with suppressed longing,
Seeming to tell of a life’s thwarted ambitions.
Head bowed, her fingers play on continuously,
Expressing all the boundless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked,
First playing *Ni Shang*, then *Liu Yao*.
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like secret confidences.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Now clear and sweet, like orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Now choked and low, like spring water trapped under ice.
The cold spring chokes, the strings seem frozen still,
Stopped and blocked, the sound momentarily ceases.
But hidden sorrow and dark resentment arise anew;
In this silence, there is more voice than sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting, water spurts out,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing loud.
When the tune ends, the plectrum draws one final stroke,
All four strings ringing together like tearing silk.
East ship, west boat—silent and unmoving;
Only the autumn moon shines white upon the river’s heart.
She muses, puts away the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her dignity.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shrimp Toad Tomb.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed among the first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a song, even great masters would bow to me;
When made up, every beauty envied my grace.
Young men of the Five Districts competed to gift me brocade,
For each piece played, countless red silks were bestowed.
Jeweled hair ornaments broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter passed,
Autumn moons and spring breezes casually consumed.
Then my brother went off to war, my aunt died,
As evening came and morning returned, my beauty faded.
The door grew cold, horsemen rare,
So, growing old, I married a merchant man.
He values profit above separation,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he departed, I wait alone on the empty boat at the river mouth,
The moon surrounds the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking with tears streaming down my painted cheeks, staining them red."

Hearing her pipa, I have long sighed;
Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.
"Both of us are fallen souls wandering the edge of heaven,
Meeting now, why need we know each other before?"
"Since last year I left the Emperor's Capital,
Banished, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Here, remote and devoid of music,
All year long, no sound of silk or bamboo is heard.
My home is near Pen River, low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow rushes and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear here, dawn to dusk?
Blood-crying cuckoos and monkeys’ mournful wails.
On spring river nights, flower morns, autumn moon evenings,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Is there truly no folk song or village flute?
Their sounds are harsh and jarring, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse; sit again, play one more piece,
And I shall compose for you 'The Song of the Pipa'."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down, tightening the strings, which played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous tones,
At the end, everyone in the room wiped their tears.
Who shed the most tears among those present?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is wet with grief.

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Six Strings.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his sleeves soaked.

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.

On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling [Frog Mound].
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through.

Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.

My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.

Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.

They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.

With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,

For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.

On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling [Frog Mound].
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through.

Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through.

message.content:
By the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell one night,
Amid rustling maple leaves and reed flowers in autumn’s chill.
I dismounted from my horse while he remained upon his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, yet lacked the music of strings and pipes.

Drunk, joy was still not found, sorrow impending at parting;
The vast river shimmered under the moon’s reflection.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa floated across the water,
Making me forget to return home and my guest delay his departure.

Following the sound, I asked softly, “Who plays this instrument?”
The pipa ceased; she hesitated, about to speak.
I moved my boat close by to invite her out,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and prepared for another feast.

After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Though no melody had formed, emotion preceded the tune.

Every string played low and suppressed, each note full of longing,
Seeming to tell of a lifetime’s unfulfilled ambitions.
With downcast eyes, she casually continued playing,
Expressing all the endless sorrows within her heart.

Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, strumming then picking,
First playing the *Rainbow Garment*, then the *Six Melodies*.
The thick strings roared loudly like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered softly like private conversations.

Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
They flowed smoothly like birdsong beneath the blossoms,
Then choked like spring water struggling under ice.

The cold spring water grew sluggish, the strings seemed frozen,
Frozen and blocked, the sound momentarily stopped.
A new kind of hidden sorrow and deep resentment arose,
In this silence, there was more sound than speech could convey.

Suddenly, as if a silver vase burst and water splashed forth,
Or iron cavalry charged with swords clashing and spears ringing.
At the end of the piece, she drew the plectrum across the center string,
All four strings sounded together, tearing like silk cloth.

To the east and west, boats lay silent without a word,
Only seeing the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, placed her plectrum into the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said that originally she was a girl from the capital city,
Her home located near the Shrimp-Frog Mound.

At thirteen, she mastered the pipa art,
Her name registered among the first rank of the imperial music bureau.
After performing a piece, even master players would admire her skill,
When dressed, every beauty envied her charm.

Young nobles from the Five Tombs vied to offer gifts,
For one song, countless red silks were thrown to her.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke beating time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.

Year after year, laughter and joy repeated,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Her brother left to join the army, her aunt died,
Days turned into nights, and her beauty faded away.

Before her gate, visitors became scarce, horses rare,
Getting older, she married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit high but love separation lightly,
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and she stayed alone guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, while the river water ran cold.
Late at night, she suddenly dreamed of events from her youth,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining her rouge down her cheeks.

Hearing the pipa, I already sighed heavily,
And hearing these words, my sighs grew deeper still.
We are both wanderers lost at the ends of the earth,
Why must we have known each other before meeting today?

Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital,
Demoted and ill, lying low in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and lacks music,
All year long, no sound of silk or bamboo instruments is heard.

Living near the Pen River in damp lowlands,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood and gibbons howling mournfully.

On spring rivers amid blooming flowers, or on autumn nights under the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it solely for myself.
Are there no local folk songs and village flutes?
Their hoarse and chaotic sounds are hard to bear listening to.

Tonight, hearing your pipa music,
It was like hearing celestial tunes, making my ears bright again.
Do not refuse to sit and play another piece;
For you, I shall compose the *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down and tightened the strings, which played faster.
The music became melancholic, unlike the previous notes,
Everyone present listened again and covered their faces in tears.

Who among us shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet with sorrow.

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

message.content:
**The Song of the Pipa**

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid a guest farewell in the night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn’s slight.
The host dismounts; the guest is aboard his craft,
We raise our cups to drink, but there is no music left.
Intoxicated yet joyless, on the verge of parting tears,
At parting time, the vast river soaks the moon in clear.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa comes through,
The host forgets to return, the guest refuses to go.
Following the sound, I quietly ask who plays with such art,
The pipa pauses, seeming hesitant to start.
I shift my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refill the wine, trim the lamps, restart the feast here.
Called a thousand times, she finally emerges from within,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her chin.
She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings’ faint sound,
Before the melody forms, emotion is already found.
Each string hides sorrow, each note carries thought,
Seeming to tell of ambitions forever thwart.
She lowers her brows, fingers move without pause,
Expressing all the infinite grief that nature draws.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, strumming then picking tight,
First the *Rainbow Garment*, then the *Six Beats* in flight.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain in haste,
The thin strings whisper as lovers do their taste.
Rumbling and whispering mixed in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling into jade plates.
Now smooth as an oriole singing under blossoms bright,
Now choked as a spring struggling beneath ice tight.
The cold spring stops, the strings seem frozen stiff,
When blocked and still, the sound takes a brief relief.
A hidden sorrow, a dark resentment arises anew,
This silence speaks louder than words ever could do.
Then silver bottles burst, water spurts in spray,
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clash in fray.
As the tune ends, the plectrum sweeps across the center,
Four strings strike together, tearing silk’s tender texture.
Boats east and west fall silent, no word is spoken,
Only the white autumn moon on the river’s bosom broken.
She hesitates, tucks the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes face, bringing peace.
She says: "I was originally a girl of the capital,
Living near Shama Ridge in my family’s portal.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s skillful art,
My name listed first in the Imperial Court’s heart.
After finishing songs, even masters praised my style,
When made up, courtesans envied me for a while.
Youths from Five Tombs vied to give me red silk,
For one song, countless bolts were their gift.
Gold hairpins and silver combs broke tapping the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine’s sweet treat.
One year laughing, next year the same old game,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed without claim.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died away,
Evenings fade, mornings come, youth turns gray.
The gate grows desolate, horsemen rare to see,
In middle age, I married a merchant’s wife to be.
Merchants value profit, little care for parting pain,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea again.
He left, I stayed guarding this empty boat alone,
Moonlight circles it, the river’s chill cuts bone.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of girlish days,
Crying in sleep, tears streak make-up’s red haze."

I heard the pipa and sighed deep in my soul,
And hearing these tales, more grief takes its toll.

Meeting now, why should we know before birth?

Banished to Xunyang, sick in bed, day and night.

All year long, no flute or zither’s rejoice.
Near Pen River, low and wet, my dwelling lies,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround the skies.

Cuckoos bleeding, monkeys wailing in fear.

Often taking wine, pouring it in solitary flights.

Like celestial music, making my ears young.

For you, I shall compose this Song of the Pipa release.

Then sat back, tightened strings, tempo turned wild.

The whole audience listened, weeping once more.

轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}
