On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Six Strings.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his sleeves soaked.

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Six Strings.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his sleeves soaked.

{"translation":"On the bank of the River Xun at night, seeing off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet unable to find joy, we face a sorrowful parting,
At this moment of farewell, the vast river bathes the moon.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa,
The host forgets to return home, and the guest does not depart.
Following the sound, I softly ask: who is playing?
The pipa stops, as if she wants to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer, inviting her to come out,
Adding wine, trimming the lamp, resuming the feast.
After countless calls, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks two or three strings,
Before the melody forms, emotion has already arrived.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled by ambition.
Lowering her brow, she plays casually, again and again,
Pouring out the infinite affairs within her heart.
Light gathering, slow rolling, wiping and picking,
First the 'Rainbow Robe', then the 'Six Strings'.
Thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
Thin strings whisper like private conversation.
Rumbling and whispering intermingled together,
Big pearls and small pearls falling onto jade plates.
Sweetly sliding, like orioles singing beneath flowers,
Choking sobs, like springs flowing under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings stop abruptly,
Stopped, blocked, the sound temporarily ceases.
But another hidden sorrow, a secret resentment arises—
At this moment, silence surpasses even voice.
Suddenly, a silver vase breaks, water bursts forth,
Like cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
The piece ends, the plectrum sweeps across the center,
Four strings sound once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent, listening intently,
Only seeing the white moon in the center of the river.
Pondering, she places the plectrum into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing herself.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital,
Her home lived near the Shrimp Mound Hill.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Renowned among the first rank of the imperial musicians.
After finishing a tune, masters would admire her skill,
When made up, other beauties felt envy.
Young men of the five tombs vied to give gifts,
For one song, red silk piles knew no count.
Hairpins and silver combs shattered keeping time,
Red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year laughing, next year also happy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Brother went to join the army, aunt died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, beauty fades.
Before the door, cold and desolate, few carriages remain,
Aging, she married a merchant.
The merchant values profit above separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving and returning, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth,
Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
In tears upon waking, makeup runs down her cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I sigh deeply,
Hearing these words, I groan anew.
We are both people lost in the corner of heaven,
Meeting here, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished to Jiujiang, sick and bedridden.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, never hearing strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling in grief.
Spring rivers, flower dawns, autumn nights—
Often taking wine, pouring alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their hoarse, jarring sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It's like heavenly music, my ears suddenly clear.
Please do not refuse; sit again and play one more tune,
To interpret for you, I shall compose this 'Song of the Pipa'.
Touched by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits back down, quickening strings, notes growing urgent.
Melancholy, unlike the earlier sound,
The whole room hears it again, everyone covering faces in tears.
Who sheds the most tears in the room?
The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou is wet."}

**The Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, at night, I bid my guest farewell,
As maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat already there,
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music’s air.
Though drunk, no joy remains before our parting tears,
When we must leave, the moonlight drowns in misty spheres.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa notes arise,
Forgetting home, I linger; guests delay their departure’s ties.
I follow the sound, asking softly who might play,
The strings fall silent, as if shy to speak or stay.
I move my vessel close, inviting her to show her face,
Refill the wine, trim lamps anew, resume the banquet’s grace.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges slow,
Still holding near her pipa, half her beauty’s glow.
She turns the pegs, then plucks two, three tentative sounds,
Before the melody begins, emotion floods the grounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep thought,
As if recounting all the dreams that life has not brought forth.
Her brows lowered low, she plays with fingers free and light,
Expressing boundless sorrows hidden in her heart’s retreat.
With gentle sweeps, slow twists, and flicks both up and down,
First playing *Rainbow Robes*, then *Six Strings’* mournful frown.
The thick strings boom like sudden rain in torrents fierce,

**The Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, at night, I bid my guest farewell,
As maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat already there,
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music’s air.
Though drunk, no joy remains before our parting tears,
When we must leave, the moonlight drowns in misty spheres.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa notes arise,
Forgetting home, I linger; guests delay their departure’s ties.
I follow the sound, asking softly who might play,
The strings fall silent, as if shy to speak or stay.
I move my vessel close, inviting her to show her face,
Refill the wine, trim lamps anew, resume the banquet’s grace.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges slow,
Still holding near her pipa, half her beauty’s glow.
She turns the pegs, then plucks two, three tentative sounds,
Before the melody begins, emotion floods the grounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep thought,
As if recounting all the dreams that life has not brought forth.
Her brows lowered low, she plays with fingers free and light,
Expressing boundless sorrows hidden in her heart’s retreat.
With gentle sweeps, slow twists, and flicks both up and down,
First playing *Rainbow Robes*, then *Six Strings’* mournful frown.
The thick strings boom like sudden rain in torrents fierce,
The thin ones whisper secrets soft, as lovers rehearse.
Thick, thin intertwined, they crash and mingle in the air,
Like large pearls falling, small pearls skipping, on jade trays rare.
Clear birdsong glides through floral shadows, smooth and sweet,
Then muffled sobbing flows beneath the ice-bound street.
The cold spring freezes stiff, the strings seem severed tight,
In silence choked, the song pauses, losing its flight.
But deeper grief and hidden hate begin to stir within,
This void of sound speaks louder than any noise can win.
Then suddenly, silver vases break, water bursts apart,
Iron cavalry charge forward, blades clash, spears impart shock.
The tune concludes; she draws her pick across the center line,
Four strings snap once—like silk tearing—to make them mine.
East boats and west barges fall into hushed repose,
Only the white autumn moon reflects upon the river’s flow.
She pauses, inserts the pick among the strings with care,
Adjusts her garments, rises, composing countenance fair.
She states she was a girl from the Imperial Capital’s core,
Her home resided below Shama Ling’s ancient door.
At thirteen, mastering the pipa, skill attained its peak,
Named first among the teaching guilds, where talents seek.
After songs ended, even master musicians bowed in awe,
When dressed, her beauty caused rival courtesans’ envy’s flaw.
Young nobles of Five Tombs contended for her favor’s prize,
For one song played, countless red silks were given as dues.
Gold-inlaid combs broken keeping time’s rhythmic beat,
Blood-colored skirts stained by spilled wine’s crimson heat.
Year after year passed laughter, spring winds and autumn moons spent idly,
Until her brother joined the army, aunt departed silently.
Day fading into dawn, her youth’s vibrant hue grew pale,
The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.
Aged beyond her prime, she wed a merchant man,
Who values profit high, disregards love’s tender span.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where waters cold display.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.
Both are exiled souls drifting at world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?
Since last year I left the imperial city’s grandeur bright,
Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.
This place remote lacks music entirely throughout the year,
No strings or bamboo flutes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp surrounds,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose my dwelling grounds.
What do I hear from dusk till dawn in this desolate place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing in mournful case.
On spring river banks under blooming flowers, autumn nights serene,
I often take my wine alone, drinking amidst the scene.
Are there no mountain songs, nor village pipes’ rough tone?
Their grating cacophony is hard for ears to own.
Tonight I hear your pipa’s voice, celestial it seems,
My ears awakened fresh, washed clean by heavenly beams.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play another song,
For you, I’ll rewrite this ballad, long and strong.
Moved by my words, she stood a while in thoughtful pause,
Sat down again, tightened strings, letting tempo draw.
Melancholy filled the air, different from sounds before,
The whole assembly wept, tears streaming on the floor.
Who shed the most tears among those listening guests?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe stains wettest.

**The Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, at night, I bid my guest farewell,
As maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat already there,
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music’s air.
Though drunk, no joy remains before our parting tears,
When we must leave, the moonlight drowns in misty spheres.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa notes arise,
Forgetting home, I linger; guests delay their departure’s ties.
I follow the sound, asking softly who might play,
The strings fall silent, as if shy to speak or stay.
I move my vessel close, inviting her to show her face,
Refill the wine, trim lamps anew, resume the banquet’s grace.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges slow,
Still holding near her pipa, half her beauty’s glow.
She turns the pegs, then plucks two, three tentative sounds,
Before the melody begins, emotion floods the grounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep thought,
As if recounting all the dreams that life has not brought forth.
Her brows lowered low, she plays with fingers free and light,
Expressing boundless sorrows hidden in her heart’s retreat.
With gentle sweeps, slow twists, and flicks both up and down,
First playing *Rainbow Robes*, then *Six Strings’* mournful frown.
The thick strings boom like sudden rain in torrents fierce,
The thin ones whisper secrets soft, as lovers rehearse.
Thick, thin intertwined, they crash and mingle in the air,
Like large pearls falling, small pearls skipping, on jade trays rare.
Clear birdsong glides through floral shadows, smooth and sweet,
Then muffled sobbing flows beneath the ice-bound street.
The cold spring freezes stiff, the strings seem severed tight,
In silence choked, the song pauses, losing its flight.
But deeper grief and hidden hate begin to stir within,
This void of sound speaks louder than any noise can win.
Then suddenly, silver vases break, water bursts apart,
Iron cavalry charge forward, blades clash, spears impart shock.
The tune concludes; she draws her pick across the center line,
Four strings snap once—like silk tearing—to make them mine.
East boats and west barges fall into hushed repose,
Only the white autumn moon reflects upon the river’s flow.
She pauses, inserts the pick among the strings with care,
Adjusts her garments, rises, composing countenance fair.
She states she was a girl from the Imperial Capital’s core,
Her home resided below Shama Ling’s ancient door.
At thirteen, mastering the pipa, skill attained its peak,
Named first among the teaching guilds, where talents seek.
After songs ended, even master musicians bowed in awe,
When dressed, her beauty caused rival courtesans’ envy’s flaw.
Young nobles of Five Tombs contended for her favor’s prize,
For one song played, countless red silks were given as dues.
Gold-inlaid combs broken keeping time’s rhythmic beat,
Blood-colored skirts stained by spilled wine’s crimson heat.
Year after year passed laughter, spring winds and autumn moons spent idly,
Until her brother joined the army, aunt departed silently.
Day fading into dawn, her youth’s vibrant hue grew pale,
The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.
Aged beyond her prime, she wed a merchant man,
Who values profit high, disregards love’s tender span.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where waters cold display.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.
Both are exiled souls drifting at world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?
Since last year I left the imperial city’s grandeur bright,
Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.
This place remote lacks music entirely throughout the year,
No strings or bamboo flutes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp surrounds,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose my dwelling grounds.

Melancholy filled the air, different from sounds before,
The whole assembly wept, tears streaming on the floor.

The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe stains wettest.

The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.

Who values profit high, disregards love’s tender span.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where waters cold display.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.

Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.

No strings or bamboo flutes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose my dwelling grounds.

Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing in mournful case.

Tonight I hear your pipa’s voice, celestial it seems,
My ears awakened fresh, washed clean by heavenly beams.

For you, I’ll rewrite this ballad, long and strong.

Sat down again, tightened strings, letting tempo draw.

The whole assembly wept, tears streaming on the floor.
Who shed the most tears among those listening guests?

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
Raised wine to drink, but no strings or pipes were heard.
Drunk yet joyless, grief awaited parting;
In the vastness, the river immersed the moon.
Suddenly, pipas sounded over the water;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed departure.
Following the sound, I asked who was playing;
The pipa paused, hesitant to speak.
We moved our boats closer to invite her out,
Added wine, lit lamps, and reopened the feast.
After countless calls, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string veiled sorrow, each note a sigh,
As if telling of a lifetime unfulfilled.
She lowered her brows and played casually,
Expressing all boundless matters of the heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking,
First 'Rainbow Feather', then 'Six Strings'.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain;
The thin ones whispered as private talk.
Intermingling loud and soft notes,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smooth as warbling orioles beneath flowers,
Choked as springs flowing under ice.
Cold seeping ice slowed the strings to stillness,
Stopped and blocked, sound temporarily paused.
Extra hidden sorrow, secret regret arose—
This silent moment surpasses any spoken word.
Then suddenly, silver bottles burst, water spraying;
Iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clashing.
Concluding the tune, she drew the plectrum across the center,
A single slash from four strings, like silk tearing.
East and west ships fell silently quiet;
Only the white autumn moon in the river's heart was seen.
Lost in thought, she put down her plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, composing her face.
She said: 'I was once a girl from the capital,
My home lay near Toad Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Renowned in the first troupe of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When my tunes ended, even great masters admired me;
When made up, every beauty envied my look.
Young nobles from Five Tombs fought for my favors,
For one tune, red silks went beyond count.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Laughter this year, next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly.
Brother joined the army, auntie died,
Day after day, youth faded away.
The door grew cold, horses rare;
Aging, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant valued profit above separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since his departure, I guard an empty boat at the mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night I dreamt of youthful days,
Waking in tears, rouge running down my cheeks.'
Hearing the pipa, I had sighed aloud;
Hearing these words, I lamented further.
Both strangers fallen to the ends of earth,
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, ill, dwelling in Xunyang City.
This place is remote, without music;
All year round, no strings or winds are heard.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo circle my home.
What do we hear here morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their rough noise is unbearable to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa language,
It sounds like celestial music, ears momentarily clear.
Please don’t refuse; sit again, play another tune,
So I may compose a Ballad of the Pipa for you.
Touched by my words, she stood long,
Then sat back, tightened strings, which grew urgent.

{"translation":"The Song of the Pipa
By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, his guest was already on the boat;
We raised our cups to drink but had no music to accompany us.
Intoxicated yet unable to find joy, we parted in sorrow;
As we left, the vast river was steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly I heard the sound of a pipa over the water;
The host forgot to return home, the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked quietly who was playing,
But the pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out, added wine, turned up the lamps, and resumed the banquet.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally came out,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
Before any tune was formed, feeling was already present.
Each string murmured with suppressed emotion, each note carried longing,
As if telling of a lifetime unfulfilled ambition.
She lowered her brows and casually continued to play,
Expressing all the boundless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, wiping then strumming,
First playing 'Rainbow Garment', then 'Six Melodies'.
The thick strings sounded noisy like rushing rain,
The thin strings whispered softly like private talk.
Noisy and soft sounds mingled together as she played,
Large pearls and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Sweetly chirping like an oriole under flowers, smooth and flowing,
Muffled and choked like a spring freezing hard under ice.
The cold ice-like spring stagnated, the strings froze and broke off,
When stuck and unable to pass, the sound temporarily ceased.
A hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then suddenly a silver vase burst, water splashing forth,
Iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
The song ended; she drew the plectrum across the center,
In one stroke of the four strings, it sounded like tearing silk.
East boats and west ships were silent without word,
Only seeing the white autumn moon in the center of the river.
She pondered, placed the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and rose with a composed expression.
She said herself that originally she was a girl from the capital city,
Her home was below Toad Mound.
At thirteen she learned to master the pipa,
Her name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, she once made even great masters admire her skill;
Once made up, she was often envied by beautiful courtesans.
The young men of the Five Tombs fought over gifts for her,
For one song, she received countless rolls of red silk.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke as they beat time,
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.
This year laughing and rejoicing, next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Her brother went off to join the army, her aunt died,
Day after day, morning after evening, her beauty faded.
Before her door became desolate, visitors on horseback grew rare,
Growing older, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant valued profit above all and cared little about partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and at the river mouth I guard an empty boat,
Around the boat shines bright moonlight, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of events from when I was young,
Waking weeping, makeup tears streak down in red lines.
Hearing the pipa I sighed already,
And hearing these words, I lamented again deeply.
Both of us are people adrift at the ends of the earth,
Since we have met now, why does it matter if we knew each other before?
I left the imperial capital last year,
Demoted and lying ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year round I do not hear the sound of silk and bamboo instruments.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow rushes and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What objects do I hear here morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, and autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Is there really no mountain songs or village pipes?
They are harsh and cacophonous, difficult to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa speech,
Like listening to celestial music, my ears are momentarily cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece;
For you, I shall compose anew this Ballad of the Pipa.
Touched by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down and tightened the strings, which played faster.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those before,
The whole room listened again and all covered their faces to weep.
Who in the audience shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked wet."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn breeze.
The host dismounts his horse while my guest is already on board,
We raise our cups to drink but have no strings or pipes.
Drunk yet joyless, we face a sorrowful parting;
At departure, the vast river gleams with moonlight.
Suddenly, pipa music drifts over the water;
The host forgets to return, and the guest delays his start.
I follow the sound and quietly ask who plays;
The pipa pauses, as if hesitant to speak.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Add wine, trim the lamp, and restart the feast.
After many calls and entreaties she finally appears,
Still holding her pipa half-covering her face.
She tunes the pegs and plucks a few tentative notes;
Before a melody forms, emotion already fills the air.
Every string sighs, every note carries longing,
As if telling a lifetime of thwarted ambition.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely one after another,
She pours out all the infinite matters in her heart.
Light presses, slow twists, sweeps, then picks;
First 'Rainbow Garments,' then 'Six Strings' dance.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like secret talks.
Rumbling and whispering tangle together:
Large beads and small pearls fall on jade plates.
Birds chirp smoothly beneath blossoms,
A spring chokes under ice, struggling to flow.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings tighten to silence;
Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceases.
Hidden sorrows and dark resentments arise anew;
In this stillness, silence speaks louder than sound.
Then silver bottles burst, water splashing forth;
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends; she strikes all four strings with a sweep—
One sharp tear, like silk ripped apart.
Boats east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects on the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she inserts her plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her face.
She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home near the Frog Hill district.
By thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Named first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After performances, great masters would admire me;
Once made up, even famous beauties grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Mausoleums competed for my favors,
One song earned countless rolls of red silk.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and beauty faded away.
Before my gate, carriages grew sparse and cold;
Getting old, I married a merchant as his wife.
The merchant values profit above all, light on partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since then, guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moon and chilling waters.
Late at night I suddenly dream of youthful days,
Waking in tears, red makeup streaking down my cheeks.'

Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, my grief intensifies.
We are both lost souls wandering the earth;
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Ever since leaving the imperial capital last year,
Exiled and ill, I've lived in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without any music;
All year round I hear not a single string or pipe.
Living near the Pen River where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos surround my home.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Dusko cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their rough, grating sounds are unbearable to hear.
Tonight hearing your pipa melodies,
Like celestial music, they clear my ears and mind.
Please don't refuse; sit again and play another tune,
For you, I'll compose this 'Ballad of the Pipa.'

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits back, tightening strings that turn urgent.
Melancholy unlike the earlier strains;
The whole audience, hearing it anew, covers their faces, weeping.
Who in the hall sheds the most tears?
The Jiangzhou Prefect, whose blue robe is soaked."}

message.content: {"translation":"On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell one night; Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill. The host dismounts while his guest stays on the boat; We raise our cups to drink, yet no music plays. Drunk but without joy, we face our gloomy parting; As we bid goodbye, the vast river is flooded with moonlight. Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifts over the water; The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays setting off. Following the sound, I ask quietly: who is playing? The pipa stops as if she hesitates to speak. I move my boat closer and invite her to meet me; More wine is poured, lamps are lit, and the feast begins again. After many calls and entreaties, she finally comes out, Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face. She turns the tuning pegs and plucks a few strings; Before the melody forms, emotion already flows. Each string sighs deeply, each note full of thought, As if telling of lifelong frustrations unfulfilled. With lowered brows, she plays casually, string after string, Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart. Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, smoothing, then picking; First 'Rainbow Garments,' then later 'Six Melodies.' The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour; The thin strings whisper like private secrets. The rumbling and whispering intermingle in complex play, Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate. Smooth as bush-warblers singing among flowers, Muffled as spring water flowing under ice. When the icy spring chills and the strings seem frozen still, This silence speaks louder than any sound. Then suddenly, like silver vases bursting open, Water splashes forth; Like armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clash. At the song's end, she draws the pick across the center, Four strings snap together with a tear like ripping silk. On boats east and west, everyone falls silent; Only the white autumn moon shines upon the river's heart. Pausing in thought, she puts down her pick and adjusts her clothes, Rising with a composed expression. She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital city, My family lived near Toad Hill. At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, Renowned in the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau. After my songs, even the greatest masters were impressed; Once made up, I often aroused the envy of famous courtesans. Young men from the Five Tombs scrambled to give gifts of silk, For one performance, I received countless red gauzes. Gold-encrusted combs snapped when keeping time to beats; Blood-red dresses stained by spilled wine. Year after year of laughter and merriment followed, Autumn moons and spring winds passed in careless ease. But my brother joined the army, my aunt died, And day by day, my beauty faded. Few horses came before my door anymore; So I married a merchant as a wife in my senior years. Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. Leaving me alone to guard this empty boat at the river mouth, Surrounded only by bright moonlight and cold river waters. Late at night, dreaming suddenly of my youthful days, I wake crying tears that stain my makeup red. Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed deeply; Hearing these words, my sorrow grows heavier. We are both lost souls wandering the ends of the earth; Why must we have known each other before meeting? Since last year I left the imperial capital, Exiled here to sickbeds in Xunyang City. Remote places lack music, And throughout the year, I hear no stringed instruments or flutes. Living near the Pen River where land is low and damp, Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home. What sounds do I hear morning and evening? Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully. In spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights, Often I take wine and pour it alone, drinking by myself. Are there folk songs and village pipes? They are harsh and discordant, hard to endure listening to tonight hearing your pipa language, It is like celestial music clearing my ears temporarily. Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune; For you, I will compose this Song of the Pipa. Touched by these words, she stands for a long time, Then sits back down, tightening strings and speeding up. Her notes are desolate, unlike those played before; Everyone present hears anew and covers their faces weeping. Who among them sheds the most tears? The Blue-robed Sima (magistrate) of Jiangzhou."}

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Six Strings.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his sleeves soaked.

message.content:
这份译文整体流畅，叙事逻辑清晰，但在文化意象的精确性和修辞力度的传达上存在几处关键问题，建议如下：

1.  **文化意象误译**：“虾蟆陵”是唐代长安著名的歌妓聚居地，具有特定的文化指代意义。译为“Shrimp Hill”不仅字面错误（“蛤蟆”非“虾”），且完全丢失了原诗暗示的身世背景与社会阶层信息，导致读者无法理解其昔日繁华与今日落魄的反差。
2.  **“秋娘”指代模糊**：“秋娘”在唐诗中常借指容貌美丽、技艺高超的歌女或才女，并非特指某个人名。直译人名会让英语读者困惑其身份，建议转化为泛指性描述以保留文学隐喻。
3.  **动词力度不足**：描写琵琶声高潮部分时，“clanged”一词显得过于平淡机械，未能充分传达“铁骑突出刀枪鸣”那种金戈铁马、惊心动魄的听觉冲击力，建议选用更具爆发力和动态感的词汇。
4.  **情感修饰词偏轻**：结尾处“sleeves soaked”虽达意，但略弱于原文“青衫湿”所承载的深沉悲怆感。作为全诗情感爆发的落点，建议增强形容词的感染力，以突显诗人闻者泪下的程度之深。

2.  **“秋娘”指代模糊**：“秋娘”在唐诗中常借指容貌美丽、技艺高超的歌女或才女，并非特指某个人名。直译人名会让英语读者困惑其身份，建议转化为泛指性描述以保留文学隐喻。

英文诗：On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling [Frog Mound].
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through.

message.content:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。

忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁？琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。

转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。

轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为《霓裳》后《六幺》。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。

间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。

银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。

沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。

弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。

去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。

其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。

莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作《琵琶行》。

感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

**1. Ambiguity Handling (Preserving Indeterminacy)**
*   **Subject/Agent:** Maintain the fluid shift between "we" (host/guest), "I" (guest/poet), and "she" (musician). Do not force rigid grammatical subjects where the original relies on context.
*   **"Tears":** The final line’s "tears wetting the blue shirt" is ambiguous as to whether it refers solely to the poet or includes the audience. Retain this collective ambiguity; do not specify "my tears."
*   **"Nameless Musician":** Keep her identity secondary to her art and fate. Avoid modernizing her social status beyond the text’s implication of a former courtesan/entertainer turned merchant’s wife.
*   **"Silence":** Translate "无声胜有声" (silence surpasses sound) as an experiential paradox rather than a logical statement, preserving the metaphysical weight without over-explaining.

**2. Imagery Relationships (Visual-Auditory-Synesthetic Links)**
*   **Sound-as-Image:** Strictly adhere to the synesthetic mapping in the music description:
    *   Thunder/rain → Loud/rapid strings.
    *   Whispers/birds → Soft/high strings.
    *   Crashing ice/jade → Sharp/staccato notes.
    *   Breaking bottle/cavalry charge → Sudden crescendo/violent climax.
    *   Tearing silk → Abrupt ending.
*   **Nature-Mood Mirroring:** Link environmental imagery directly to emotional states:
    *   Autumn wind/maple/reeds → Melancholy separation.
    *   Moon on river → Isolation and clarity after chaos.
    *   Cold water/barren reeds/wailing apes → Poet’s exile despair.
*   **Contrast Pairing:** Juxtapose past grandeur (Chang’an, red gauze, silver combs) with present desolation (empty boat, cold moon, aged face) using parallel syntactic structures to highlight temporal decay.

    *   Slow down during biographical narration and the final reflective moments (longer sentences, caesuras).

message.content: {"translation":"At dusk by the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest; Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill. The host dismounts while the guest waits on the boat; We raise our cups but have no music for the drink. Drunk yet joyless, sorrowful at parting, we see only the moon submerged in the vast river mist. Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa; The host forgets to return, and the guest delays his departure. Following the sound, I quietly ask who plays; The pipa ceases, hesitant as if about to speak. I move my boat closer and invite her out; More wine is added, lamps trimmed, and the feast resumes. After countless calls, she finally emerges, Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face. She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times; Before forming a melody, feelings already stir. Each string suppresses sighs, each note carries longing, As if telling of a life unfulfilled. With lowered brows, she plays casually and continuously, Expressing the boundless thoughts within her heart. Light touches, slow twists, sweeps, and picks— First 'Rainbow Garment,' then 'Six Melodies.' The thick strings roar like sudden rain; The thin strings whisper like private talk. Loud and soft notes intermingle, Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate. Smoothly flowing like orioles singing beneath blossoms, Then choked like springs ice-bound under coldness. When the icy spring freezes up, the strings seem to stop; In this silence, hidden grief and secret resentment arise. Indeed, silence speaks more than sound ever could. Then suddenly—like a silver vase bursting, water splashing forth, Or iron cavalry charging with swords clashing and spears ringing. At the song’s end, she draws the plectrum across all four strings, A single sharp cry like tearing silk. Boats east and west fall silent, unaware of time passing; Only the white moon of autumn reflects in the center of the river. She hesitates, inserts the plectrum into the strings, Straightens her clothes, composes herself, and speaks. She says she was originally a daughter of the capital city, Her home near Shrimp Mound Hill. At thirteen she mastered the pipa, Named first in the Imperial Music Bureau’s top troupe. Once finished with a tune, even great masters admired her skill; Upon arranging her makeup, other beauties grew envious. Young nobles from Five Villages competed to gift her red silks; For each song played, countless bolts of fabric were given away. Gold-inlaid hairpins shattered keeping rhythm; Red-dyed skirts stained with spilled wine. This year laughter, next year also laughter; Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly. Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died; Days turn to nights, beauty fades. Doorway deserted, horsemen rare; Growing old, she married a merchant as his wife. Merchants value profit above separation; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. Leaving me behind at the river mouth to guard an empty boat, Wrapped around by bright moonlight and cold river waters. Deep in night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days; Waking with tears streaming down reddened cheeks. Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply; Hearing these words, my sorrow doubled again. Both are wanderers cast adrift at world’s edge— Why must strangers need prior acquaintance? Since last year I left the imperial capital, Banished and ill in Xunyang City. Remote here, without any music; All year long, never hear strings or flutes. Living near Pen River where land is low and damp, Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house. What do I hear morning and evening? Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully. Though spring flowers, summer tides, autumn moons exist, Often I take wine alone, pouring drinks myself. Are there mountain songs and village pipes? Yes—but harsh, discordant, unbearable to listen to. Tonight hearing your pipa language feels like celestial music; My ears cleared momentarily. Do not refuse to sit and play one more piece; I shall compose this 'Ballad of the Pipa' for you. Moved by my words, she stands long before returning; Sitting back, she tightens strings, which now play faster. Sad sounds unlike those heard earlier; Everyone present weeps anew. Who among us sheds most tears? The humid blue robe of Jiangzhou’s Prefect."}

浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。

忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。

千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。

轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为《霓裳》后《六幺》。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。

间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。

别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。

曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。

沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。

弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。

商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。

其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。

莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作《琵琶行》。

感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

message.content: {"translation":"By the Xunyang River, at night I see off a friend; maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill. The host dismounts his horse as the guest boards his ship; raising wine to drink, yet lacking music's sound. Drunk but joyless, sorrowful near parting; when we say goodbye, the vast river reflects the moon. Suddenly I hear pipa strings from over water; the host forgets to return, and the guest stays his departure. Following the sound, I ask softly who plays it; the pipa pauses, the player hesitates to speak. I move my boat closer and invite her to meet; add wine, turn up lamps, and reopen the banquet. Called ten thousand times, she finally emerges, still holding the pipa half-covering her face. Turning pegs and plucking strings two or three notes; before the tune forms, feeling is already present. Each string muffled, each note full of thought, seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled. Head lowered, fingers play continuously, saying out endless things in her heart. Light strokes, slow twists, sweeps, and picks; first the 'Rainbow Skirt', then the 'Six Whistles'. Big strings roar like sudden rain; small strings whisper like secret talk. Roaring and whispering mixed together; big pearls and small pearls falling into a jade plate. Birdsong slides through under flowers; choked spring flows hard beneath ice. Ice spring cold and sluggish, strings freeze and stop; frozen and blocked, sound temporarily ceases. Another kind of hidden sorrow and dark hatred arises; here, silence surpasses sound. A silver vase suddenly breaks, water bursts forth; iron cavalry charges out, swords and spears clang. The song ends; she draws the pick across the center; one strike on four strings sounds like tearing silk. East boats and west ships are quiet with no speech; only seeing the white autumn moon in the middle of the river. **The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.

On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling [Frog Mound].
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through.

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.

Use functional equivalents or transliteration with glossary notes if strict fidelity is required, but for flow, render as dynamic verbs: *"She swept, plucked, strummed, and picked..."*
