On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Six Strings.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his sleeves soaked.

{
  "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell by night,
Maple leaves and reeds rustling in the chill of autumn's might.
The host dismounts from horse while the guest sits aboard his boat;
We raise our wine to drink, but hear no flute or lute’s soft note.
Drunk yet not joyful, we face parting sad and deep,
The moon drowned in the vast river makes us want to weep.
Suddenly, across the water, a pipa’s sound is heard,
The host forgets to go home, the guest stays put undeterred.
We seek the source, asking softly who plays such strains,
The music stops; she wants to speak but hesitates with pains.
We move our boats close together, invite her to appear,
Add more wine, trim the lamps, and start the feast anew here.
Called out many times, she finally emerges shy,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face and eye.
She turns the pegs and plucks three strings, few notes so true,
Before a melody forms, emotion shines through.
Each string suppressed, every sound carries thought,
As if telling a life of ambition thwarted and caught.
Brows lowered, fingers moving gently, one after another,
She tells the endless sorrow hidden in her heart’s cover.
Lightly pinching, slowly rolling, sweeping then picking tight,
First 'Rainbow Robe', then 'Six Beats' fill the night.
The thick strings roar like heavy rain pouring down fast,
The thin strings whisper like private talks held past.
Loud and soft, mixed together, they interweave,
Large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate leave.
Smooth as orioles singing among flowers bright,
Choking as springs flowing under ice at night.
Cold and rough, the stream freezes, strings seem to cease,
Frozen still, no sound comes, only silence’s peace.
Other secret sorrows and hidden hatreds arise,
At this moment, silence speaks better than any cries.
Then suddenly, a silver vase bursts, water spurts out loud,
Iron cavalry charges forth, swords and spears clash proud.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center string,
One sharp sound rips silk, making hearts quiver and sing.
East boats and west barges fall silent, no word is said,
Only the white moon in the middle of the river spread.
She pauses, puts the plectrum between the strings’ hold,
Straightens her clothes, composes herself, becoming cold.
She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My family lived below Shrimp Mound Hill, amidst beauty.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, skillful and keen,
Named first in the Teaching Bureau’s finest scene.
After playing tunes, even great masters were impressed,
When made up, courtesans often felt distressed.
Young nobles from Five Tombs fought over me with gifts,
For one song, countless red silks came in swift shifts.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke keeping time’s beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine, never neat.
This year laughter returned, next year too, passing by,
Autumn moons and spring winds wasted, neither high nor low.
My brother joined the army, my aunt passed away,
Days went by, mornings came, youth faded day by day.
Front door deserted, horses rare, visitors few,
In old age, I became a merchant’s wife, through.
The merchant values profit more than love’s bond,
Last month he went to Fuliang for tea beyond.
He left me alone guarding an empty boat at the mouth,
Moonlight surrounds the ship, river water cold south.
Deep in night, I dream of youthful days gone by,
Wake crying, makeup tears running red down the sky.'
Hearing the pipa, I sighed already deeply moved,
Hearing these words, I murmured again, grief improved.
'We are both people lost at the edge of the world,
Meeting each other now, why did we need old bonds unfurled?'
Since last year, I left the imperial capital behind,
Banished and sick, living in Xunyang, weary mind.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of musical grace,
All year round, no strings or pipes touch this place.
I live near Pen River where land is low and wet,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my set.
What do I hear morning and evening within?
Cuckoo bleeding its voice, apes wailing their din.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often take wine alone, pouring cups in sights.
Are there no village songs and mountain flutes played?
Hoarse and chaotic sounds, difficult for ears displayed.
Tonight hearing your pipa’s language pure and clear,
Like listening to fairy music, ears brighten near.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more tune,
For you, I compose this 'Song of the Pipa' soon.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while still,
Then sat back down, tightened strings, growing shrill.
Sad and mournful, unlike the previous sound,
Everyone present hid faces, tears streaming down.
Who among them shed most tears, drowning in grief?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked beneath."
}

On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling [Frog Mound].
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through.

On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling [Frog Mound].
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through.

*   **四段式结构**:

    2.  **主奏 (Lines 9-24)**: 快速多变。译文采用短促、密集的节奏，模仿琵琶指法的变化（轻拢慢捻抹复挑），在“无声胜有声”处设置明显的排版留白或短句断行。

On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling [Frog Mound].
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through.

    *   **译文问题**："The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour; / The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private."

When we must leave, the moonlight drowns in misty spheres.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa notes arise,
Forgetting home, I linger; guests delay their departure’s ties.
I follow the sound, asking softly who might play,
The strings fall silent, as if shy to speak or stay.
I move my vessel close, inviting her to show her face,
Refill the wine, trim lamps anew, resume the banquet’s grace.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges slow,
Still holding near her pipa, half her beauty’s glow.
She turns the pegs, then plucks two, three tentative sounds,
Before the melody begins, emotion floods the grounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep thought,
As if recounting all the dreams that life has not brought forth.
Her brows lowered low, she plays with fingers free and light,
Expressing boundless sorrows hidden in her heart’s retreat.
With gentle sweeps, slow twists, and flicks both up and down,
First playing *Rainbow Robes*, then *Six Strings’* mournful frown.
The thick strings boom like sudden rain in torrents fierce,
The thin ones whisper secrets soft, as lovers rehearse.
Thick, thin intertwined, they crash and mingle in the air,
Like large pearls falling, small pearls skipping, on jade trays rare.
Clear birdsong glides through floral shadows, smooth and sweet,
Then muffled sobbing flows beneath the ice-bound street.
The cold spring freezes stiff, the strings seem severed tight,
In silence choked, the song pauses, losing its flight.
But deeper grief and hidden hate begin to stir within,
This void of sound speaks louder than any noise can win.
Then suddenly, silver vases break, water bursts apart,
Iron cavalry charge forward, blades clash, spears impart shock.
The tune concludes; she draws her pick across the center line,
Four strings snap once—like silk tearing—to make them mine.
East boats and west barges fall into hushed repose,
Only the white autumn moon reflects upon the river’s flow.
She pauses, inserts the pick among the strings with care,
Adjusts her garments, rises, composing countenance fair.
She states she was a girl from the Imperial Capital’s core,
Her home resided below Shama Ling’s ancient door.
At thirteen, mastering the pipa, skill attained its peak,
Named first among the teaching guilds, where talents seek.
After songs ended, even master musicians bowed in awe,
When dressed, her beauty caused rival courtesans’ envy’s flaw.
Young nobles of Five Tombs contended for her favor’s prize,
For one song played, countless red silks were given as dues.
Gold-inlaid combs broken keeping time’s rhythmic beat,
Blood-colored skirts stained by spilled wine’s crimson heat.
Year after year passed laughter, spring winds and autumn moons spent idly,
Until her brother joined the army, aunt departed silently.
Day fading into dawn, her youth’s vibrant hue grew pale,
The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.
Aged beyond her prime, she wed a merchant man,
Who values profit high, disregards love’s tender span.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where waters cold display.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.
Both are exiled souls drifting at world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?
Since last year I left the imperial city’s grandeur bright,
Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.
This place remote lacks music entirely throughout the year,
No strings or bamboo flutes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp surrounds,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose my dwelling grounds.
What do I hear from dusk till dawn in this desolate place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing in mournful case.
On spring river banks under blooming flowers, autumn nights serene,
I often take my wine alone, drinking amidst the scene.
Are there no mountain songs, nor village pipes’ rough tone?
Their grating cacophony is hard for ears to own.
Tonight I hear your pipa’s voice, celestial it seems,
My ears awakened fresh, washed clean by heavenly beams.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play another song,
For you, I’ll rewrite this ballad, long and strong.
Moved by my words, she stood a while in thoughtful pause,
Sat down again, tightened strings, letting tempo draw.
Melancholy filled the air, different from sounds before,
The whole assembly wept, tears streaming on the floor.
Who shed the most tears among those listening guests?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe stains wettest.

《琵琶行》

浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁？琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为《霓裳》后《六幺》。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作《琵琶行》。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

*   **“虾蟆陵” (Xiama Ling):** 直译 *Toad Tomb Hill* 或音译 *Xiamaling*。保留地名原貌，不强加“墓地”的负面联想（在唐代为长安名胜），维持中性地理标识。

**2. 意象关系构建**
*   **核心三元组：** *Moon-Water-Pipa*。

    *   “秋月白” → *white autumn moon on the river’s heart*：将视觉聚焦于江心，形成静谧闭环。
    *   “绕船月明” → *moonlight encircling the empty boat*：突出孤独感的空间包围性。
*   **声音具象化链：**
    *   急雨/私语 → *hurricane rain / whispers*
    *   珠落玉盘 → *pearls falling into a jade plate* (保留“珠”与“玉”的材质对比)
    *   冰下难 → *trapped beneath ice* (强调阻滞感)

**1. 歧义处理与不确定处保留**

*   **“虾蟆陵” (Hama Ling):** 直译为 “Toad Hill” 并保留地名音译。此名在中文语境中带有长安繁华与世俗气息的双重隐喻，英语中难以完全对应，故保留字面意象以维持原作的地缘特异性。
*   **“青衫” (Qing Shan):** 译为 “blue/green robe”。白居易当时官阶低微，服色为青绿。保留颜色的视觉冲击，不强加“低级官员”的解释性翻译，让读者通过上下文推断身份落差。

*   **自然与音乐的互文:** 强化“月”、“水”、“风”作为背景音轨的角色。前段江浸月、后段秋月白，形成冷色调闭环；中段将琵琶声直接映射为自然声响（急雨、私语、莺啼、泉流、崩瓶、骑鸣），建立通感体系。

*   **色彩与触觉:** 聚焦“红”（枫叶、罗裙、泪）与“白/冷”（荻花、月、江水、青衫）的对冲，象征热烈过往与凄清现状的张力。

*   **序曲 (Stanzas 1-4):** 缓慢、叙事性。使用长句描绘环境，节奏沉郁，模拟送别的滞重感。“忽闻”二字需单独成行或加强停顿，制造转折。
*   **演奏 (Stanzas 5-16):** 动态、多变。前半段轻柔连贯（如珠落玉盘），中段凝滞压抑（冰泉冷涩），后半段爆发激烈（银瓶乍破）。译文句式长度应随乐势起伏：短句表现急促，长句表现绵延，断句表现休止。
*   **自述 (Stanzas 17-28):** 平稳、哀婉。转为第一人称叙述，节奏趋于平缓但情感浓度增加。今昔对比部分需保持平行结构，强化时间流逝的无情。
*   **共鸣 (Stanzas 29-End):** 紧凑、终结。由个人感慨升华为普遍命运。“同是天涯沦落人”一句需独立突出，具有格言般的重量。结尾“青衫湿”需简洁有力，留有余韵，避免过度修饰。

**4. 风格建议**
*   采用自由体诗 (Free Verse) 而非严格押韵，以避免为了韵脚牺牲意象准确性。
*   语言风格应兼具古典雅致与现代清晰度，避免维多利亚式的陈词滥调。
*   保留原文中数字的精确性（十三、五陵、四弦等），以体现纪实感与艺术细节的真实。

刚才的译文在整体意境和叙事流畅度上表现不错，但存在一处明显的**未翻译残留**，以及几处可以优化以更贴合原诗韵律或精确语义的地方。

以下是具体问题及修改建议：

### 1. 严重错误：混合语言残留
**涉及原文：** `终岁不闻丝竹声`
**英文片段：** `All year long, I hear not the sound of丝竹 (strings and flutes).`
**问题说明：** 译文中直接保留了中文词汇“丝竹”及其拼音/注释形式，这在纯英文诗歌翻译中是不允许的，属于未完成翻译。
**依据：** 题目要求“将给定完整作品译成英语诗”，应全篇使用英语。
**修改建议：** 改为 `All year long, no sound of strings or pipes is heard.` 或 `No music reaches my ears throughout the year.`

### 2. 意象与动词的精确性
**涉及原文：** `铁骑突出刀枪鸣`
**英文片段：** `Iron cavalry surged forth, swords and spears clashing.`
**问题说明：** “surged forth”（涌出）略显平淡，未能完全体现“突出”那种突然爆发、冲破阻碍的力度和金属撞击的尖锐感。“clashing”尚可，但可以更强有力。
**依据：** “突”意为突然冲出，“鸣”指兵器碰撞发出的清脆响声，形容琵琶乐音高亢激越。
**修改建议：** 可调整为 `Iron cavalry bursts forth; steel blades ring out.` 以增强节奏感和冲击力。

### 3. 文化专有名词的处理风格一致性
**涉及原文：** `初为霓裳后六幺`
**英文片段：** `First "Rainbow Robes," then "Six Flutes" followed.`
**问题说明：** 《霓裳羽衣曲》通常译为 *Rainbow Garments* 或保留拼音 *Nishangyuyi*；《六幺》（又称《绿腰》），直译 "Six Flutes" 虽能达意，但在古典诗词英译中，有时保留拼音或更通用的音乐术语可能更好。不过此处并非错误，只是风格选择。鉴于前文有“丝竹”的错误，这里需要确保后续没有类似的中文字符残留。此句本身语法正确。
**修改建议：** 无需强制修改，但需注意与前文“丝竹”问题的区别，这里是意译了曲名，是可以接受的。若要更精准，可考虑 `Playing first the 'Rainbow Garments,' then the 'Six Strings' tune.` (*六幺* 本意并非六支笛子，而是曲调名，因结构变化多端如六种花样，故称六幺，也有说法指其节奏快慢变化。"Six Flutes" 是常见的误译或简化译法，严格来说 *Liu Yao* 是曲目名。若追求学术准确，建议用拼音或注明。但若作为诗歌，"Six Flutes" 易读性强，可保留，但需意识到其局限性。)
*注：考虑到用户主要关注明显错误，此处重点在于确认是否还有其他非英文字符。*

### 4. “青衫”的翻译
**涉及原文：** `江州司马青衫湿`
**英文片段：** `The Blue-Robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou, whose robe was wet.`
**问题说明：** “Blue-Robed” 是对“青衫”的一种常见解释（唐代官服制度中，八九品官员穿青色服装）。这里的处理是合适的，能够传达出白居易当时被贬谪、职位低微的身份象征。
**修改建议：** 无需修改。

### 5. 韵律与措辞的微调建议（可选）
**涉及原文：** `寻声暗问弹者谁`
**英文片段：** `Tracing the sound, I asked discreetly who was playing;`
**问题说明：** “discreetly” 对应 “暗问”（暗中询问/悄悄地问），处理得当。但 “Tracing the sound” 稍显生硬，原文是“顺着声音去探寻”。
**修改建议：** 可改为 `Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing;` 更自然。

---

**总结反馈：**

主要必须修改的是第1点中的 **“丝竹”** 未翻译问题。其他部分多为风格优化。

**修正后的关键段落示例：**

> ...
> Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
> **All year long, no sound of strings or pipes is heard.**
> Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
> ...

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Six Strings.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his sleeves soaked.

    *   **问题类型**：无依据增补 / 翻译未完成

    *   **修改建议**：改为 `...I hear not the sound of strings and pipes.` 或 `...no music of silk and bamboo reaches my ears.`

2.  **语气/意象偏差：“呕哑嘲哳”的翻译过于直白且带贬义过头**
    *   **涉及片段**：`Their harsh, grating sounds are painful to the ear.`
    *   **问题类型**：语气/修辞失当
    *   **依据**：原文“呕哑嘲哳难为听”。白居易此处是委婉地表示本地音乐粗糙、不成调，难以入耳，并非单纯的“刺耳疼痛”。译文“grating... painful”略显过度负面，削弱了诗人借以衬托琵琶仙乐之美的对比张力，但尚可接受。若求更精准，可强调其杂乱无章。
    *   **修改建议**：可微调为 `Crude and chaotic, they are hard for the ear to bear.` （保持原意即可，此条为可选优化，非硬伤）。

3.  **遗漏/简化：“名属教坊第一部”的身份表述不够精确**
    *   **涉及片段**：`My name belonged to the First Division of the Imperial Troupe.`
    *   **问题类型**：文化意象准确性
    *   **依据**：原文“名属教坊第一部”。“教坊”在唐代是宫廷雅乐机构，地位极高，“第一部”代表顶尖水平。译文用 `Imperial Troupe` 大致对应，但 `First Division` 稍显现代行政化。不过在诗歌翻译中，此处理解尚可接受。

4.  **关键误译风险：“虾蟆陵”的处理**
    *   **涉及片段**：`My home lay near Shrimp Mound Ridge.`
    *   **问题类型**：专有名词处理

    *   **修改建议**：应保留拼音并加注释或意译。例如：`My home was by the Xiamaling district in Chang'an.` 或 `Living below the famous Xiamaling mound.` （因英文读者不知此地，通常采用音译+模糊方位词处理，避免滑稽的“虾蟆山脊”意象）。

5.  **“同是天涯沦落人”的经典句式处理略平淡**
    *   **涉及片段**：`We are both down-and-out wanderers under heaven’s wide sky;`
    *   **问题类型**：修辞力度减弱
    *   **依据**：原文极具概括力和感染力。译文 `down-and-out` 带有较强的美国俚语色彩（意为穷困潦倒），虽语义接近，但与古诗庄重悲凉的语境略有隔膜。
    *   **修改建议**：可改为更文学化的表达，如 `Both of us are castaways drifting from the ends of the earth;`

---

*   **原句**：`...I hear not the sound of丝竹 (strings and flutes).`
    **改**：`...I hear no sound of strings or pipes.`

    **改**：`My home was down by the Xiamaling landmark.` (注：Xiamaling 为音译，避免歧义)

*   **原句**：`We are both down-and-out wanderers under heaven’s wide sky;`
    **改**：`Both of us, wandering souls adrift at the world's edge;`

其余部分基本符合诗意传达，无需强制修改。

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Six Strings.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his sleeves soaked.

这份译文整体流畅，叙事逻辑清晰，但在文化意象的精确性和修辞力度的传达上存在几处关键问题，建议如下：

1.  **文化意象误译**：“虾蟆陵”是唐代长安著名的歌妓聚居地，具有特定的文化指代意义。译为“Shrimp Hill”不仅字面错误（“蛤蟆”非“虾”），且完全丢失了原诗暗示的身世背景与社会阶层信息，导致读者无法理解其昔日繁华与今日落魄的反差。
2.  **“秋娘”指代模糊**：“秋娘”在唐诗中常借指容貌美丽、技艺高超的歌女或才女，并非特指某个人名。直译人名会让英语读者困惑其身份，建议转化为泛指性描述以保留文学隐喻。
3.  **动词力度不足**：描写琵琶声高潮部分时，“clanged”一词显得过于平淡机械，未能充分传达“铁骑突出刀枪鸣”那种金戈铁马、惊心动魄的听觉冲击力，建议选用更具爆发力和动态感的词汇。
4.  **情感修饰词偏轻**：结尾处“sleeves soaked”虽达意，但略弱于原文“青衫湿”所承载的深沉悲怆感。作为全诗情感爆发的落点，建议增强形容词的感染力，以突显诗人闻者泪下的程度之深。

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting's sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played "Rainbow Robes," then followed by "Six Strings."

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears rang out sharply.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river's heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Hama Ling, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.

Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.

候选1：**英译方案：琵琶行 (Pipa Xing)**

**1. 歧义处理与不确定处保留**
*   **“瑟瑟” (Sese):** 译为 “rustling/shivering” 而非仅指颜色。保留听觉上的风声/叶声双关，暗示秋意寒凉与心境萧瑟的模糊界限。
*   **“霓裳后六幺” (Nishang/Yaozhong Qu):** 音译 *Nishang* 和 *Liuyao*（或 *Six Strings*），加注说明其为唐代著名舞曲。不强行解释其具体旋律特征，保留音乐专有名词的异域感与历史距离感。
*   **“虾蟆陵” (Hama Ling):** 直译为 “Toad Hill” 并保留地名音译。此名在中文语境中带有长安繁华与世俗气息的双重隐喻，英语中难以完全对应，故保留字面意象以维持原作的地缘特异性。
*   **“青衫” (Qing Shan):** 译为 “blue/green robe”。白居易当时官阶低微，服色为青绿。保留颜色的视觉冲击，不强加“低级官员”的解释性翻译，让读者通过上下文推断身份落差。

**2. 意象关系构建**
*   **自然与音乐的互文:** 强化“月”、“水”、“风”作为背景音轨的角色。前段江浸月、后段秋月白，形成冷色调闭环；中段将琵琶声直接映射为自然声响（急雨、私语、莺啼、泉流、崩瓶、骑鸣），建立通感体系。
*   **空间转换:** 突出从“开阔江面”到“封闭船舱”再到“回忆中的长安”最后回归“现实浔阳”的空间收缩与扩张节奏。强调“空船”与“满座”的对比。
*   **色彩与触觉:** 聚焦“红”（枫叶、罗裙、泪）与“白/冷”（荻花、月、江水、青衫）的对冲，象征热烈过往与凄清现状的张力。

**3. 篇章及节奏安排**
*   **序曲 (Stanzas 1-4):** 缓慢、叙事性。使用长句描绘环境，节奏沉郁，模拟送别的滞重感。“忽闻”二字需单独成行或加强停顿，制造转折。
*   **演奏 (Stanzas 5-16):** 动态、多变。前半段轻柔连贯（如珠落玉盘），中段凝滞压抑（冰泉冷涩），后半段爆发激烈（银瓶乍破）。译文句式长度应随乐势起伏：短句表现急促，长句表现绵延，断句表现休止。
*   **自述 (Stanzas 17-28):** 平稳、哀婉。转为第一人称叙述，节奏趋于平缓但情感浓度增加。今昔对比部分需保持平行结构，强化时间流逝的无情。
*   **共鸣 (Stanzas 29-End):** 紧凑、终结。由个人感慨升华为普遍命运。“同是天涯沦落人”一句需独立突出，具有格言般的重量。结尾“青衫湿”需简洁有力，留有余韵，避免过度修饰。

**4. 风格建议**
*   采用自由体诗 (Free Verse) 而非严格押韵，以避免为了韵脚牺牲意象准确性。
*   语言风格应兼具古典雅致与现代清晰度，避免维多利亚式的陈词滥调。
*   保留原文中数字的精确性（十三、五陵、四弦等），以体现纪实感与艺术细节的真实。
候选2：**英译方案：The Song of the Pipa (Li Bai / Bai Juyi)**

**1. 歧义处理与不确定处保留**
*   **“瑟瑟” (Sè sè):** 译为 *rustling chill*。既指风声，也暗含秋意萧瑟感；不强行区分拟声或形容词，保留感官模糊性。
*   **“半遮面” (Bàn zhē miàn):** 译为 *half-hiding her face behind the pipa*。保留动作的羞涩与乐器的遮挡关系，不解释心理状态。
*   **“霓裳/六幺” (Ni Chang / Liu Yao):** 音译 *Neichang* and *Liuyao*，并加注 *(court dances/melodies)*。避免过度归化破坏异域文化质感，承认其作为特定曲目名的不可通约性。
*   **“虾蟆陵” (Xiama Ling):** 直译 *Toad Tomb Hill* 或音译 *Xiamaling*。保留地名原貌，不强加“墓地”的负面联想（在唐代为长安名胜），维持中性地理标识。

**2. 意象关系构建**
*   **核心三元组：** *Moon-Water-Pipa*。
    *   “江浸月” → *the river soaking in moonlight*：强调月影在水中的弥漫感，而非倒影。
    *   “秋月白” → *white autumn moon on the river’s heart*：将视觉聚焦于江心，形成静谧闭环。
    *   “绕船月明” → *moonlight encircling the empty boat*：突出孤独感的空间包围性。
*   **声音具象化链：**
    *   急雨/私语 → *hurricane rain / whispers*
    *   珠落玉盘 → *pearls falling into a jade plate* (保留“珠”与“玉”的材质对比)
    *   冰下难 → *trapped beneath ice* (强调阻滞感)
    *   裂帛 → *tearing silk* (保留清脆刺耳的瞬间爆发力)
*   **色彩隐喻：**
    *   “血色罗裙” → *crimson skirt stained by wine*：连接青春放纵与当下污浊/遗憾。
    *   “青衫湿” → *wet blue robe*：以官职服色代指诗人身份，泪渍象征共情之深。

**3. 篇章及节奏安排**
*   **结构分段：** 分为五幕，对应叙事逻辑转折。
    1.  *The Setting & The Sound* (Lines 1-4): 短促、冷寂句式，模拟秋夜寒意。
    2.  *The Encounter & The Performance* (Lines 5-20): 节奏渐快，多用动词连缀 (*plucking, sliding, breaking*)，模拟琵琶曲由缓至急再骤停的过程。
    3.  *The Silence & The Aftermath* (Lines 21-22): 极简短句，留白大，镜像“无声胜有声”。
    4.  *The Storyteller’s Tale* (Lines 23-44): 叙事语调转为低沉、绵长，使用过去时态堆叠，体现回忆的重量。
    5.  *The Resonance & Conclusion* (Lines 45-End): 主客视角交融，句式复沓 (*Both are...*, *Hearing...*)，结尾单句定格 (*Blue robe wet*)，余韵悠长。
*   **韵律策略：** 采用自由体诗 (Free Verse) 但注重内部重音 (Stress-based rhythm)。关键对仗句 (如“大弦...小弦...”) 保持平行结构 (Parallelism) 以还原中文整齐感；长段落允许跨行 (Enjambment) 以模拟流水般的倾诉感。
本轮只回答“候选N”，不返回裸数字或JSON。

*   **“虾蟆陵” (Xiama Ling):** 直译 *Toad Tomb Hill* 或音译 *Xiamaling*。保留地名原貌，不强加“墓地”的负面联想（在唐代为长安名胜），维持中性地理标识。

**2. 意象关系构建**
*   **核心三元组：** *Moon-Water-Pipa*。
    *   “江浸月” → *the river soaking in moonlight*：强调月影在水中的弥漫感，而非倒影。
    *   “秋月白” → *white autumn moon on the river’s heart*：将视觉聚焦于江心，形成静谧闭环。
    *   “绕船月明” → *moonlight encircling the empty boat*：突出孤独感的空间包围性。
*   **声音具象化链：**
    *   急雨/私语 → *hurricane rain / whispers*

    *   “青衫湿” → *wet blue robe*：以官职服色代指诗人身份，泪渍象征共情之深。

**3. 篇章及节奏安排**
*   **结构分段：** 分为五幕，对应叙事逻辑转折。

    2.  *The Encounter & The Performance* (Lines 5-20): 节奏渐快，多用动词连缀 (*plucking, sliding, breaking*)，模拟琵琶曲由缓至急再骤停的过程。
    3.  *The Silence & The Aftermath* (Lines 21-22): 极简短句，留白大，镜像“无声胜有声”。
    4.  *The Storyteller’s Tale* (Lines 23-44): 叙事语调转为低沉、绵长，使用过去时态堆叠，体现回忆的重量。
    5.  *The Resonance & Conclusion* (Lines 45-End): 主客视角交融，句式复沓 (*Both are...*, *Hearing...*)，结尾单句定格 (*Blue robe wet*)，余韵悠长。
*   **韵律策略：** 采用自由体诗 (Free Verse) 但注重内部重音 (Stress-based rhythm)。关键对仗句 (如“大弦...小弦...”) 保持平行结构 (Parallelism) 以还原中文整齐感；长段落允许跨行 (Enjambment) 以模拟流水般的倾诉感。

**The Song of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell one night,
Beneath autumn’s chill, maple leaves and reed flowers sighed in the breeze.
I dismounted from my horse while he waited on his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but lacked the music of flutes and strings.
Though drunk, joy failed us, and sorrow marked our parting;
Looking away, we saw nothing but the river soaking the moonlight.

Suddenly, sounds of a pipa drifted across the water,
And both host and guest forgot their duties: I stayed, he did not depart.
Tracing the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa ceased, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my ship closer and invited her to come out,
Adding more wine, trimming the lamps, and resuming the feast.
After much calling and urging, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face behind it.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before any melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note carried longing,
As if narrating a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
Head bowed low, fingers moving with ease,
Voicing all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played "Rainbow Robe," then followed with "Six Strings."

The big strings thundered like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whispered like hushed private talk.
Loud and soft notes intermingled,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Melodies slid smooth as orioles singing among blooming branches,
Then choked like spring streams struggling through ice beneath.
Ice-cold water stiffened, strings froze into silence,
The flow blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

Yet hidden grief and deep resentment were born anew—
At this moment, silence spoke louder than words.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water spewed forth,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing loud.
As the song ended, she drew the plectrum sharply across the center,
The four strings sounded once, like silk tearing apart.

Boats to the east and west fell silent, no word spoken,
Only the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her features.

She said herself: "Originally, I was a woman of the capital,
My home lay near Shama Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first among the courtesans of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire me;
When made up, every beauty envied my charm.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to toss silks at my feet,
For one song, they gave countless bundles of red silk.
Gold hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Years of laughter passed into other years,
Autumn moons and spring winds spent carelessly.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Time stole my youth, fading my beauty day by day.
Front gate grew cold, fewer horses visited,
Aged now, I married a merchant man.
He values profits over affection, parting lightly,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now he is gone, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and the chill river waters.
Late at night, I often dream of youthful days,
Waking with tears that ruin my makeup, running down my face."

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her story, I grieved even more.
We are both fallen souls drifting at the world's edge,
Why must we have known each other before meeting today?

"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled here, sick in bed in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear neither silk nor bamboo instruments.
Living near the Pen River, in low, damp land,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring evenings with flowers, under autumn moons,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
Their coarse and harsh tones are painful to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightened the strings, which played faster now.
Melancholy, unlike the previous tunes,
As everyone present listened again, all covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.

By the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell one night,
Beneath autumn’s chill, maple leaves and reed flowers sighed in the breeze.
I dismounted from my horse while he waited on his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but lacked the music of flutes and strings.
Though drunk, joy failed us, and sorrow marked our parting;
Looking away, we saw nothing but the river soaking the moonlight.

Suddenly, sounds of a pipa drifted across the water,
And both host and guest forgot their duties: I stayed, he did not depart.
Tracing the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa ceased, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my ship closer and invited her to come out,
Adding more wine, trimming the lamps, and resuming the feast.
After much calling and urging, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face behind it.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before any melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note carried longing,
As if narrating a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
Head bowed low, fingers moving with ease,
Voicing all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played "Rainbow Robe," then followed with "Six Strings."

The big strings thundered like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whispered like hushed private talk.
Loud and soft notes intermingled,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Melodies slid smooth as orioles singing among blooming branches,
Then choked like spring streams struggling through ice beneath.
Ice-cold water stiffened, strings froze into silence,
The flow blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

Yet hidden grief and deep resentment were born anew—
At this moment, silence spoke louder than words.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water spewed forth,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing loud.
As the song ended, she drew the plectrum sharply across the center,
The four strings sounded once, like silk tearing apart.

Boats to the east and west fell silent, no word spoken,
Only the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her features.

She said herself: "Originally, I was a woman of the capital,
My home lay near Shama Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first among the courtesans of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire me;
When made up, every beauty envied my charm.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to toss silks at my feet,
For one song, they gave countless bundles of red silk.
Gold hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Years of laughter passed into other years,
Autumn moons and spring winds spent carelessly.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Time stole my youth, fading my beauty day by day.
Front gate grew cold, fewer horses visited,
Aged now, I married a merchant man.
He values profits over affection, parting lightly,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now he is gone, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and the chill river waters.
Late at night, I often dream of youthful days,
Waking with tears that ruin my makeup, running down my face."

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her story, I grieved even more.
We are both fallen souls drifting at the world's edge,
Why must we have known each other before meeting today?

"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled here, sick in bed in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear neither silk nor bamboo instruments.
Living near the Pen River, in low, damp land,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring evenings with flowers, under autumn moons,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
Their coarse and harsh tones are painful to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightened the strings, which played faster now.
Melancholy, unlike the previous tunes,
As everyone present listened again, all covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.

**检查意见：**

当前译文在整体叙事流畅度上尚可，但在以下三个视角存在影响原诗核心神韵与准确性的问题，建议修改：

**1. 语义文化视角（关键意象误读）**
*   **乐器术语混淆**：译文中混用了“丝竹”这一中文概念对应的英文直译或泛化词。在英语语境中，“strings and flutes”虽可理解，但未能传达出中国古代文人音乐审美中“丝”（弦乐）与“竹”（管乐）的特定分类美感及排比修辞力度，且前文已明确为琵琶（Pipa），此处应统一语境或强化对比，避免让读者产生乐器类型混乱的歧义。
*   **身份称谓偏差**：“Magistrate”一词过于行政化，削弱了“司马”作为唐代闲职、带有贬谪意味的文化内涵。白居易自指时强调的不仅是官职，更是士大夫在政治失意后的边缘人身份。建议使用更能体现其官僚等级却隐含闲置状态的词汇，或通过上下文强化这种反差。
*   **地名与文化典故处理**：“虾蟆陵”等专有名词若仅音译或意译不当，可能丢失其作为长安繁华娱乐区象征的文化负载意义。需确保译文保留其作为“昔日繁华之地”的隐喻功能，而非仅仅是一个地理坐标。

**2. 情绪修辞视角（张力缺失）**
*   **“无声胜有声”的处理不足**：原诗在此处达到情感高潮，即通过音乐的停顿来烘托内心压抑的痛苦。现有译文虽表达了意思，但缺乏修辞上的顿挫感。建议调整句式节奏，使其在英语中也形成一种“静默中的爆发力”，而不仅仅是陈述句。
*   **悲剧色彩的层次递进**：从女伶的身世到诗人的共鸣，情绪应是层层叠加直至崩溃。现有译文部分段落语气过于平铺直叙，未能充分展现由“技艺展示”转入“身世悲凉”再至“同病相怜”的情感转折剧烈程度。建议在描述哭泣和沉默的场景时，使用更具感染力和画面感的动词。

**3. 英语表达视角（诗意与韵律）**
*   **比喻的陈旧与生硬**：如“Silver bottles burst...”等比喻直接对应中文意象，但在英语中显得突兀且不符合诗歌习惯。英语诗歌更倾向于融合听觉与视觉的通感，建议优化这些比喻的表达方式，使其更符合英语读者的审美直觉，避免机械对译造成的阅读障碍。
*   **节奏单调**：全诗多为松散的自由体长句，缺乏内在的节奏变化来模拟琵琶声的急缓错落。特别是描写音乐演奏的段落，译文未能通过短句、重音或头韵等手段重现原诗的音乐性。建议根据音乐情节调整诗句长短与断句，使语言本身具有乐感。
*   **语域不协调**：部分用词过于现代口语化（如某些连接词或感叹），破坏了古典诗歌应有的庄重与哀婉氛围。需提升词汇的文学性，保持语域的一致性。

**总结建议**：重点修正涉及中国文化特有概念（如官职、乐器类别、地标象征）的翻译准确性；重构音乐描写段落的节奏以匹配原诗的声情之美；打磨关键情感节点（如无声处、泪湿青衫）的英语表达，使其兼具语义深度与修辞感染力。

*   **悲剧色彩的层次递进**：从女伶的身世到诗人的共鸣，情绪应是层层叠加直至崩溃。现有译文部分段落语气过于平铺直叙，未能充分展现由“技艺展示”转入“身世悲凉”再至“同病相怜”的情感转折剧烈程度。建议在描述哭泣和沉默的场景时，使用更具感染力和画面感的动词。

**3. 英语表达视角（诗意与韵律）**
*   **比喻的陈旧与生硬**：如“Silver bottles burst...”等比喻直接对应中文意象，但在英语中显得突兀且不符合诗歌习惯。英语诗歌更倾向于融合听觉与视觉的通感，建议优化这些比喻的表达方式，使其更符合英语读者的审美直觉，避免机械对译造成的阅读障碍。
*   **节奏单调**：全诗多为松散的自由体长句，缺乏内在的节奏变化来模拟琵琶声的急缓错落。特别是描写音乐演奏的段落，译文未能通过短句、重音或头韵等手段重现原诗的音乐性。建议根据音乐情节调整诗句长短与断句，使语言本身具有乐感。
*   **语域不协调**：部分用词过于现代口语化（如某些连接词或感叹），破坏了古典诗歌应有的庄重与哀婉氛围。需提升词汇的文学性，保持语域的一致性。

**The Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, at night, I bid my guest farewell,
As maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat already there,
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music’s air.
Though drunk, no joy remains before our parting tears,
When we must leave, the moonlight drowns in misty spheres.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa notes arise,
Forgetting home, I linger; guests delay their departure’s ties.
I follow the sound, asking softly who might play,
The strings fall silent, as if shy to speak or stay.
I move my vessel close, inviting her to show her face,
Refill the wine, trim lamps anew, resume the banquet’s grace.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges slow,
Still holding near her pipa, half her beauty’s glow.
She turns the pegs, then plucks two, three tentative sounds,
Before the melody begins, emotion floods the grounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep thought,
As if recounting all the dreams that life has not brought forth.
Her brows lowered low, she plays with fingers free and light,
Expressing boundless sorrows hidden in her heart’s retreat.
With gentle sweeps, slow twists, and flicks both up and down,
First playing *Rainbow Robes*, then *Six Strings’* mournful frown.
The thick strings boom like sudden rain in torrents fierce,
The thin ones whisper secrets soft, as lovers rehearse.
Thick, thin intertwined, they crash and mingle in the air,
Like large pearls falling, small pearls skipping, on jade trays rare.
Clear birdsong glides through floral shadows, smooth and sweet,
Then muffled sobbing flows beneath the ice-bound street.
The cold spring freezes stiff, the strings seem severed tight,
In silence choked, the song pauses, losing its flight.
But deeper grief and hidden hate begin to stir within,
This void of sound speaks louder than any noise can win.
Then suddenly, silver vases break, water bursts apart,
Iron cavalry charge forward, blades clash, spears impart shock.
The tune concludes; she draws her pick across the center line,
Four strings snap once—like silk tearing—to make them mine.
East boats and west barges fall into hushed repose,
Only the white autumn moon reflects upon the river’s flow.
She pauses, inserts the pick among the strings with care,
Adjusts her garments, rises, composing countenance fair.
She states she was a girl from the Imperial Capital’s core,
Her home resided below Shama Ling’s ancient door.
At thirteen, mastering the pipa, skill attained its peak,
Named first among the teaching guilds, where talents seek.
After songs ended, even master musicians bowed in awe,
When dressed, her beauty caused rival courtesans’ envy’s flaw.
Young nobles of Five Tombs contended for her favor’s prize,
For one song played, countless red silks were given as dues.
Gold-inlaid combs broken keeping time’s rhythmic beat,
Blood-colored skirts stained by spilled wine’s crimson heat.
Year after year passed laughter, spring winds and autumn moons spent idly,
Until her brother joined the army, aunt departed silently.
Day fading into dawn, her youth’s vibrant hue grew pale,
The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.
Aged beyond her prime, she wed a merchant man,
Who values profit high, disregards love’s tender span.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where waters cold display.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.
Both are exiled souls drifting at world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?
Since last year I left the imperial city’s grandeur bright,
Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.
This place remote lacks music entirely throughout the year,
No strings or bamboo flutes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp surrounds,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose my dwelling grounds.
What do I hear from dusk till dawn in this desolate place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing in mournful case.
On spring river banks under blooming flowers, autumn nights serene,
I often take my wine alone, drinking amidst the scene.
Are there no mountain songs, nor village pipes’ rough tone?
Their grating cacophony is hard for ears to own.
Tonight I hear your pipa’s voice, celestial it seems,
My ears awakened fresh, washed clean by heavenly beams.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play another song,
For you, I’ll rewrite this ballad, long and strong.
Moved by my words, she stood a while in thoughtful pause,
Sat down again, tightened strings, letting tempo draw.
Melancholy filled the air, different from sounds before,
The whole assembly wept, tears streaming on the floor.
Who shed the most tears among those listening guests?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe stains wettest.

message.content:
A Song of the Pipa

On the Xunyang River, that night I saw a guest off;
The maples and reeds rustled in autumn’s chill.
The host dismounted; the guest boarded his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no lute or string.

Drunk, yet uncheerful, we parted in sorrow;
And in parting, the vast river swallowed the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.

Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boats nearer, invited her to meet;
Added wine, relit the lamp, and reopened the feast.

After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
Turning the pegs, plucking the strings, a few sounds,
Before the tune was formed, the emotion was already there.

Each string, subdued and sorrowful; each note, full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, at ease, she played on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking, and flicking,
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.
The bass strings roared like a sudden rain;
The treble strings whispered like private talk.

Roaring and whispering, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding smoothly under the flowers,
Or a choked spring trickling under ice.

The icy spring grew cold, the strings as if frozen;
Frozen, unpassable, the sound paused for a time.
A separate sorrow, a hidden resentment rose;
At this moment, silence was more powerful than sound.

Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth;
Or an iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ended; a stroke of the拨 (plectrum) at the center;
The four strings, as one, sounded like tearing silk.

In the boats east and west, all were silent;
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river.
Pensively, she tucked the plectrum into the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her countenance.

She said she was a girl from the capital,
Living under the Toad Mound.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After a tune, even the best musicians were impressed;
Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.
The young men of the five tombs competed to offer gifts;
For one song, she received countless red silks.
Ornaments and silver combs shattered to the beat;
Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.

Year after year, with laughter and joy,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed without care.
My brother went to the army, my aunt died;
Day after day, her youth faded.
Before her gate, carriages grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit over parting;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She comes and goes by the river mouth, guarding an empty boat;
The moon shines around the boat, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreamed of her youth;
In the dream, she wept, her tears staining her rouge-streaked cheeks.

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again.
Both of us are fallen souls at the end of the world;
Why must we have known each other to meet?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital;
Banished, I lie ill in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year, I hear no strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear, morning and evening?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry, the gibbon’s mourn.
On spring river flower days, autumn moon nights,
I often take wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s words,
It is like hearing immortal music, my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse; sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose a *Song of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then she sat back, tightened the strings, and the tempo quickened.
Desolate, unlike the sound before,
Hearing it again, all present covered their faces and wept.
Who wept the most among the guests?
The Jiangzhou司马, his blue robe wet with tears.

Song of the Pipa

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night,
Where maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn breeze.
I dismounted from my horse while he stayed aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, yet lacked the sound of strings and pipes.
Drunk but joyless, sorrow filled the parting hour,
As moonlight drowned in the vast, misty expanse of the river.

Suddenly, above the water, a pipa’s music rose,
Forgetting home, I lingered; my guest held back his sails.
Seeking the source, I asked softly who played thus,
The music paused as if the player wished to speak, then hesitated.
We moved our boats closer, inviting her to meet us,
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and resumed the feast.

After countless calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa to half-conceal her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few preliminary notes,
Before any melody formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note conveyed longing,
Seeming to tell the tale of ambitions thwarted in life.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving casually, she continued playing,
Pouring out all the endless sorrows within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking again,
First she played the *Rainbow Feather*, then followed with the *Six Strings*.
The thick strings thundered like a sudden rainstorm,
The thin ones whispered soft secrets between lovers.
Thunders and whispers intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Melodious warbling slid like orioles singing among blossoms,
Muffled sobs choked like spring water trapped beneath ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed, then froze the strings into silence,
When motion ceased, the music too came briefly to rest.
A hidden grief, a silent resentment now arose,
At this moment, no sound was louder than any sound.

Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water sprayed,
Like iron cavalry charging forth, swords and spears clashed loudly.
The song ended; with a single stroke across the center,
Four strings snapped together, tearing silk in one sharp cry.

East and west, the boats fell into quietude,
Only the white autumn moon reflected on the river’s heart remained.
Lost in thought, she set down her plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, composing her expression.

"She says: 'Once I was a girl of the capital city,
Living near Shama Ling, by the old terraces.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa’s art,
My name listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau.
When songs ended, even great masters bowed in admiration;
With makeup done, I made Autumn Flower jealous of my grace.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to give me gifts,
For one performance, bolts of red silk piled high beyond count.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke marking time for dance,
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine during revelry.

Year after year passed in laughter and gaiety,
Autumn moons and spring breezes wasted away carelessly.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and beauty faded with age.
Deserted front gate saw few horses or carriages,
So when older, I married a merchant’s wife.

He values profit more than love, indifferent to separation,
Last month he went floating Liang to buy tea, leaving me alone.
Returning, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river waters cold.
Deep in the night, I dream vividly of youthful days,
Waking weeping, tears streaming through red makeup.'"

Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
And hearing her words, I lamented anew.
"We are both wanderers lost at the edge of heaven,
What need have we to know each other before today?

Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital behind,
Demoted, sick, lying low in Xunyang City’s confines.
This place is remote, devoid of music’s charm,
All year long, never heard strings nor bamboo flutes.
Near the Peng River, where land lies low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring my dwelling.

What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing mournfully.
On spring river mornings, flower-filled dawns, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine, pouring it alone.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, noisy tunes are painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears find clarity anew.

Do not refuse to sit further and play another tune;
For you, I shall compose this *Song of the Pipa*."

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat again, tightening strings that played faster still.
Mournful tones unlike those played before,
Filled the room once more; all listeners covered their faces, weeping.

Who shed the most tears among them?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou—his blue robe soaked through.
