译文：At night by the Xunyang River I bid a guest farewell,
As autumn winds rustled through maple leaves and reeds.
The host dismounts, the guest is on his boat;
We raise our cups, but lack the music of strings and pipes.
Drunk yet joyless, we face this sorrowful parting,
And at our farewell, the vast river soaks the moon in its depths.

Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays,
But the pipa falls silent, and she hesitates to speak.
I move my boat close to invite her out,
Add more wine, bring back lanterns, and reopen the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally appears,
Holding the pipa still half-covering her face.

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times,
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string suppressed, every note filled with longing,
Seeming to tell of a life unmet in ambition.
With lowered brows, casually continuing to play,
She speaks out all the boundless thoughts within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and plucking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Strings."

The thick strings rumble loudly like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper softly like private talk.
Loud and soft notes intermingle in complex strumming,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as an oriole’s song beneath flowers,
Choked as spring water flowing under ice, struggling against coldness.
Ice-bound springs chill and stall, strings freeze and stop,
Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceases.

Another kind of hidden sorrow and secret resentment arises;
In this silence, quietness surpasses even sound.
Then suddenly, as if a silver vase bursts, water spurt s forth,
Or iron cavalry charges out, swords and spears ringing clash.
When the tune ends, she draws the plectrum down the center,
All four strings strike once, tearing silk apart.
Boats east and west fall quietly speechless,
Only seeing the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pauses, inserts the plectrum between the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises, composing her expression.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living in a house near Shama Ling (Frog Mound).
By age thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau performers.
After finishing a piece, I could make skilled masters admire;
Once made up, I was often envied by Qi Niang (a famous courtesan).
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to give me gifts,
For one song, red silk scarves received were beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs broke timekeeping with rhythm beats,
Blood-red silk skirts spilled wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent casually.
Then my brother went off to war, my aunt died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, my beauty fades away.
Before my gate, visitors dwindle, scarce are horses and carriages,
Getting older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit highly, take separation lightly,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamt of affairs of my youth,
Waking crying, makeup tears running down my red cheeks."

Having heard the pipa, I already sighed deeply,
Now hearing these words, I sigh again with heavy lament.
We are both people fallen from grace, wandering the edge of heaven,
Since we meet now, why need we have known each other before?
I, since last year, bid farewell to the imperial capital,
Demoted and lying ill here in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year round, I hear not the sound of silk and bamboo instruments.
Living near the Pen River, low land damp and wet,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my dwelling.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower dawns, autumn nights,
Often taking wine alone to pour and drink.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant sounds are unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune for me,
For you, I will compose this Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits back down, tightens the strings, which turn urgent.
The melancholy sound differs from what came before,
Everyone in the room hears it anew and covers their faces weeping.
Who sheds the most tears among those seated?
The Blue-robed official, Sima of Jiangzhou, has his garment soaked.

At Xunyang River's edge, I bid a guest goodbye,

The host dismounts, the guest boards the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but no lute or flute to note.
Drunk without joy, we grieve at parting,
The river merges with the moon, vast and parting.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound;
The host forgets to leave, the guest delays his round.
Following the sound, I softly ask, "Who plays?"
The music stops, she hesitates, words slow to blaze.
We move our boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight the lamp, the feast again to hear.
After a thousand calls, she emerges at last,
Still holding her pipa, half her face hid fast.
She turns the pegs, plucks strings, two or three sounds,
Before the tune begins, emotion already resounds.
Each string's suppressed notes, each sound a sigh,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled desires.
Brows low, fingers loose, she plays on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart alone.
Light touches, slow rubs, strokes and plucks in turn,
First "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Yao" to discern.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings murmur like a private strain.
Rumbling and whispering, mixed in the play,
Like pearls large and small falling on a jade tray.
Like orioles singing smoothly under flowers,
Or a choked spring trickling under icy bowers.
Ice-cold spring, strings stiffen, sound breaks off,
Stuck, impassable, the music takes a pause.
A hidden sorrow, a deep resentment grows,
In this silence, more than any sound that flows.
Then a silver vase shatters, water bursts forth,
Armored cavalry charges, swords and spears clash forth.
The tune ends with a sweep across the center,
Four strings snap as one, like tearing silk asunder.
In all the boats, east and west, a hushed profound,
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart, bright and round.
She ponders, tucks the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, solemnity she brings.
She says, "I was a girl from the capital's heart,
My home lay beneath Toad Hill, a part.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
My name was listed first in the music school's chart.
When a tune ended, even the best players admired,

Young men from the Five Tombs competed for my favor,

Jeweled combs snapped to the beat, red skirts stained with wine,

My brother went to war, my aunt died in her youth,

Before my door, horses grew sparse, visitors few,

I wait at the river's mouth, in an empty boat,

Hearing her words, I sighed again, deeply inside.
Both of us exiles, adrift in this world,

By the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount to meet him on his boat; we raise our wine,
Yet no pipes or strings accompany this drink.
Drunk but not joyful, gloom hangs over parting;
At the moment of goodbye, the moon drowns in the vast river.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifts across the water;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;

After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerges,

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the melody forms, emotion already breathes.
Every string sighs with suppressed longing,

Head bowed, her fingers play on continuously,
Expressing all the boundless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked,

The cold spring chokes, the strings seem frozen still,
Stopped and blocked, the sound momentarily ceases.
But hidden sorrow and dark resentment arise anew;
In this silence, there is more voice than sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting, water spurts out,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing loud.
When the tune ends, the plectrum draws one final stroke,
All four strings ringing together like tearing silk.
East ship, west boat—silent and unmoving;
Only the autumn moon shines white upon the river’s heart.
She muses, puts away the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her dignity.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shrimp Toad Tomb.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed among the first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a song, even great masters would bow to me;

Since he departed, I wait alone on the empty boat at the river mouth,

Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.

Blood-crying cuckoos and monkeys’ mournful wails.

Often I take wine and pour it alone.

Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down, tightening the strings, which played faster.

At the end, everyone in the room wiped their tears.

译文：**The Song of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount to meet him on his boat; we raise our wine,
Yet no pipes or strings accompany this drink.
Drunk but not joyful, gloom hangs over parting;
At the moment of goodbye, the moon drowns in the vast river.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifts across the water;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The music stops, as if she hesitates to speak.
We move our boats closer, inviting her to appear;
More wine is poured, the lamps are turned up bright, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the melody forms, emotion already breathes.
Every string sighs with suppressed longing,
Seeming to tell of a life’s thwarted ambitions.
Head bowed, her fingers play on continuously,
Expressing all the boundless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked,
First playing *Ni Shang*, then *Liu Yao*.
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like secret confidences.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Now clear and sweet, like orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Now choked and low, like spring water trapped under ice.
The cold spring chokes, the strings seem frozen still,
Stopped and blocked, the sound momentarily ceases.
But hidden sorrow and dark resentment arise anew;
In this silence, there is more voice than sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting, water spurts out,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing loud.
When the tune ends, the plectrum draws one final stroke,
All four strings ringing together like tearing silk.
East ship, west boat—silent and unmoving;
Only the autumn moon shines white upon the river’s heart.
She muses, puts away the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her dignity.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shrimp Toad Tomb.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed among the first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a song, even great masters would bow to me;
When made up, every beauty envied my grace.
Young men of the Five Districts competed to gift me brocade,
For each piece played, countless red silks were bestowed.
Jeweled hair ornaments broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter passed,
Autumn moons and spring breezes casually consumed.
Then my brother went off to war, my aunt died,
As evening came and morning returned, my beauty faded.
The door grew cold, horsemen rare,
So, growing old, I married a merchant man.
He values profit above separation,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he departed, I wait alone on the empty boat at the river mouth,
The moon surrounds the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking with tears streaming down my painted cheeks, staining them red."

Hearing her pipa, I have long sighed;
Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.
"Both of us are fallen souls wandering the edge of heaven,
Meeting now, why need we know each other before?"
"Since last year I left the Emperor's Capital,
Banished, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Here, remote and devoid of music,
All year long, no sound of silk or bamboo is heard.
My home is near Pen River, low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow rushes and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear here, dawn to dusk?
Blood-crying cuckoos and monkeys’ mournful wails.
On spring river nights, flower morns, autumn moon evenings,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Is there truly no folk song or village flute?
Their sounds are harsh and jarring, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse; sit again, play one more piece,
And I shall compose for you 'The Song of the Pipa'."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down, tightening the strings, which played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous tones,
At the end, everyone in the room wiped their tears.

译文：**The Song of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell one night,
Beneath autumn’s chill, maple leaves and reed flowers sighed in the breeze.
I dismounted from my horse while he waited on his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but lacked the music of flutes and strings.
Though drunk, joy failed us, and sorrow marked our parting;
Looking away, we saw nothing but the river soaking the moonlight.

Suddenly, sounds of a pipa drifted across the water,
And both host and guest forgot their duties: I stayed, he did not depart.
Tracing the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa ceased, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my ship closer and invited her to come out,
Adding more wine, trimming the lamps, and resuming the feast.
After much calling and urging, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face behind it.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before any melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note carried longing,
As if narrating a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
Head bowed low, fingers moving with ease,
Voicing all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played "Rainbow Robe," then followed with "Six Strings."

The big strings thundered like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whispered like hushed private talk.
Loud and soft notes intermingled,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Melodies slid smooth as orioles singing among blooming branches,
Then choked like spring streams struggling through ice beneath.
Ice-cold water stiffened, strings froze into silence,
The flow blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

Yet hidden grief and deep resentment were born anew—
At this moment, silence spoke louder than words.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water spewed forth,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing loud.
As the song ended, she drew the plectrum sharply across the center,
The four strings sounded once, like silk tearing apart.

Boats to the east and west fell silent, no word spoken,
Only the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her features.

She said herself: "Originally, I was a woman of the capital,
My home lay near Shama Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first among the courtesans of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire me;
When made up, every beauty envied my charm.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to toss silks at my feet,
For one song, they gave countless bundles of red silk.
Gold hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Years of laughter passed into other years,
Autumn moons and spring winds spent carelessly.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Time stole my youth, fading my beauty day by day.
Front gate grew cold, fewer horses visited,
Aged now, I married a merchant man.
He values profits over affection, parting lightly,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now he is gone, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and the chill river waters.
Late at night, I often dream of youthful days,
Waking with tears that ruin my makeup, running down my face."

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her story, I grieved even more.
We are both fallen souls drifting at the world's edge,
Why must we have known each other before meeting today?

"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled here, sick in bed in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear neither silk nor bamboo instruments.
Living near the Pen River, in low, damp land,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring evenings with flowers, under autumn moons,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
Their coarse and harsh tones are painful to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightened the strings, which played faster now.
Melancholy, unlike the previous tunes,
As everyone present listened again, all covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.

After ten thousand calls and summons, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She twists the pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before the melody forms, the emotion is already there.

Each string suppresses sighs, each note carries thought,
Seeming to tell of a lifetime’s unfulfilled ambitions.
Head bowed low, she strums continuously with ease,
Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twirling, brushing and picking,
First playing "Rainbow Robe," then "Six Strings" dance.
The thick strings thunder loudly like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper softly like private talk.

Loud and soft notes intertwine as she plays,
Like large and small pearls falling into a plate of jade.
Smooth like orioles singing beneath flowers,
Muffled like springs flowing under ice, struggling to pass.

When the icy spring turns cold and sluggish, the strings seem frozen;
Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceases.
A hidden sorrow and silent hatred arise anew;
In this moment, silence speaks louder than sound.

Then suddenly, as if a silver bottle breaks and water bursts forth,
It sounds like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clanging.
The song ends; she draws the pick across the center;
One final strike from the four strings, tearing silk-like.

Boats east and west fall silent; no one speaks,
Only seeing the autumn moon white upon the river’s heart.
She contemplates deeply, inserts the pick between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her expression.

She tells me: "Originally, I was a girl from the capital,
My family lived near Shrimp Mound Hill.
By thirteen, I mastered my skill on the pipa,
And was ranked first among the court musicians.

After finishing songs, even great masters admired me;
Once dressed up, every beauty grew envious of me.
Young men of power competed to give me gifts,
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.

Gold-inlaid hairpins broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter followed,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed by idly.

Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turn to nights, and my beauty fades away.
The front door grows desolate; horses and riders are scarce,
So, growing old, I married a merchant for a wife.

Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guard the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river waters cold.

Late in the night, I dream of youthful affairs,
Weeping in dreams, my makeup tears stain the railings red."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words, my sighs grow deeper still.
We are both wanderers fallen far from home,
Meeting now—why need we have known each other before?

Since last year, I left the imperial city,
Banished to lie ill here in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year round, I hear not a single string or flute.

Living near the Pen River, on low, damp ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around the house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing sadly.

On spring days with flowers, autumn nights with moons,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, difficult to listen to.

Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this "Ballad of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits back down and tightens the strings; they play faster.
Melancholy sounds unlike those played before,
Everyone present hears them again and covers their faces in weeping.

Who among the listeners sheds the most tears?
The Blue-robed Prefect of Jiangzhou, wet through with salt.

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.
请检查刚才的英译，说明问题和修改建议，并指出涉及的原文、英文片段。无需另给论证依据。反馈也可能出错，不要因措辞不同就报错。确实没有需要修改的问题时，只回答“无需修改”；否则用自然语言说明。

译文整体忠实且流畅，但存在几处关键误译和风格不一致的问题，建议修改如下：

1.  **误译“呕哑嘲哳”为物理伤害**
    *   **原文**：呕哑嘲哳难为听。
    *   **现译**：They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
    *   **问题**：“呕哑嘲哳”形容声音嘈杂、刺耳、不和谐，“难为听”意为难以入耳/不好听。译为 "painful"（痛苦）虽可接受，但略显夸张；更严重的是前句 "harsh and jarring" 尚可，但整句语感稍硬。不过，最大的问题在于对“山歌与村笛”的否定语气处理得不够委婉或准确，原意是“难道没有……吗？（有的话也）……”。
    *   **建议**：虽无致命错误，但若追求更精准的文化对应，可考虑调整语气。*注：经复核，此条并非严重误译，暂保留，重点看下一条。*

2.  **“名属教坊第一部”的归属误解**
    *   **原文**：名属教坊第一部。
    *   **现译**：My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
    *   **问题**：“教坊” (Jiaofang) 是唐代的宫廷音乐机构，译为 "imperial academy"（帝国学院/皇家学院）不准确，容易让人联想到学术机构而非艺术培训机构。通常译为 "Music Bureau" 或保留拼音并加注，或译为 "Imperial Music Academy/Bureau"。此外，“第一部”指第一梯队/头牌位置，"first troupe" 尚可，但 "name belonged to" 有点生硬。
    *   **建议**：改为 "I was listed in the top tier of the Imperial Music Bureau." 或 "My name was recorded in the First Division of the Jiaofang (Music Bureau)."

3.  **“五陵年少争缠头”的文化意象缺失**
    *   **原文**：五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
    *   **现译**：Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade, / For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
    *   **问题**：“缠头”是唐代习俗，指赠送给歌伎的锦帛等礼物，作为赏赐。译文中 "fought to wrap me in brocade" 字面意思变成了“争着把我包在绸缎里”，这是严重的误译，产生了歧义甚至不当联想。应理解为“争相赠我缠头之礼（锦帛）”。
    *   **建议**：改为 "The young nobles of the Five Mausoleums vied to give me silks as rewards; / A single song earned me countless bolts of red gauze."

4.  **“血色罗裙翻酒污”的主被动关系不清**
    *   **原文**：血色罗裙翻酒污。
    *   **现译**：Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
    *   **问题**：这句诗描写的是年轻时的狂放生活，酒洒在裙子上弄脏了裙子。译文用名词短语 "stained by..." 略显静态，未能完全还原原诗的叙事画面感，但基本达意。若与前句并列，需注意语法平行。此处可接受，但若能与上一句 "vied to give me..." 形成更好的节奏呼应会更好。

5.  **“江州司马青衫湿”的身份标识**
    *   **原文**：江州司马青衫湿。
    *   **现译**：The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.
    *   **问题**：“青衫”特指唐代低阶官员的服色，白居易当时被贬官，职位较低。译作 "blue robe" 正确，但为了体现文学性，有时也会直译 "green robe" (因古代青色包含蓝绿)，但在英语语境中 blue 更通用。主要问题是 "Magistrate"（行政长官/法官）对于“司马”这个特定唐代官职来说，虽然功能上有重叠，但 "Sima" 或 "Vice-Magistrate" / "Military Governor's Aide" 可能更精确？其实 "Magistrate" 在此处常被用来泛指地方主管官员，鉴于白居易是“江州司马”，实际上是闲职副手。不过在诗歌翻译中，"Magistrate" 是可接受的通用译法。**关键错误点不在这里**。

6.  **重大误译：“大弦嘈嘈如急雨”**
    *   **原文**：大弦嘈嘈如急雨。
    *   **现译**：The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
    *   **问题**："Rumble" 通常指低沉的轰鸣声（如雷声或引擎），而琵琶的大弦（低音弦）发出的声音应该是浑厚有力的，但不一定是 "rumble"。更重要的是下一句对比。不过最大的问题在 **"小弦切切如私语"** 的翻译。
    *   **修正关注点**：见第7条。

7.  **“银瓶乍破水浆迸”的比喻失真**
    *   **原文**：银瓶乍破水浆迸。
    *   **现译**：Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
    *   **问题**：原文强调的是声音的突然爆发和清脆激烈。译文 "water bursting forth" 侧重于水的视觉流动，稍微偏离了听觉焦点，但尚可接受。然而，后半句 "iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud" 很好地对应了“铁骑突出刀枪鸣”。

8.  **最严重的误译：**
    *   **原文**：犹抱琵琶半遮面。
    *   **现译**：Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
    *   **问题**：这句非常经典，译文基本正确。但是看前面的 **"千呼万唤始出来"** -> **"After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,"**。这里的 "appears" 很好。

    **重新检查发现的一个明显逻辑/翻译错误：**
    *   **原文**：浔阳江头夜送客... 主人下马客在船...
    *   **现译**：At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang... I dismount; my guest is already on board...
    *   **分析**：原文“主人下马客在船”是一种互文修辞，意思是主人和客人都下了马，然后登上船（或者主人在岸上骑马到达，客人在船上等待，最终汇合于船）。译文 "my guest is already on board" 暗示客人一直在船上，这不符合常理（客人通常是来送别或聚会的人，之前可能在岸上）。更准确的互文理解是：Both host and guest alight/dismount and proceed to the boat. 或者 Host gets off horse, guest is on boat (meaning they meet there). 现有译文造成了细微的场景误解，但不算致命。

    **确实存在的硬伤：**
    *   **原文**：莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
    *   **现译**：Please, sit again and play another tune; / For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'
    *   **问题**：“翻作”在这里的意思是“依韵改写”或“创作一首新诗来记录这件事/回应你的演奏”，不仅仅是 “compose for you”（为你作曲）。而且 “莫辞” 是 “Do not refuse/decline”。译文 "Please, sit again" 丢失了 "Do not refuse" 这种恳请对方不要推辞的语气，显得过于随意。
    *   **建议**：改为 "Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece; / I shall write for you this 'Ballad of the Pipa'."

    *   **原文**：感我此言良久立
    *   **现译**：Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
    *   **问题**：原文是诗人说“莫辞...”，琵琶女听到后“感我此言良久立”。译文正确。

    **另一个硬伤：**
    *   **原文**：秋月春风等闲度
    *   **现译**：Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
    *   **问题**："Treated casually" 语法怪异，应为 "passed casually" 或 "spent idly"。"度" 是度过时光。译文把主语搞混了，像是“明月清风被对待得很随意”。
    *   **建议**：改为 "I passed autumn moons and spring breezes idly."

    **再一个硬伤：**
    *   **原文**：绕船月明江水寒
    *   **现译**：Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
    *   **问题**：原文意境很美，译文尚可。

    **关于“同是天涯沦落人”：**
    *   **现译**："Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;"
    *   **问题**：加了引号，表示这是引用，但后面紧接着 "Since we meet here..."，导致段落结构混乱。原文是对话，译文混合了叙述和直接引语。前面有 She says, "Once I was..."，这一段应该明确是谁在说话。根据上下文，这是白居易的感慨，或者两人的共鸣。如果是白居易说的话，不应放在 She says 的引号内延续。看译文结构：
        `She says, "Once I was... [long quote] ...dreamed of youthful days...`
        然后突然断开：`Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;` (这是白居易的旁白)
        然后 `"Both of us are exiles..."` (这句没标明是谁说的，看意思像白居易)。
        如果 `Both of us...` 也是 She says 的一部分，那就不对了，因为这是白居易的感叹。
        **格式错误**：译文将白居易的议论部分直接接在琵琶女的自述引号之后或混淆了。
        检查译文：
        `She says, "...red streaked with tears.` (引号结束)
        `Hearing the pipa...` (白居易旁白)
        `"Both of us...` (开始新引号? 还是继续?)
        看标点：`"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth; / Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?` 这两句显然是白居易的心声/诗句，不是琵琶女说的。但译文没有明确指出说话人切换，或者将其置于引号内容易让读者误以为是琵琶女说的。
        **建议**：需明确标示这部分是诗人的独白，或去掉引号表示诗人内心活动，或在前面加 "I thought:"。

    **总结需要修改的具体点：**

    1.  **语义误译**：“五陵年少争缠头” 译为 "fought to wrap me in brocade" 错误，易产生歧义。应改为 "vied to give me silks/rewards"。
    2.  **语法/搭配不当**：“秋月春风等闲度” 译为 "Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually" 不通顺，主语错位。应改为 "I spent autumn moons and spring breezes idly/casually."
    3.  **视角/说话人混淆**：“同是天涯沦落人...” 这一节紧接在琵琶女自述之后，译文未清晰区分这是白居易的感悟，仍带有引号或处于连续语境中，极易误导读者认为是琵琶女所说。需表明这是诗人的心声。
    4.  **语气减弱**：“莫辞更坐弹一曲” 译为 "Please, sit again..." 丢失了 "Do not refuse" 的原意。
    5.  **词汇精度**：“教坊” 译为 "imperial academy" 不够准确，建议用 "Music Bureau"。

    基于以上分析，给出反馈。
请对照原作核实上面的检查意见，只修正确实存在的问题，允许保留原稿。给出完整英文译文。

{"translation":"At night, I saw off a guest by the Xunyang River;
Maple leaves and reeds shivered in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted to board the ship where his friend waited,
Raising wine to drink, yet lacking pipes and strings.
Drunk but joyless, we mourned our parting soon,
Bidding farewell as the vast river bathed the moon.
Suddenly, from over the water, came sounds of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed departure.
Following the sound, I softly asked who was playing;
The pipa paused, hesitating, as if it wished to speak.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine was poured, lamps turned up, and the feast resumed.
After many calls, she finally emerged,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa held close to her chest.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few notes first;
Before the tune formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string sighed low, every note carried thought
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled, ambitions thwarted.
With lowered brows, fingers moving freely on,
She voiced all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept then struck—
First 'Rainbow Shirt,' then 'Six Melodies' followed.
The thick strings rumbled like rain falling fast,
The thin strings whispered like private talk at last.
Mixed together, loud and soft, they intertwined,
Like pearls large and small dropping into a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blooming flowers,
Choked like springs flowing under ice, struggling to find their way.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seemed frozen tight;
When blocked completely, sound ceased for a moment.
Other hidden griefs and resentments were thus born;
In this silence, no sound surpassed the sound before.
As suddenly as a silver vase bursting with liquid spray,
Or iron cavalry charging forth, swords clashing away.
The song ended; the pick drew across the center string;
All four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fell silent, words unheard,
Only the white autumn moon seen on the river's breast.
Pondering deeply, she put the pick among the strings,
Straightened her dress, rose, composed her look.
She said: "Once I was a girl of capital fame,
My home lay near Shama Ridge, not far from the gate.
Mastered the pipa at thirteen years of age,
My name listed first in the Music Bureau's stage.
After finishing songs, even masters felt inferior;
When made-up, rival beauties envied my attire.
Young men of Five Tombs vied to give me gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red gauze they offered.
Gold-inlaid combs broke keeping time to beats,
Blood-red skirts stained when spilling wine repeated.
Year after year passed laughter and delight,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent idly through the night.
Then brother went to war, aunt died too soon,
Days turned to nights, beauty faded, youth undone.
Front door became cold, horsemen rare to see,
Aged now, I married a merchant's wife to be.
The merchant values profit, cares little for parting,
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and chilling river flow.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in dreams, tears streaking rouge down my face."
Hearing the pipa, I had long since sighed,
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"We are both wanderers fallen to the ends of earth;
Meeting here, why need we have known each other beforehand?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished, sick, lying in Xunyang city.
This place is remote, without any music,
All year round, never hear strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the camp.
What do I hear there morning and evening so?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
On spring rivers' flowering mornings, autumn nights with moon,
Often take wine alone, pour it down without company.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
Harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is as if listening to celestial music, ears newly clear.
Please sit again and play another tune;
For you, I shall write this 'Ballad of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Returned to sit, tightened strings, played faster still.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before,
Everyone in the room, hearing anew, wiped away tears.
Who shed most tears among those seated there?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, blue robe wet with care."}

候选1：Ballad of the Pipa

By night at Xunyang River’s head, I saw a guest depart;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn’s chill.
The Host dismounted from his horse, the Guest stood on his boat,
We raised our cups to drink, yet lacked strings and pipes to cheer.
Drunk but not joyful, sorrow loomed as parting drew near;
At farewell, vast and boundless, the river soaked the moon.
Suddenly, over the water, pipas sounded clear—
The Host forgot to return, the Guest set sail no more.
I followed the sound, asking softly: Who plays here?
The pipa paused; she wished to speak, yet hesitated long.
I moved my ship close by her side, inviting her to see;
Added wine, brought back the lamp, and opened up the feast anew.
Called out ten thousand times, she finally came forth,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face in shy restraint.

She turned the tuning pegs, plucked three or four notes first,
Before the melody formed, emotion already stirred.
Every string suppressed a sigh, every tone carried longing deep,
As if telling of a lifetime thwarted, hopes lost in sleep.
Lowered brows, fingers moving with practiced ease,
Pouring out all infinite matters held within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing and then picking—
First the "Neon Robes," then the "Six Beats" began their striking.

The great strings clattered loud like sudden, rushing rain,
The small strings whispered soft like private talk between lovers’ ears.
Clattering and whispering mixed in intricate play,
Like beads of jade, great and small, clatter on a silver plate.
Smooth and fluid like orioles singing beneath blossoms’ shade,
Choked and sobbing like springs flowing under ice’s cold blade.
Ice-cold and stiff, the strings froze, sound ceased abruptly there,
But hidden sorrows and secret hatreds rose from silence rare.
At that moment, wordlessness spoke louder than song,
Then suddenly the silver flask broke, water bursting forth strong!
Cavalry charged with iron hooves, swords and spears rang out sharp,
When the tune ended, she gathered the plectrum for a final scrape.
One sharp cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart—
East ships and west boats fell silent, hearts held tight.
Only one thing remained visible in the quiet night:
The autumn moon over the river center, shining white.

She pondered long, inserted the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, composed her face’s expressions.
She told me: “I was born a girl in the capital’s streets,
My home lay near Hama Ling, where noble spirits meet.
At thirteen, my pipa skill was fully grown,
My name listed among the first rank of the Imperial Troupe.
After finishing a piece, even masters bowed in awe,
When dressed, my beauty sparked envy in Qiuniang’s law.
Young men of Wuling vied to wrap red silk around my neck,
For one single song, they gave silks without reckoning check.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs shattered keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spills of wine during revelry’s prime.
Year after year laughter continued, season after season passed,
Autumn moons and spring winds spent idly, joy lasting last.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died away,
Evenings faded, mornings came, color left my face grey.
Gate grew lonely, horses sparse, visitors few,
Aging maiden married a merchant, fate led me through.
He valued profit high, separation light, carefree,
Last month went to Fuliang to buy tea, far from me.
Gone and come, I guard an empty boat at river’s mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river waters cold south.
Deep in the night, I dreamt of youthful days once more,
Waking with tears, makeup streaked red, washing down my floor.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply at its woe,
Then heard her words, my own grief swelling higher flow.
“Both we are wanderers fallen from the edge of sky,
Meeting now, why must we have known each other in passing by?”
Since last year I left the Emperor’s City behind,
Exiled to sickbed rest in this remote, damp town confined.
Xunyang is isolated, devoid of music’s art,
All year round, no silk and bamboo sounds touch the heart.
Near the Pen River, land low and wet surrounds my home,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos encircle where I roam.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk within these walls?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, and monkeys’ mournful calls.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights under moon,
Often take wine alone, pouring it down, drinking sorrow soon.
Are there no mountain songs or village flute tunes here?
Rough, harsh, discordant noises—hard to bear, unclear.
Tonight I hear your pipa speech, so pure and sweet,
As if hearing celestial music, making ears complete.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another strain,
For you, I compose this Ballad of the Pipa’s pain.

Touched by my words, she stood for a long while still,
Then sat back down, tightened strings, played with urgent thrill.
Mournful tones unlike those before, sadder, deeper, darker hue,
Everyone in the room listened again, tears covering view.
Who among the guests shed most tears, soaking their eyes?
It was the Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue official robe dries—
No, the blue robe remains wet, stained by sorrow’s tide.

Loud and soft together, they intermingle and clash,
Like pearls, great and small, clattering on a jade dish’s flash.

Choked as a spring flowing under ice, hard to wade.
The cold spring freezes, the strings seem to cease,
A blockage halts the flow, bringing moments of peace.
Then springs forth hidden grief, unspoken hate anew—
At this silent pause, sound surpasses what words can do.

Iron cavalry charges, swords clash in battle’s fray.

Only the autumn moon over the river center shone white instead.

Straightens her clothes, rises with a composed face.

Living near Hama Ling, where music and dance abide.
Thirteen years old, I mastered the pipa’s art,
Named among the First Section, a standout heart.
My songs made skilled musicians bow in shame,
My makeup stirred envy in Beauty Qiuniang’s flame.

The young men of Wuling fought to drape me in brocade,
For one song alone, red silk came in a huge trade.
Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped keeping time’s beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine’s heat.
Year after year of laughter, joy’s fleeting reign,
Autumn moons and spring winds passed without care or pain.

But my brother joined the army, my auntie died away,
Dusk comes, dawn goes, my beauty fades to gray.
My door grows desolate, horses rare and few,
In age, I married a merchant, bound for business new.
He values profit high, cares little for goodbye,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, leaving me dry.

Gone and going back, I guard an empty boat here,
Moonlight circles the hull, the river water chills fear.
Late at night, I dream of youthful days gone by,
Waking, tears stain my rouge, wetting the pillow’s dye.”

Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply before,
Now hearing these words, my grief weighs more.
We are both people lost at the world’s far edge,
Why must we have known each other to feel this pledge?

Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital’s throne,
Demoted, sick, lying low in Xunyang City alone.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of musical grace,
All year round, no silk-string sounds fill the place.
My home lies near the Pen River’s damp, low ground,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo all around.

What do I hear there, morning or evening’s call?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, gibbons’ mournful howl.
On spring rivers when flowers bloom, or autumn nights bright,
I often take my wine and drink it alone, out of sight.
Are there no mountain songs or village flute tunes?
They are rough, cacophonous, harsh to listen to soon.

Tonight I heard your pipa speech, its heavenly tone,
My ears cleared as if listening to gods upon their throne.
Do not refuse to sit down and play another tune,
For you, I shall compose this Ballad of the Pipa’s swoon.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while still,
Returned to sit, tightened strings, playing with urgent skill.
Her gloom is different now from the voice before,
The whole audience hears, covers faces, weeping sore.

Who in the room sheds the most abundant tear?
The Jiangzhou Sima’s blue official robe is wet with severe fear.

译文：At the head of Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest was on board;
We raised our wine cups, longing to drink, but lacked music—no flutes or strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy, only sorrow before parting;
As we parted, the vast river immersed the moon in its depths.

Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifted over the water;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing;
The pipa paused, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And though the melody had not yet begun, emotion was already there.
Each string was suppressed, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a lifetime spent unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, she played with flowing ease,
Expressing all the endless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and plucking again,
First playing *Ni Chang*, then *Liu Yao*.

The thick strings rumbled like heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like intimate murmurs.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in mixed play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Bird-like chirps slid smoothly beneath flowers,
Trickling springs choked difficultly under ice.
The cold, sticky spring froze, and the strings seemed to break;
When broken and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

But another secret sorrow and hidden resentment arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Suddenly, silver bottles burst, water splashing forth,
Iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clashing loudly.
As the tune ended, she drew the pick across the center,
The four strings struck together, tearing like silk cloth.

East boats and west ships fell silent,
Only the white moon in the heart of the river remained visible.
She pondered, set down the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and arranged her expression.

She said herself that she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed in the first rank of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing songs, even skilled masters would admire her;
Once made up, every beauty envied her.
Young men from the Five Mausoleums fought to give her gifts,
One song earned her unknown quantities of crimson silk.
Gold-inlaid combs were shattered keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by overturned wine.

This year laughter and merriment, next year too,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
Her brother enlisted in the army, her aunt died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, and her beauty fades.
Before her gate, visitors became few, horses sparse,
Aging, she married a merchant as his wife.
That merchant values profit lightly regarding separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and she guards the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.

Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days,
Waking crying, makeup tears stain the red railings.

Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
Then hearing these words, I lamented anew.
Both are people fallen into wandering fate beyond the sky’s edge,
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long, no sound of silk and bamboo is heard.
My dwelling is near Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries and apes wailing sadly.
On spring rivers’ flower mornings and autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.

Is there no mountain song and village flute?
They are hoarse, harsh, and unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I shall compose the Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, which grew faster.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those before,
The whole audience listened again, covering their faces and weeping.
Who among the guests wept the most?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose green robe was wet.

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.

这份译文整体流畅，很好地传达了原诗的叙事脉络和主要情感，但在**意象的精确对应、修辞力度的还原以及部分关键细节的准确性**上存在若干明显问题。以下是具体的检查结果与修改建议：

### 1. 意象与动词的误译（中等严重程度）
*   **原文**：“枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟”
    *   **现译**："Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill."
    *   **问题**：“Shiver”通常指因寒冷或恐惧而颤抖，用于植物略显拟人化过度且偏离“瑟瑟”作为风声或树叶摩擦声的本意。白居易此处是用声音烘托凄清氛围。
    *   **建议**改为："Maple leaves and reeds rustle, a cold autumn wind sighing." 或保留 "rustle" 以体现听觉意象。

*   **原文**：“犹抱琵琶半遮面”
    *   **现译**："Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face."
    *   **问题**：漏掉了“抱”的姿态感以及“遮”的动作方向性。虽然意思对，但略显平淡。更重要的是，“holding... before her”不如“embracing the pipa, covering half her face”来得具有古典美感和羞涩的动态。
    *   **建议**改为："Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face."

### 2. 典故与专有名词的处理偏差（高严重程度）
*   **原文**：“五陵年少争缠头”
    *   **现译**："Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,"
    *   **问题**：**严重误译**。“缠头”在唐代指赠给歌伎的锦帛（赏赐），并非指用锦缎把人“包裹起来”。译者望文生义，将隐喻变成了字面动作，导致画面荒谬。
    *   **建议**改为："The young nobles from the Five Mausoleums vied to offer me silk rewards," 或 "...vied to throw jewels at my head," (注：缠头具体指赏赐之物)。

*   **原文**：“钿头银篦击节碎”
    *   **现译**："Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,"
    *   **问题**：这里“钿头银篦”确实是发饰，但“snapped”暗示是梳子本身断了。历史上这是形容演奏激烈，打拍子的器物碎裂，或者更常见的是形容酒席上狂欢时，金翠首饰随节奏撞击破碎（极言奢华与狂放）。译文尚可接受，但“Gold-inlaid”对应“钿头”略显宽泛，“silver comb”对应“银篦”。
    *   **微调建议**："Silver combs with jeweled heads shattered keeping time,"

### 3. 语气与情感的弱化（中等严重程度）
*   **原文**：“同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！”
    *   **现译**："Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth; Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?"
    *   **问题**：原文是一种强烈的共鸣与感叹，带有宿命感。译文用了 "Since we meet here..." 这种逻辑连接词，削弱了那种“无需多言，心意相通”的瞬间爆发力。
    *   **建议**改为："We are both wanderers cast to the horizon's edge; Meeting thus, what need was there for prior acquaintance?"

*   **原文**：“呕哑嘲哳难为听”
    *   **现译**："They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to."
    *   **问题**：“Painful”太重了，原文更多是表达那些音乐粗俗、杂乱、不堪入耳，令人皱眉而非痛苦。
    *   **建议**改为："Their sounds are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear."

### 4. 细节遗漏或增补无据（轻微至中等）
*   **原文**：“主人下马客在船”
    *   **现译**："I dismount; my guest is already on board;"
    *   **问题**：这是互文见义，意思是“我和客人都下了马/上了船”或者描述一种送别的场景交错。译者处理成“I dismount”和“guest is on board”，虽然符合语境，但略微丢失了原句紧凑的画面感。不过为了英语通顺，此处理解可接受，不算硬伤。

*   **原文**：“曲罢曾教善才服”
    *   **现译**："When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;"
    *   **问题**：“善才”是当时著名的琵琶师曹善才，也可泛指技艺高超的乐师。译为 "great musicians" 可以，但 "bowed in admiration" 属于增补。原文只是说让他们“服气/佩服”。
    *   **建议**改为："...made even master players concede,"

*   **原文**：“暮去朝来颜色故”
    *   **现译**："Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away."
    *   **问题**：语序颠倒。原文是“暮去朝来”（时间流逝，傍晚过去清晨到来），译文写成了“Days turned to nights”（白天变黑夜），虽然都是时间流逝，但与原文意象相反。
    *   **建议**改为："As evenings pass and mornings come, my looks grew old."

### 5. 结尾的高潮处理
*   **原文**：“江州司马青衫湿”
    *   **现译**："The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet."
    *   **问题**：非常忠实，但缺乏一点诗意张力。考虑到前文“满座重闻皆掩泣”，最后一句应更具象。
    *   **建议**保持原样即可，或者微调为："The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Magistrate, dampened by tears."

Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
The young nobles of the Five Mausoleums vied to bestow silks upon me,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
As evenings fade and mornings rise, my beauty waned;
My brother went off to war, and my aunt died.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"We are both exiles drifting to the world's end;
Meeting thus, what need had we to know each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Harsh and discordant, they are unpleasant to the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Magistrate, dampened by tears.

message.content:
这份译文在上一轮修正后已经非常准确，主要误译（如“缠头”）和逻辑错误（如时间流逝方向）均已纠正。然而，若以严格对照原作的标准审视，仍有几处细节存在**意象流失、语气偏差或微小的增补问题**，建议进一步优化。

以下是具体检查结果：

### 1. 意象与修辞的弱化（轻微至中等）
*   **原文**：“似诉平生不得志”
    *   **现译**："As if telling of a life frustrated by fate."
    *   **问题**：“Fate”（命运/宿命）带有强烈的不可抗拒感，而“不得志”更多指仕途不顺、抱负未展的社会性挫折。用 "fate" 略显消极被动，原诗强调的是才华被埋没的愤懑。
    *   **建议**改为："As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition," 或 "...of thwarted aspirations,"

*   **原文**：“弦弦掩抑声声思”
    *   **现译**："Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,"
    *   **问题**：“Sighs”（叹息）是增加的动作，原文“掩抑”意为压抑、含蓄、低沉。虽然音乐常伴叹息，但这里侧重的是演奏技法带来的情感克制。“Restrain”尚可，但“Sighs”属于无依据增补。
    *   **建议**改为："Every string is suppressed, every sound holds sorrow,"

*   **原文**：“东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白”
    *   **现译**："Boats to the east and west fall silent; Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart."
    *   **问题**：译文基本准确，但“reflects”（倒影）是物理描述。原诗“江心秋月白”是一种视觉印象——月光洒满江心，一片洁白。这种“空寂”的美感稍显平淡。不过此处理解可接受，不算硬伤。

### 2. 专有名词与文化背景的精确度（中等）
*   **原文**：“名属教坊第一部”
    *   **现译**："My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy."
    *   **问题**：“Imperial academy”通常指太学或国子监（教育机构），而“教坊”（Jiaofang）是管理宫廷音乐的机构。译为 "imperial music bureau" 或 "first division of the Imperial Music Bureau" 更准确。
    *   **建议**改为："I was ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau,"

*   **原文**：“曲罢曾教善才服”
    *   **现译**："When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;"
    *   **问题**：“Bowed in admiration”（鞠躬致敬）是动作描写，原文“服”是心理状态（折服/佩服）。乐师不一定都鞠躬，而是心悦诚服。
    *   **建议**改为："Even master players were convinced by my skill," 或 "...won the acclaim of skilled masters,"

### 3. 语气与情感的细微差别（轻微）
*   **原文**：“商人重利轻别离”
    *   **现译**："Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;"
    *   **问题**：“Over love”（胜过爱）是对“重利”的引申。原文仅说重视利益、轻视离别。虽然语境中隐含了感情淡薄，但直接加“love”略有过度解读之嫌。
    *   **建议**改为："The merchant cares only for profit, disregarding partings;"

*   **原文**：“杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣”
    *   **现译**："Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief."
    *   **问题**：“Bleeding from their cries”直译了“啼血”，但在英语文化中可能显得过于血腥或奇幻。不过为了保留中国典故意象，此翻译是可以接受的文学化处理。无需修改。

### 4. 节奏与连贯性（风格优化）
*   **原文**：“我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。”
    *   **现译**："Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago; Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply."
    *   **问题**：“Long ago”对应“已”（以前/刚才），但“sighed”时态略乱。且“again I lament deeply”不如“my sighs redoubled”来得紧凑。
    *   **建议**改为："I had already sighed at the pipa's tune; Now hearing her story, my grief doubles."

### 总结
整体而言，译文质量很高，上述问题多为**精益求精的风格调整**或**文化术语的微调**。其中，“帝京/教坊”的机构名称准确性、“不得志”的内涵表达值得注意。

**是否需要修改？**
是的，建议针对“教坊”、“不得志”和“善才服”这几处进行微调，以更贴合历史背景和情感原意。其他部分可保留。

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;

Here, silence surpasses all sound.

All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.

She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;

"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;

"I left the imperial capital last year,

Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.

请对照原作检查刚才的英译，找出误译、遗漏、无依据增补、意象修辞或语气方面的实际问题，指出涉及的片段、问题类型和严重程度，并给出修改建议。反馈也可能出错，不要因措辞不同就报错。确实没有需要修改的问题时，只回答“无需修改”；否则用自然语言说明。

这份译文整体流畅，很好地传达了原诗的叙事脉络和主要情感，但在**意象的精确对应、修辞力度的还原以及部分关键细节的准确性**上存在若干明显问题。以下是具体的检查结果与修改建议：

### 1. 意象与动词的误译（中等严重程度）
*   **原文**：“枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟”
    *   **现译**："Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill."
    *   **问题**：“Shiver”通常指因寒冷或恐惧而颤抖，用于植物略显拟人化过度且偏离“瑟瑟”作为风声或树叶摩擦声的本意。白居易此处是用声音烘托凄清氛围。
    *   **建议**改为："Maple leaves and reeds rustle, a cold autumn wind sighing." 或保留 "rustle" 以体现听觉意象。

*   **原文**：“犹抱琵琶半遮面”
    *   **现译**："Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face."
    *   **问题**：漏掉了“抱”的姿态感以及“遮”的动作方向性。虽然意思对，但略显平淡。更重要的是，“holding... before her”不如“embracing the pipa, covering half her face”来得具有古典美感和羞涩的动态。
    *   **建议**改为："Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face."

### 2. 典故与专有名词的处理偏差（高严重程度）
*   **原文**：“五陵年少争缠头”
    *   **现译**："Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,"
    *   **问题**：**严重误译**。“缠头”在唐代指赠给歌伎的锦帛（赏赐），并非指用锦缎把人“包裹起来”。译者望文生义，将隐喻变成了字面动作，导致画面荒谬。
    *   **建议**改为："The young nobles from the Five Mausoleums vied to offer me silk rewards," 或 "...vied to throw jewels at my head," (注：缠头具体指赏赐之物)。

*   **原文**：“钿头银篦击节碎”
    *   **现译**："Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,"
    *   **问题**：这里“钿头银篦”确实是发饰，但“snapped”暗示是梳子本身断了。历史上这是形容演奏激烈，打拍子的器物碎裂，或者更常见的是形容酒席上狂欢时，金翠首饰随节奏撞击破碎（极言奢华与狂放）。译文尚可接受，但“Gold-inlaid”对应“钿头”略显宽泛，“silver comb”对应“银篦”。
    *   **微调建议**："Silver combs with jeweled heads shattered keeping time,"

### 3. 语气与情感的弱化（中等严重程度）
*   **原文**：“同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！”
    *   **现译**："Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth; Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?"
    *   **问题**：原文是一种强烈的共鸣与感叹，带有宿命感。译文用了 "Since we meet here..." 这种逻辑连接词，削弱了那种“无需多言，心意相通”的瞬间爆发力。
    *   **建议**改为："We are both wanderers cast to the horizon's edge; Meeting thus, what need was there for prior acquaintance?"

*   **原文**：“呕哑嘲哳难为听”
    *   **现译**："They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to."
    *   **问题**：“Painful”太重了，原文更多是表达那些音乐粗俗、杂乱、不堪入耳，令人皱眉而非痛苦。
    *   **建议**改为："Their sounds are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear."

### 4. 细节遗漏或增补无据（轻微至中等）
*   **原文**：“主人下马客在船”
    *   **现译**："I dismount; my guest is already on board;"
    *   **问题**：这是互文见义，意思是“我和客人都下了马/上了船”或者描述一种送别的场景交错。译者处理成“I dismount”和“guest is on board”，虽然符合语境，但略微丢失了原句紧凑的画面感。不过为了英语通顺，此处理解可接受，不算硬伤。

*   **原文**：“曲罢曾教善才服”
    *   **现译**："When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;"
    *   **问题**：“善才”是当时著名的琵琶师曹善才，也可泛指技艺高超的乐师。译为 "great musicians" 可以，但 "bowed in admiration" 属于增补。原文只是说让他们“服气/佩服”。
    *   **建议**改为："...made even master players concede,"

*   **原文**：“暮去朝来颜色故”
    *   **现译**："Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away."
    *   **问题**：语序颠倒。原文是“暮去朝来”（时间流逝，傍晚过去清晨到来），译文写成了“Days turned to nights”（白天变黑夜），虽然都是时间流逝，但与原文意象相反。
    *   **建议**改为："As evenings pass and mornings come, my looks grew old."

### 5. 结尾的高潮处理
*   **原文**：“江州司马青衫湿”
    *   **现译**："The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet."
    *   **问题**：非常忠实，但缺乏一点诗意张力。考虑到前文“满座重闻皆掩泣”，最后一句应更具象。

At night I bid farewell to a guest by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn wind.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
The young nobles of the Five Mausoleums vied to bestow silks upon me,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
As evenings fade and mornings rise, my beauty waned;
My brother went off to war, and my aunt died.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"We are both exiles drifting to the world's end;
Meeting thus, what need had we to know each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Harsh and discordant, they are unpleasant to the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Magistrate, dampened by tears.

译文：At night by the Xunyang River I bid a guest farewell,
As autumn winds rustled through maple leaves and reeds.
The host dismounts, the guest is on his boat;
We raise our cups, but lack the music of strings and pipes.
Drunk yet joyless, we face this sorrowful parting,
And at our farewell, the vast river soaks the moon in its depths.

Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays,
But the pipa falls silent, and she hesitates to speak.
I move my boat close to invite her out,
Add more wine, bring back lanterns, and reopen the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally appears,
Holding the pipa still half-covering her face.

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times,
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string suppressed, every note filled with longing,
Seeming to tell of a life unmet in ambition.
With lowered brows, casually continuing to play,
She speaks out all the boundless thoughts within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and plucking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Strings."

The thick strings rumble loudly like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper softly like private talk.
Loud and soft notes intermingle in complex strumming,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as an oriole’s song beneath flowers,
Choked as spring water flowing under ice, struggling against coldness.
Ice-bound springs chill and stall, strings freeze and stop,
Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceases.

Another kind of hidden sorrow and secret resentment arises;
In this silence, quietness surpasses even sound.
Then suddenly, as if a silver vase bursts, water spurt s forth,
Or iron cavalry charges out, swords and spears ringing clash.
When the tune ends, she draws the plectrum down the center,
All four strings strike once, tearing silk apart.
Boats east and west fall quietly speechless,
Only seeing the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pauses, inserts the plectrum between the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises, composing her expression.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living in a house near Shama Ling (Frog Mound).
By age thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau performers.
After finishing a piece, I could make skilled masters admire;
Once made up, I was often envied by Qi Niang (a famous courtesan).
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to give me gifts,
For one song, red silk scarves received were beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs broke timekeeping with rhythm beats,
Blood-red silk skirts spilled wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent casually.
Then my brother went off to war, my aunt died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, my beauty fades away.
Before my gate, visitors dwindle, scarce are horses and carriages,
Getting older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit highly, take separation lightly,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamt of affairs of my youth,
Waking crying, makeup tears running down my red cheeks."

Having heard the pipa, I already sighed deeply,
Now hearing these words, I sigh again with heavy lament.
We are both people fallen from grace, wandering the edge of heaven,
Since we meet now, why need we have known each other before?
I, since last year, bid farewell to the imperial capital,
Demoted and lying ill here in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year round, I hear not the sound of silk and bamboo instruments.
Living near the Pen River, low land damp and wet,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my dwelling.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower dawns, autumn nights,
Often taking wine alone to pour and drink.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant sounds are unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune for me,
For you, I will compose this Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits back down, tightens the strings, which turn urgent.
The melancholy sound differs from what came before,
Everyone in the room hears it anew and covers their faces weeping.
