译文：**The Song of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount, my guest remains aboard his boat;
We raise our cups, but there is no music to accompany the drink.
Tipsy yet joyless, we part in sorrow,
And as we leave, the vast river soaks the moon’s reflection.
Suddenly, from across the water, comes the sound of pipa strings,
Making me forget to return home and my guest forget to set sail.

Following the sound, I ask quietly who plays,
But the pipas stop, and she hesitates, reluctant to speak.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Refill the wine, trim the lamp, and resume the feast.
After countless calls and pleas, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.

She turns the pegs and plucks just two or three notes,
And before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string restrains its voice, every note carries longing,
Seeming to recount a lifetime of thwarted ambitions.
Head bowed low, she plays with casual ease,
Expressing all the boundless matters of her heart.
With light sweeps, slow twists, slides, and picks,
First playing "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Strings."

The thick strings roar like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private murmurs.
Roaring and whispering intermingle in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Now sweet like orioles singing smoothly beneath flowers,
Now choked like spring water struggling under ice.
When the cold, sticky ice halts the flow, the strings seem frozen,
And this stillness cuts off the sound for a brief pause.
But within that silence arise hidden sorrows and secret resentments—
At this moment, silence speaks louder than sound.

Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water spurts forth,
Or iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ends, she draws the plectrum across the center,
All four strings strike one final note, tearing silk apart.

East boats and west barges fall silent, no word spoken,
Only the white autumn moon seen in the middle of the river.
She pauses, inserts the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her solemn face.

She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My home was near the Shrimp Mound Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
My performances impressed even master musicians,
And when made up, my beauty incited the envy of courtesans.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to gift me brocade,
For one song, red silk received beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins snapped keeping time to the rhythm,
Blood-red skirts stained by overturned wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and merriment,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent idly away.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned into nights, and my youth faded.
Before my door, visitors grew rare, horses few,
So, grown old, I married a merchant for security.
He values profit over sentiment, caring little for partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
While he is away, I guard an empty ship at the river mouth,
Bathed in bright moonlight, surrounded by cold river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream of my boyhood days,
Waking to find tears staining my makeup red across the pillow."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
And upon hearing these words, my sighs grew deeper.
We are both exiles lost at the edge of the earth,
What need was there for us to have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished to Jiujiang, sick and bedridden.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, no strings or pipes are heard.
Living near the Peng River on damp, low ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
I often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, harsh sounds are painful to the ear.
Tonight I heard your pipa’s language,
It felt like celestial music, clearing my ears anew.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I shall compose the "Song of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits back down, quickening the tempo, the strings growing urgent.
Her mournful tones differ from those heard before;
Everyone present covers their faces and weeps.
Who sheds the most tears in the audience?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is soaked dry.

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid a guest farewell by night,

Expressing endless matters within, like wind in clover.

First "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Melodies" in the chain.
The big strings thundered loudly like a sudden rainstorm’s crash,
The small strings whispered gently like lovers’ soft flash.
Thundering and whispering mingled in complex play,
Like pearls large and small falling onto jade plate’s array.
Cuckoo-like birds sang sweetly beneath flowers, smooth and bright,
Then choked sobs like spring water flowing under ice, tight.
Ice-cold springs, stiffened strings, music ceased for a breath,
A new hidden grief arose, silencing death before life.
At this moment, silence surpassed the sound’s own claim,
Then suddenly a silver vase burst, water spurring flame.
Iron cavalry charged forth, blades clashing, spears ringing,
The song ended; with a final stroke, the silk tore, stinging.
Four strings struck as one, like tearing cloth’s sharp cry,
East ships and west barges fell silent, under the sky.
Only the moon’s white reflection upon the river’s heart remained,
While she paused, put down the plectrum, in the strings constrained.
Adjusting her clothes, she stood up, composing her face,
Telling her story, revealing her past’s trace.
"I was born a girl in the capital’s grand domain,
My home lay near Xiama Ling, amidst wealth and fame’s reign.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s intricate art,

Hearing her words, I added sighs beyond relief.

Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.

Her home located near the Shrimp-Frog Mound.

Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Her brother left to join the army, her aunt died,
Days turned into nights, and her beauty faded away.

Before her gate, visitors became scarce, horses rare,
Getting older, she married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit high but love separation lightly,
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

Surrounded by bright moonlight, while the river water ran cold.
Late at night, she suddenly dreamed of events from her youth,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining her rouge down her cheeks.

And hearing these words, my sighs grew deeper still.
We are both wanderers lost at the ends of the earth,
Why must we have known each other before meeting today?

Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital,
Demoted and ill, lying low in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and lacks music,
All year long, no sound of silk or bamboo instruments is heard.

Living near the Pen River in damp lowlands,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood and gibbons howling mournfully.

On spring rivers amid blooming flowers, or on autumn nights under the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it solely for myself.
Are there no local folk songs and village flutes?
Their hoarse and chaotic sounds are hard to bear listening to.

Tonight, hearing your pipa music,
It was like hearing celestial tunes, making my ears bright again.
Do not refuse to sit and play another piece;
For you, I shall compose the *Song of the Pipa*.

译文：The Song of the Pipa

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid a guest farewell by night,
When autumn winds rustled through maple leaves and reeds so slight.
I dismounted to the boat where my guest was bound to stay;
We raised our cups, but no music came to grace the play.
Though drunk on wine, joy failed us as parting drew near,
And we saw only the moon drowned in the river’s clear.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa strings began to sing;
I forgot my return, he his departure, captivated by its ring.
We traced the sound, asking softly who could be the player,
But the music stopped; hesitation hung in the air.
We moved our boats close together, inviting her to show,
Refilled our cups, lit the lamps, renewed the feast below.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-hiding her face, reserved.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three tentative notes,
Before a melody formed, her sorrow already floats.
Each string restrained, each note laden with thought deep,
As if telling of a lifetime’s failures, silent and steep.
Brow lowered, fingers moving freely, one after another,
Expressing endless matters within, like wind in clover.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, strummed and picked again,
First "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Melodies" in the chain.
The big strings thundered loudly like a sudden rainstorm’s crash,
The small strings whispered gently like lovers’ soft flash.
Thundering and whispering mingled in complex play,
Like pearls large and small falling onto jade plate’s array.
Cuckoo-like birds sang sweetly beneath flowers, smooth and bright,
Then choked sobs like spring water flowing under ice, tight.
Ice-cold springs, stiffened strings, music ceased for a breath,
A new hidden grief arose, silencing death before life.
At this moment, silence surpassed the sound’s own claim,
Then suddenly a silver vase burst, water spurring flame.
Iron cavalry charged forth, blades clashing, spears ringing,
The song ended; with a final stroke, the silk tore, stinging.
Four strings struck as one, like tearing cloth’s sharp cry,
East ships and west barges fell silent, under the sky.
Only the moon’s white reflection upon the river’s heart remained,
While she paused, put down the plectrum, in the strings constrained.
Adjusting her clothes, she stood up, composing her face,
Telling her story, revealing her past’s trace.
"I was born a girl in the capital’s grand domain,
My home lay near Xiama Ling, amidst wealth and fame’s reign.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s intricate art,
Named first among the Imperial Music Troupe’s smart.
After finishing a tune, skilled masters bowed to my skill,
My makeup finished, even famed beauties felt ill.
Young men of Five Mounds vied to wrap me in brocade heads,
For one song, red silk bolts piled high, unknown counts spread.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time’s beat,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine, wild and fleet.
This year of laughter passed into next year’s delight,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent carelessly in flight.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died away,
As twilight faded into dawn, beauty lost its day.
The gate grew cold, horse hooves rare, visitors few,
Growing old, I married a merchant, true to his cue.
He valued profit more than separation’s pain,
Last month to Fuliang he went, buying tea again.
When he returns, I guard the empty boat at river mouth,
Moonlight circles the ship, cold waters flow south.
Late at night, dreams of youth come crashing back to start,
Crying in sleep, tears ruin makeup, staining the heart."
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply, overcome with grief,
Hearing her words, I added sighs beyond relief.
Both are wanderers fallen to the ends of earth’s expanse,
Meeting now, why should we need prior acquaintance?
Since last year I left the Emperor’s Capital City,
Exiled here to Xunyang, sick, alone, pity.
Xunyang is remote, no music fills the air,
All year long, no strings or flutes can be heard there.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp, wet ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my abode found.
What do I hear morning and evening in this place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing with sad grace.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights’ glow,
Often take out wine, drink alone, feelings slow.
Are there no mountain songs or village flute’s tune?
Hoarse and harsh sounds, painful to listen soon.
Tonight hearing your pipa speak its language pure,
Like celestial music, my ears brighten, cure.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more song,
For you I’ll compose this Ballad of the Pipa, strong.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence profound,
Then sat down, tightened strings, playing faster, bound.
Mournful and desolate, nothing like the former sound,
Everyone present covered faces, tears pouring round.
Who shed most tears among them? Ask if you must know:
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet in woe.

At the head of Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest was on board;
We raised our wine cups, longing to drink, but lacked music—no flutes or strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy, only sorrow before parting;
As we parted, the vast river immersed the moon in its depths.

Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifted over the water;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing;
The pipa paused, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And though the melody had not yet begun, emotion was already there.
Each string was suppressed, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a lifetime spent unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, she played with flowing ease,
Expressing all the endless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and plucking again,
First playing *Ni Chang*, then *Liu Yao*.

The thick strings rumbled like heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like intimate murmurs.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in mixed play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Bird-like chirps slid smoothly beneath flowers,
Trickling springs choked difficultly under ice.
The cold, sticky spring froze, and the strings seemed to break;
When broken and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

But another secret sorrow and hidden resentment arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Suddenly, silver bottles burst, water splashing forth,
Iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clashing loudly.
As the tune ended, she drew the pick across the center,
The four strings struck together, tearing like silk cloth.

East boats and west ships fell silent,
Only the white moon in the heart of the river remained visible.
She pondered, set down the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and arranged her expression.

She said herself that she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed in the first rank of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing songs, even skilled masters would admire her;
Once made up, every beauty envied her.
Young men from the Five Mausoleums fought to give her gifts,
One song earned her unknown quantities of crimson silk.
Gold-inlaid combs were shattered keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by overturned wine.

This year laughter and merriment, next year too,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
Her brother enlisted in the army, her aunt died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, and her beauty fades.
Before her gate, visitors became few, horses sparse,
Aging, she married a merchant as his wife.
That merchant values profit lightly regarding separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and she guards the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.

Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days,
Waking crying, makeup tears stain the red railings.

Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
Then hearing these words, I lamented anew.
Both are people fallen into wandering fate beyond the sky’s edge,
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long, no sound of silk and bamboo is heard.
My dwelling is near Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries and apes wailing sadly.
On spring rivers’ flower mornings and autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.

Is there no mountain song and village flute?
They are hoarse, harsh, and unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I shall compose the Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, which grew faster.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those before,
The whole audience listened again, covering their faces and weeping.
Who among the guests wept the most?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose green robe was wet.

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?

At night I bid farewell to a guest by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn wind.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
The young nobles of the Five Mausoleums vied to bestow silks upon me,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
As evenings fade and mornings rise, my beauty waned;
My brother went off to war, and my aunt died.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"We are both exiles drifting to the world's end;
Meeting thus, what need had we to know each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Harsh and discordant, they are unpleasant to the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Magistrate, dampened by tears.

    *   **问题**：“Fate”（命运/宿命）带有强烈的不可抗拒感，而“不得志”更多指仕途不顺、抱负未展的社会性挫折。用 "fate" 略显消极被动，原诗强调的是才华被埋没的愤懑。
    *   **建议**改为："As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition," 或 "...of thwarted aspirations,"

*   **原文**：“弦弦掩抑声声思”
    *   **现译**："Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,"
    *   **问题**：“Sighs”（叹息）是增加的动作，原文“掩抑”意为压抑、含蓄、低沉。虽然音乐常伴叹息，但这里侧重的是演奏技法带来的情感克制。“Restrain”尚可，但“Sighs”属于无依据增补。
    *   **建议**改为："Every string is suppressed, every sound holds sorrow,"

*   **原文**：“东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白”
    *   **现译**："Boats to the east and west fall silent; Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart."
    *   **问题**：译文基本准确，但“reflects”（倒影）是物理描述。原诗“江心秋月白”是一种视觉印象——月光洒满江心，一片洁白。这种“空寂”的美感稍显平淡。不过此处理解可接受，不算硬伤。

### 2. 专有名词与文化背景的精确度（中等）
*   **原文**：“名属教坊第一部”
    *   **现译**："My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy."
    *   **问题**：“Imperial academy”通常指太学或国子监（教育机构），而“教坊”（Jiaofang）是管理宫廷音乐的机构。译为 "imperial music bureau" 或 "first division of the Imperial Music Bureau" 更准确。
    *   **建议**改为："I was ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau,"

*   **原文**：“曲罢曾教善才服”
    *   **现译**："When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;"
    *   **问题**：“Bowed in admiration”（鞠躬致敬）是动作描写，原文“服”是心理状态（折服/佩服）。乐师不一定都鞠躬，而是心悦诚服。
    *   **建议**改为："Even master players were convinced by my skill," 或 "...won the acclaim of skilled masters,"

### 3. 语气与情感的细微差别（轻微）
*   **原文**：“商人重利轻别离”
    *   **现译**："Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;"
    *   **问题**：“Over love”（胜过爱）是对“重利”的引申。原文仅说重视利益、轻视离别。虽然语境中隐含了感情淡薄，但直接加“love”略有过度解读之嫌。
    *   **建议**改为："The merchant cares only for profit, disregarding partings;"

*   **原文**：“杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣”
    *   **现译**："Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief."
    *   **问题**：“Bleeding from their cries”直译了“啼血”，但在英语文化中可能显得过于血腥或奇幻。不过为了保留中国典故意象，此翻译是可以接受的文学化处理。无需修改。

### 4. 节奏与连贯性（风格优化）
*   **原文**：“我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。”
    *   **现译**："Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago; Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply."
    *   **问题**：“Long ago”对应“已”（以前/刚才），但“sighed”时态略乱。且“again I lament deeply”不如“my sighs redoubled”来得紧凑。
    *   **建议**改为："I had already sighed at the pipa's tune; Now hearing her story, my grief doubles."

### 总结
整体而言，译文质量很高，上述问题多为**精益求精的风格调整**或**文化术语的微调**。其中，“帝京/教坊”的机构名称准确性、“不得志”的内涵表达值得注意。

**是否需要修改？**
是的，建议针对“教坊”、“不得志”和“善才服”这几处进行微调，以更贴合历史背景和情感原意。其他部分可保留。

**Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, at night I bid a guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The Host dismounts; the Guest waits on his boat below,
We raise our cups to drink, yet no strings play nor pipes blow.
Drunk, we cannot be joyful; sorrow hangs before parting,
At this moment, the vast river is soaked in moonlight’s haunting.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa notes arise—
The Host forgets to return; the Guest delays his departure’s ties.

I move my boat closer to invite her sight,
Pour fresh wine, trim the lamp, restart the light.
After a thousand calls, ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding her pipa, half-hiding her face in fears.

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings—a few preliminary tries,

Every string suppresses a sigh, every note carries longing deep,
As if telling of a lifetime where promises fail to keep.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving with practiced ease,

Playing first “Neon Robes,” then “Six Beats”’ refrain.
The thick strings clamor like a sudden storm’s heavy rain,
The thin strings whisper like lovers’ murmurs in pain.
Loud and soft together, they intermingle and clash,
Like pearls, great and small, clattering on a jade dish’s flash.

Smooth as an oriole singing beneath blossoms’ shade,
Choked as a spring flowing under ice, hard to wade.
The cold spring freezes, the strings seem to cease,
A blockage halts the flow, bringing moments of peace.

Four chords ring out once, tearing silk’s sharp sing.

Living near Hama Ling, where music and dance abide.

The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays departure.

The pipa music stops, hesitant to speak.

Adding more wine, lighting lamps again, reopening the feast.

Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She twists the pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before the melody forms, the emotion is already there.

Each string suppresses sighs, each note carries thought,
Seeming to tell of a lifetime’s unfulfilled ambitions.
Head bowed low, she strums continuously with ease,
Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart.

First playing "Rainbow Robe," then "Six Strings" dance.
The thick strings thunder loudly like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper softly like private talk.

Muffled like springs flowing under ice, struggling to pass.

A hidden sorrow and silent hatred arise anew;

One final strike from the four strings, tearing silk-like.

Only seeing the autumn moon white upon the river’s heart.
She contemplates deeply, inserts the pick between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her expression.

My family lived near Shrimp Mound Hill.
By thirteen, I mastered my skill on the pipa,
And was ranked first among the court musicians.

After finishing songs, even great masters admired me;
Once dressed up, every beauty grew envious of me.
Young men of power competed to give me gifts,
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.

Gold-inlaid hairpins broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter followed,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed by idly.

Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turn to nights, and my beauty fades away.

So, growing old, I married a merchant for a wife.

Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guard the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river waters cold.

Late in the night, I dream of youthful affairs,
Weeping in dreams, my makeup tears stain the railings red."

Hearing these words, my sighs grow deeper still.

Meeting now—why need we have known each other before?

Banished to lie ill here in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year round, I hear not a single string or flute.

Living near the Pen River, on low, damp ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around the house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing sadly.

On spring days with flowers, autumn nights with moons,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, difficult to listen to.

Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this "Ballad of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits back down and tightens the strings; they play faster.
Melancholy sounds unlike those played before,
Everyone present hears them again and covers their faces in weeping.

Who among the listeners sheds the most tears?
The Blue-robed Prefect of Jiangzhou, wet through with salt.

Only the autumn moon shines white upon the river’s heart.

Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her dignity.

Living near Shrimp Toad Tomb.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed among the first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a song, even great masters would bow to me;
When made up, every beauty envied my grace.
Young men of the Five Districts competed to gift me brocade,
For each piece played, countless red silks were bestowed.
Jeweled hair ornaments broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.

Autumn moons and spring breezes casually consumed.
Then my brother went off to war, my aunt died,
As evening came and morning returned, my beauty faded.
The door grew cold, horsemen rare,
So, growing old, I married a merchant man.
He values profit above separation,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he departed, I wait alone on the empty boat at the river mouth,
The moon surrounds the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking with tears streaming down my painted cheeks, staining them red."

Hearing her pipa, I have long sighed;
Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.
"Both of us are fallen souls wandering the edge of heaven,
Meeting now, why need we know each other before?"
"Since last year I left the Emperor's Capital,
Banished, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Here, remote and devoid of music,
All year long, no sound of silk or bamboo is heard.
My home is near Pen River, low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow rushes and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear here, dawn to dusk?
Blood-crying cuckoos and monkeys’ mournful wails.
On spring river nights, flower morns, autumn moon evenings,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Is there truly no folk song or village flute?
Their sounds are harsh and jarring, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse; sit again, play one more piece,
And I shall compose for you 'The Song of the Pipa'."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down, tightening the strings, which played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous tones,
At the end, everyone in the room wiped their tears.
Who shed the most tears among those present?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is wet with grief.

"Since last year I left the Emperor's Capital,
Banished, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Here, remote and devoid of music,
All year long, no sound of silk or bamboo is heard.
My home is near Pen River, low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow rushes and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear here, dawn to dusk?
Blood-crying cuckoos and monkeys’ mournful wails.
On spring river nights, flower morns, autumn moon evenings,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Is there truly no folk song or village flute?
Their sounds are harsh and jarring, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse; sit again, play one more piece,
And I shall compose for you 'The Song of the Pipa'."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down, tightening the strings, which played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous tones,
At the end, everyone in the room wiped their tears.
Who shed the most tears among those present?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is wet with grief.

{"translation":"**The Song of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount to meet him on his boat; we raise our wine,
Yet no pipes or strings accompany this drink.
Drunk but not joyful, gloom hangs over parting;
At the moment of goodbye, the moon drowns in the vast river.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifts across the water;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The music stops, as if she hesitates to speak.
We move our boats closer, inviting her to appear;
More wine is poured, the lamps are turned up bright, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the melody forms, emotion already breathes.
Every string sighs with suppressed longing,
Seeming to tell of a life’s thwarted ambitions.
Head bowed, her fingers play on continuously,
Expressing all the boundless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked,
First playing *Ni Shang*, then *Liu Yao*.
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like secret confidences.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Now clear and sweet, like orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Now choked and low, like spring water trapped under ice.
The cold spring chokes, the strings seem frozen still,
Stopped and blocked, the sound momentarily ceases.
But hidden sorrow and dark resentment arise anew;
In this silence, there is more voice than sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting, water spurts out,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing loud.
When the tune ends, the plectrum draws one final stroke,
All four strings ringing together like tearing silk.
East ship, west boat—silent and unmoving;
Only the autumn moon shines white upon the river’s heart.
She muses, puts away the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her dignity.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shrimp Toad Tomb.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed among the first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a song, even great masters would bow to me;
When made up, every beauty envied my grace.
Young men of the Five Districts competed to gift me brocade,
For each piece played, countless red silks were bestowed.
Jeweled hair ornaments broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter passed,
Autumn moons and spring breezes casually consumed.

As evening came and morning returned, my beauty faded.
The door grew cold, horsemen rare,
So, growing old, I married a merchant man.
He values profit above separation,

Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.

Banished, lying ill in Xunyang City.

At the end, everyone in the room wiped their tears.

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet.
请对照原作检查刚才的英译，找出误译、遗漏、无依据增补、意象修辞或语气方面的实际问题，指出涉及的片段、问题类型和严重程度，并给出修改建议。反馈也可能出错，不要因措辞不同就报错。确实没有需要修改的问题时，只回答“无需修改”；否则用自然语言说明。

这份译文整体流畅，很好地传达了原诗的叙事脉络和主要情感，但在**意象的精确对应、修辞力度的还原以及部分关键细节的准确性**上存在若干明显问题。以下是具体的检查结果与修改建议：

### 1. 意象与动词的误译（中等严重程度）
*   **原文**：“枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟”
    *   **现译**："Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill."
    *   **问题**：“Shiver”通常指因寒冷或恐惧而颤抖，用于植物略显拟人化过度且偏离“瑟瑟”作为风声或树叶摩擦声的本意。白居易此处是用声音烘托凄清氛围。
    *   **建议**改为："Maple leaves and reeds rustle, a cold autumn wind sighing." 或保留 "rustle" 以体现听觉意象。

*   **原文**：“犹抱琵琶半遮面”
    *   **现译**："Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face."
    *   **问题**：漏掉了“抱”的姿态感以及“遮”的动作方向性。虽然意思对，但略显平淡。更重要的是，“holding... before her”不如“embracing the pipa, covering half her face”来得具有古典美感和羞涩的动态。
    *   **建议**改为："Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face."

### 2. 典故与专有名词的处理偏差（高严重程度）
*   **原文**：“五陵年少争缠头”
    *   **现译**："Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,"
    *   **问题**：**严重误译**。“缠头”在唐代指赠给歌伎的锦帛（赏赐），并非指用锦缎把人“包裹起来”。译者望文生义，将隐喻变成了字面动作，导致画面荒谬。
    *   **建议**改为："The young nobles from the Five Mausoleums vied to offer me silk rewards," 或 "...vied to throw jewels at my head," (注：缠头具体指赏赐之物)。

*   **原文**：“钿头银篦击节碎”
    *   **现译**："Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,"
    *   **问题**：这里“钿头银篦”确实是发饰，但“snapped”暗示是梳子本身断了。历史上这是形容演奏激烈，打拍子的器物碎裂，或者更常见的是形容酒席上狂欢时，金翠首饰随节奏撞击破碎（极言奢华与狂放）。译文尚可接受，但“Gold-inlaid”对应“钿头”略显宽泛，“silver comb”对应“银篦”。
    *   **微调建议**："Silver combs with jeweled heads shattered keeping time,"

### 3. 语气与情感的弱化（中等严重程度）
*   **原文**：“同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！”
    *   **现译**："Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth; Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?"
    *   **问题**：原文是一种强烈的共鸣与感叹，带有宿命感。译文用了 "Since we meet here..." 这种逻辑连接词，削弱了那种“无需多言，心意相通”的瞬间爆发力。
    *   **建议**改为："We are both wanderers cast to the horizon's edge; Meeting thus, what need was there for prior acquaintance?"

*   **原文**：“呕哑嘲哳难为听”
    *   **现译**："They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to."
    *   **问题**：“Painful”太重了，原文更多是表达那些音乐粗俗、杂乱、不堪入耳，令人皱眉而非痛苦。
    *   **建议**改为："Their sounds are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear."

### 4. 细节遗漏或增补无据（轻微至中等）
*   **原文**：“主人下马客在船”
    *   **现译**："I dismount; my guest is already on board;"
    *   **问题**：这是互文见义，意思是“我和客人都下了马/上了船”或者描述一种送别的场景交错。译者处理成“I dismount”和“guest is on board”，虽然符合语境，但略微丢失了原句紧凑的画面感。不过为了英语通顺，此处理解可接受，不算硬伤。

*   **原文**：“曲罢曾教善才服”
    *   **现译**："When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;"
    *   **问题**：“善才”是当时著名的琵琶师曹善才，也可泛指技艺高超的乐师。译为 "great musicians" 可以，但 "bowed in admiration" 属于增补。原文只是说让他们“服气/佩服”。
    *   **建议**改为："...made even master players concede,"

*   **原文**：“暮去朝来颜色故”
    *   **现译**："Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away."
    *   **问题**：语序颠倒。原文是“暮去朝来”（时间流逝，傍晚过去清晨到来），译文写成了“Days turned to nights”（白天变黑夜），虽然都是时间流逝，但与原文意象相反。
    *   **建议**改为："As evenings pass and mornings come, my looks grew old."

### 5. 结尾的高潮处理
*   **原文**：“江州司马青衫湿”
    *   **现译**："The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet."
    *   **问题**：非常忠实，但缺乏一点诗意张力。考虑到前文“满座重闻皆掩泣”，最后一句应更具象。
    *   **建议**保持原样即可，或者微调为："The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Magistrate, dampened by tears."

### 总结修改建议清单

| 原文片段 | 问题类型 | 严重程度 | 建议修改 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟 | 意象不准 | 中 | Maple leaves and reeds rustle in the autumn wind. |
| 五陵年少争缠头 | **严重误译** | **高** | The young nobles of the Five Mausoleums vied to bestow silks upon me. |
| 暮去朝来颜色故 | 逻辑/意象反 | 中 | As evenings fade and mornings rise, my beauty waned. |
| 同是天涯沦落人... | 语气弱化 | 中 | We are both exiles drifting to the world's end; What need had we to know each other before? |
| 呕哑嘲哳难为听 | 程度过重 | 轻 | Harsh and discordant, they are unpleasant to the ear. |

**结论**：译文需要修正“五陵年少争缠头”这一处明显的文化意象误读，并调整几处关于时间流逝和自然声响的描写以更贴合原诗意境。其他部分大体准确。

请对照原作核实上面的检查意见，只修正确实存在的问题，允许保留原稿。给出完整英文译文。

Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Magistrate, dampened by tears.

这份译文在上一轮修正后已经非常准确，主要误译（如“缠头”）和逻辑错误（如时间流逝方向）均已纠正。然而，若以严格对照原作的标准审视，仍有几处细节存在**意象流失、语气偏差或微小的增补问题**，建议进一步优化。

以下是具体检查结果：

### 1. 意象与修辞的弱化（轻微至中等）
*   **原文**：“似诉平生不得志”
    *   **现译**："As if telling of a life frustrated by fate."
    *   **问题**：“Fate”（命运/宿命）带有强烈的不可抗拒感，而“不得志”更多指仕途不顺、抱负未展的社会性挫折。用 "fate" 略显消极被动，原诗强调的是才华被埋没的愤懑。
    *   **建议**改为："As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition," 或 "...of thwarted aspirations,"

*   **原文**：“弦弦掩抑声声思”
    *   **现译**："Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,"
    *   **问题**：“Sighs”（叹息）是增加的动作，原文“掩抑”意为压抑、含蓄、低沉。虽然音乐常伴叹息，但这里侧重的是演奏技法带来的情感克制。“Restrain”尚可，但“Sighs”属于无依据增补。
    *   **建议**改为："Every string is suppressed, every sound holds sorrow,"

*   **原文**：“东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白”
    *   **现译**："Boats to the east and west fall silent; Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart."
    *   **问题**：译文基本准确，但“reflects”（倒影）是物理描述。原诗“江心秋月白”是一种视觉印象——月光洒满江心，一片洁白。这种“空寂”的美感稍显平淡。不过此处理解可接受，不算硬伤。

### 2. 专有名词与文化背景的精确度（中等）
*   **原文**：“名属教坊第一部”
    *   **现译**："My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy."
    *   **问题**：“Imperial academy”通常指太学或国子监（教育机构），而“教坊”（Jiaofang）是管理宫廷音乐的机构。译为 "imperial music bureau" 或 "first division of the Imperial Music Bureau" 更准确。
    *   **建议**改为："I was ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau,"

*   **原文**：“曲罢曾教善才服”
    *   **现译**："When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;"
    *   **问题**：“Bowed in admiration”（鞠躬致敬）是动作描写，原文“服”是心理状态（折服/佩服）。乐师不一定都鞠躬，而是心悦诚服。

### 3. 语气与情感的细微差别（轻微）
*   **原文**：“商人重利轻别离”
    *   **现译**："Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;"
    *   **问题**：“Over love”（胜过爱）是对“重利”的引申。原文仅说重视利益、轻视离别。虽然语境中隐含了感情淡薄，但直接加“love”略有过度解读之嫌。
    *   **建议**改为："The merchant cares only for profit, disregarding partings;"

*   **原文**：“杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣”
    *   **现译**："Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief."
    *   **问题**：“Bleeding from their cries”直译了“啼血”，但在英语文化中可能显得过于血腥或奇幻。不过为了保留中国典故意象，此翻译是可以接受的文学化处理。无需修改。

### 4. 节奏与连贯性（风格优化）
*   **原文**：“我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。”
    *   **现译**："Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago; Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply."
    *   **问题**：“Long ago”对应“已”（以前/刚才），但“sighed”时态略乱。且“again I lament deeply”不如“my sighs redoubled”来得紧凑。
    *   **建议**改为："I had already sighed at the pipa's tune; Now hearing her story, my grief doubles."

### 总结
整体而言，译文质量很高，上述问题多为**精益求精的风格调整**或**文化术语的微调**。其中，“帝京/教坊”的机构名称准确性、“不得志”的内涵表达值得注意。

**是否需要修改？**
是的，建议针对“教坊”、“不得志”和“善才服”这几处进行微调，以更贴合历史背景和情感原意。其他部分可保留。

At night I bid farewell to a guest by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn wind.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Every string is suppressed, every note carries deep sorrow,
As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
I was ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
When I finished a piece, even master players were convinced by my skill;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
The young nobles of the Five Mausoleums vied to bestow silks upon me,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
As evenings fade and mornings rise, my beauty waned;
My brother went off to war, and my aunt died.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
The merchant cares only for profit, disregarding partings;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
I had already sighed at the pipa's tune;
Now hearing her story, my grief doubles.
"We are both exiles drifting to the world's end;
Meeting thus, what need had we to know each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Harsh and discordant, they are unpleasant to the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Magistrate, dampened by tears.

**The Song of the Pipa**

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?

请对照原作检查刚才的英译，找出误译、遗漏、无依据增补、意象修辞或语气方面的实际问题，指出涉及的片段、问题类型和严重程度，并给出修改建议。反馈也可能出错，不要因措辞不同就报错。确实没有需要修改的问题时，只回答“无需修改”；否则用自然语言说明。

这份译文整体流畅，很好地传达了原诗的叙事脉络和主要情感，但在**意象的精确对应、修辞力度的还原以及部分关键细节的准确性**上存在若干明显问题。以下是具体的检查结果与修改建议：

### 1. 意象与动词的误译（中等严重程度）
*   **原文**：“枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟”
    *   **现译**："Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill."
    *   **问题**：“Shiver”通常指因寒冷或恐惧而颤抖，用于植物略显拟人化过度且偏离“瑟瑟”作为风声或树叶摩擦声的本意。白居易此处是用声音烘托凄清氛围。
    *   **建议**改为："Maple leaves and reeds rustle, a cold autumn wind sighing." 或保留 "rustle" 以体现听觉意象。

*   **原文**：“犹抱琵琶半遮面”
    *   **现译**："Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face."
    *   **问题**：漏掉了“抱”的姿态感以及“遮”的动作方向性。虽然意思对，但略显平淡。更重要的是，“holding... before her”不如“embracing the pipa, covering half her face”来得具有古典美感和羞涩的动态。
    *   **建议**改为："Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face."

### 2. 典故与专有名词的处理偏差（高严重程度）
*   **原文**：“五陵年少争缠头”
    *   **现译**："Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,"
    *   **问题**：**严重误译**。“缠头”在唐代指赠给歌伎的锦帛（赏赐），并非指用锦缎把人“包裹起来”。译者望文生义，将隐喻变成了字面动作，导致画面荒谬。
    *   **建议**改为："The young nobles from the Five Mausoleums vied to offer me silk rewards," 或 "...vied to throw jewels at my head," (注：缠头具体指赏赐之物)。

*   **原文**：“钿头银篦击节碎”
    *   **现译**："Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,"
    *   **问题**：这里“钿头银篦”确实是发饰，但“snapped”暗示是梳子本身断了。历史上这是形容演奏激烈，打拍子的器物碎裂，或者更常见的是形容酒席上狂欢时，金翠首饰随节奏撞击破碎（极言奢华与狂放）。译文尚可接受，但“Gold-inlaid”对应“钿头”略显宽泛，“silver comb”对应“银篦”。
    *   **微调建议**："Silver combs with jeweled heads shattered keeping time,"

### 3. 语气与情感的弱化（中等严重程度）
*   **原文**：“同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！”
    *   **现译**："Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth; Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?"
    *   **问题**：原文是一种强烈的共鸣与感叹，带有宿命感。译文用了 "Since we meet here..." 这种逻辑连接词，削弱了那种“无需多言，心意相通”的瞬间爆发力。
    *   **建议**改为："We are both wanderers cast to the horizon's edge; Meeting thus, what need was there for prior acquaintance?"

*   **原文**：“呕哑嘲哳难为听”
    *   **现译**："They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to."
    *   **问题**：“Painful”太重了，原文更多是表达那些音乐粗俗、杂乱、不堪入耳，令人皱眉而非痛苦。
    *   **建议**改为："Their sounds are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear."

### 4. 细节遗漏或增补无据（轻微至中等）
*   **原文**：“主人下马客在船”
    *   **现译**："I dismount; my guest is already on board;"
    *   **问题**：这是互文见义，意思是“我和客人都下了马/上了船”或者描述一种送别的场景交错。译者处理成“I dismount”和“guest is on board”，虽然符合语境，但略微丢失了原句紧凑的画面感。不过为了英语通顺，此处理解可接受，不算硬伤。

*   **原文**：“曲罢曾教善才服”
    *   **现译**："When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;"
    *   **问题**：“善才”是当时著名的琵琶师曹善才，也可泛指技艺高超的乐师。译为 "great musicians" 可以，但 "bowed in admiration" 属于增补。原文只是说让他们“服气/佩服”。
    *   **建议**改为："...made even master players concede,"

*   **原文**：“暮去朝来颜色故”
    *   **现译**："Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away."
    *   **问题**：语序颠倒。原文是“暮去朝来”（时间流逝，傍晚过去清晨到来），译文写成了“Days turned to nights”（白天变黑夜），虽然都是时间流逝，但与原文意象相反。

At night I bid farewell to a guest by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn wind.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
The young nobles of the Five Mausoleums vied to bestow silks upon me,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
As evenings fade and mornings rise, my beauty waned;
My brother went off to war, and my aunt died.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"We are both exiles drifting to the world's end;
Meeting thus, what need had we to know each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Harsh and discordant, they are unpleasant to the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Magistrate, dampened by tears.

The Song of the Pipa

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid a guest farewell by night,
When autumn winds rustled through maple leaves and reeds so slight.
I dismounted to the boat where my guest was bound to stay;
We raised our cups, but no music came to grace the play.
Though drunk on wine, joy failed us as parting drew near,
And we saw only the moon drowned in the river’s clear.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa strings began to sing;

Refilled our cups, lit the lamps, renewed the feast below.

Still holding the pipa, half-hiding her face, reserved.

Before a melody formed, her sorrow already floats.
Each string restrained, each note laden with thought deep,
As if telling of a lifetime’s failures, silent and steep.
Brow lowered, fingers moving freely, one after another,
Expressing endless matters within, like wind in clover.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, strummed and picked again,
First "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Melodies" in the chain.
The big strings thundered loudly like a sudden rainstorm’s crash,
The small strings whispered gently like lovers’ soft flash.
Thundering and whispering mingled in complex play,
Like pearls large and small falling onto jade plate’s array.
Cuckoo-like birds sang sweetly beneath flowers, smooth and bright,
Then choked sobs like spring water flowing under ice, tight.
Ice-cold springs, stiffened strings, music ceased for a breath,
A new hidden grief arose, silencing death before life.
At this moment, silence surpassed the sound’s own claim,
Then suddenly a silver vase burst, water spurring flame.
Iron cavalry charged forth, blades clashing, spears ringing,
The song ended; with a final stroke, the silk tore, stinging.

East ships and west barges fell silent, under the sky.

Telling her story, revealing her past’s trace.

My home lay near Xiama Ling, amidst wealth and fame’s reign.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s intricate art,
Named first among the Imperial Music Troupe’s smart.
After finishing a tune, skilled masters bowed to my skill,
My makeup finished, even famed beauties felt ill.
Young men of Five Mounds vied to wrap me in brocade heads,
For one song, red silk bolts piled high, unknown counts spread.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time’s beat,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine, wild and fleet.
This year of laughter passed into next year’s delight,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent carelessly in flight.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died away,
As twilight faded into dawn, beauty lost its day.
The gate grew cold, horse hooves rare, visitors few,
Growing old, I married a merchant, true to his cue.
He valued profit more than separation’s pain,
Last month to Fuliang he went, buying tea again.
When he returns, I guard the empty boat at river mouth,
Moonlight circles the ship, cold waters flow south.
Late at night, dreams of youth come crashing back to start,
Crying in sleep, tears ruin makeup, staining the heart."
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply, overcome with grief,
Hearing her words, I added sighs beyond relief.
Both are wanderers fallen to the ends of earth’s expanse,
Meeting now, why should we need prior acquaintance?
Since last year I left the Emperor’s Capital City,
Exiled here to Xunyang, sick, alone, pity.
Xunyang is remote, no music fills the air,
All year long, no strings or flutes can be heard there.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp, wet ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my abode found.
What do I hear morning and evening in this place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing with sad grace.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights’ glow,
Often take out wine, drink alone, feelings slow.
Are there no mountain songs or village flute’s tune?
Hoarse and harsh sounds, painful to listen soon.
Tonight hearing your pipa speak its language pure,
Like celestial music, my ears brighten, cure.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more song,
For you I’ll compose this Ballad of the Pipa, strong.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence profound,
Then sat down, tightened strings, playing faster, bound.
Mournful and desolate, nothing like the former sound,
Everyone present covered faces, tears pouring round.
Who shed most tears among them? Ask if you must know:
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet in woe.

Do not refuse to sit again and play one more song,
For you I’ll compose this Ballad of the Pipa, strong.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence profound,
Then sat down, tightened strings, playing faster, bound.

将下面已选中的完整英文译文作为最终结果，保留原文措辞和诗行，不添加说明：
On the Xunyang River at night, I saw a guest off,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest stayed on his boat;
He raised his cup to drink, yet no strings or pipes.
Too drunk for joy, sad at our parting—
At farewell the river was a blur, soaked in moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go back, the guest delayed his sailing.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The playing stopped, and she hesitated before she spoke.
We drew our boats nearer and invited her to meet;
Wine was poured, lamps relit, and the feast began again.
After countless calls she finally came out,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before a tune was formed, feeling was already there.
String after string, muted and brooding, each note a thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
With downcast brows she played on, unceasingly,
Telling all the countless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping, then flicking—
First the *Rainbow Garment*, then the *Six Yao*.
The great strings thundered like sudden rain,
The small strings whispered like private talk.
Thunder and whisper, mixed and interlarded—
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling, smooth beneath the flowers,
Or a choked spring, hard to pass beneath the ice.
The icy spring froze, the strings congealed and broke;
The break, the silence—sound for a while suspended.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment rose;
At this moment, silence was better than sound.
Then a silver flask cracked open, water bursting forth,
Armored riders charging out, blades and spears ringing.
At the end of the tune she drew the pick across the center—
Four strings together, like tearing silk apart.
Boats to east and west were hushed and mute;
Only the autumn moon, white at the heart of the river.
She pondered, set the pick between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, composed her face.
"I was once a girl of the capital," she said,
"My home stood beneath Hama Hill."
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
And my name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a tune, even the best masters were humbled;
When I made up my face, even Qiu Niang was jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to send me gifts;
For one song, red silk—countless, I cannot say.
Ornamental combs and silver hairpins beat time till they broke,
Blood-red silk skirts stained and spotted with wine.
Year after year of laughter, year after year of mirth;
Autumn moons and spring winds, idly I passed them by.
My younger brother left to join the army, my elder sister died;
Dusk went, dawn came, and my beauty faded.
Before my gate, the stirrups and horses grew sparse;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant thought of profit, not of parting;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone I wait at the river mouth in an empty boat;
Around the boat, the moon shines bright, the river water cold.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream I weep, and tears streak my rouge.
I had sighed already at the sound of the pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, and again.
Both of us, drifters at the ends of the earth—
Why must we have met before to understand?
I left the emperor's capital last year;
Banished, I lie ill here in Xunyang.
This place is remote, with no music;
All year I hear no strings, no flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful cry.
On flower-filled spring days, on moonlit autumn nights,
I often take a cup of wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs, no village pipes?
Their harsh, discordant sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa's speech—
Like celestial music, my ears were cleared.
Do not refuse; sit and play once more—
For you, I'll turn it into a "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood a long while,
Then sat back, tightened the strings—the pace grew swift.
Mournful, unlike the sound before;
The whole audience, hearing it again, wept with hands covering faces.
Who among us wept the most?
The Master of Jiangzhou, his blue robe drenched.

将给定完整作品译成英语诗。待译作品数据：
{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}
只给英文译文正文。
